rules.title: Use of applicant-provided reusable screening reports
rules.requirement: Use a reusable screening report when the tenant provides one.
rules.coverage_conditions: An applicant supplies a report that qualifies as a reusable screening report under the missing governing provision. D005 frames this as a screening-fee right under state law, but does not define qualification or reconcile1950.6(a)/(g).
rules.exemptions: The source does not establish the applicable report-qualification exceptions. A generic applicant-presented credit report is not automatically a qualified reusable report.
rules.quoted_span: If the tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.
rules.conflict_note: Merge review: D005 expressly says a landlord MUST use a tenant-provided reusable screening report. D026 section 1950.6(a) expressly says a landlord MAY, but is NOT REQUIRED to, accept an applicant-presented consumer credit report, and subdivision (g) preserves accepting reusable reports under section 1950.1. Reusable screening reports may be a distinct qualified subset; section 1950.1 is not reproduced. This is an unresolved relationship requiring that missing definition/provision, not an established legal contradiction or authorization to override either claim. Keep both statements and their source boundaries. External status review: the statewide mandatory reusable-screening-report requirement remains unverified against the cited Civil Code. Source scope and section 1950.1 require substantive review before a conclusive applicability result.

conditions.description: The guide conditions mandatory use on the tenant providing the report.

limitations: The guide does not define a reusable screening report, specify qualifying criteria, or reproduce the statutory language.

evidence.quote:
For more information, see
California Civil Code Section 1950.6
.
If the tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.

Screening Fee
The maximum tenant screening fee for 2026 is
$68.96
Landlords may use screening fees to obtain information about a prospective tenant like a consumer credit report. Prospective tenants should expect to receive a copy of their credit report within 7 days of receipt by the landlord, a receipt for the fee paid and an itemized list of any out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord on the screening, and a refund of any unused portion of the fee. If the tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.
The landlord cannot charge a prospective tenant a screening fee if no rental unit is actually available. The landlord must also return a screening fee to any applicant not selected, or have a policy under which they: (1) review applications in the order received and the first qualified applicant gets the unit, and (2) do not charge a screening fee to any applicant not considered.
For more information, see
California Civil Code Section 1950.6

(a) Notwithstanding Section 1950.5, when a landlord or their agent receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant, the landlord or their agent may charge, pursuant to subdivision (c), that applicant an application screening fee to cover the costs of obtaining information about the applicant. The information requested and obtained by the landlord or their agent may include, but is not limited to, personal reference checks and consumer credit reports produced by consumer credit reporting agencies as defined in Section 1785.3. A landlord or their agent may, but is not required to, accept and rely upon a consumer credit report presented by an applicant.
(g) Nothing in this section prevents a landlord from accepting a reusable screening report pursuant to Section 1950.1.

rules.title: Five-year restriction after permanent-removal notice
rules.requirement: After vacancy caused by notice of permanent boarding, demolition or retirement from residential use, the property cannot resume residential use for five years. It also cannot be registered as a planned real estate development during five years after a notice-induced vacancy.

rules.title: Limits on deductions not identified during the initial inspection
rules.requirement: If an initial inspection occurs without tenant possessions preventing identification of repairs or cleaning, the landlord generally may not deduct for repairs or cleaning absent from the inspection statement. Authorized deductions for listed but uncured deficiencies, later-arising conditions, and conditions obscured by tenant possessions are preserved as stated in subdivision (f)(5)-(6).
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security deductions following an initial inspection under subdivision (f), with the itemized statement required by (f)(2). Deductions must remain for purposes permitted by (b)(1)-(4) and comply with the general reasonable-amount and ordinary-wear restrictions.
rules.exemptions: Subdivision (f)(5) preserves itemized uncured deductions only for damage authorized by the section. Paragraph (6) refers to authorized purposes arising in a post-inspection interval whose endpoint wording is unclear in the supplied source, and preserves deductions for matters not identified because of tenant possessions; subdivision (f) does not apply to terminations under Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(2), (3), or (4).
rules.interaction: Inspection-based limits supplement the permissible-purpose and reasonable-amount limits rather than authorizing otherwise impermissible deductions.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The original onset is not specified; the supplied version was amended effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: The supplied wording of (f)(6) has an awkward interval phrase between inspection completion and return of possession. The exact source is preserved and the temporal reading needs review rather than silent correction.

(f) (1) Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before
the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. The purpose of the initial inspection shall be to allow the tenant an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies, in a manner consistent with the rights and obligations of the parties under the rental agreement, in order to avoid deductions from the security. If a tenant chooses not to request an initial inspection, the duties of the landlord under this subdivision are discharged. If an inspection is requested, the parties shall attempt to schedule the inspection at a mutually acceptable date and time. The landlord shall give at least 48 hours’ prior written notice of the date and time of the inspection if either a mutual time is
agreed upon, or if a mutually agreed time cannot be scheduled but the tenant still wishes an inspection. rules.title: Failure to sign a substantially similar renewal lease is not an eviction ground
rules.requirement: A landlord may not evict a tenant for failing to sign a substantially similar lease when a fixed-term lease expires.
rules.coverage_conditions: Expiration of a fixed-term lease for a tenancy subject to Berkeley's Rent Ordinance eviction protections. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.
rules.exemptions: The section addresses fully and partially covered units, not ordinance-exempt units. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord cannot evict a tenant for failing to sign a substantially similar lease upon expiration of a fixed-term lease.
rules.interaction: Eliminates the specified eviction ground within the local just-cause framework.
rules.temporal_notes: Identified as a Measure BB change; no operative date is given.
limitations: No complete renewal or lease-conversion rules are supplied.

rules.title: Civil immunity for renting to persons with records or foregoing screening
rules.requirement: Landlords subject to the Act are immune from civil liability arising from a decision to rent to individuals with criminal records or convictions, or a decision not to perform criminal-background screening.
rules.key_value: Civil immunity for specified rental and screening decisions
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential landlords subject to the Act; immunity is tied to civil actions arising from the specified decisions.
rules.exemptions: Units in owner-occupied premises with no more than four dwelling units are excluded from the Act. Subsection (b) preserves immunity otherwise conferred by law for renting to persons convicted of the listed serious offenses or crimes resulting in lifetime sex-offender registration.

rules.title: Rent increases require lease-end procedure and continued-tenancy offer
rules.requirement: A landlord cannot raise rent during the lease term. To increase rent, terminate the old lease by proper written notice and offer a new lease at the increased rent, explaining that the tenant may continue renting at that rate.
rules.key_value: No mid-lease increase; written termination and increased-rent offer
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rent increases described under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(f); Anti-Eviction Act coverage limitations apply where eviction enforcement is invoked.
rules.exemptions: The guide does not state an exception permitting a mid-term increase.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord cannot raise the 
rent mid-lease term. The old lease must be terminated, and the new lease must have the increased 
rental payment. The landlord has to offer the tenant a new lease with the increased rent once the 
old lease has been terminated.
rules.interaction: Legal increases also must satisfy unconscionability and applicable municipal limits; eviction for refusal has separate notice requirements.
rules.temporal_notes: Triggered by the existing lease's termination, not a fixed calendar date.
limitations: No general advance-notice duration is supplied here beyond the separately described eviction procedure.

A landlord cannot raise the 
rent mid-lease term. The old lease must be terminated, and the new lease must have the increased 
rental payment. The landlord has to offer the tenant a new lease with the increased rent once the 
old lease has been terminated.

Landlord must give the tenant proper written notice, which informs the tenant that the current 
lease is terminated, and the tenant can remain in the premises by signing a new lease at an 
increased rent.

Written notice must also state that  end of the current lease, tenant has the right to continue

regulations, and court cases that concern landlord-tenant relations; however, this publication is not

and will be posted on the Department’s website accordingly.

Although the State of New Jersey does not have any laws that establish, govern, or control 
rents, a landlord can increase rents if they follow certain procedures. A landlord cannot raise the 
rent mid-lease term. The old lease must be terminated, and the new lease must have the increased 
rental payment. The landlord has to offer the tenant a new lease with the increased rent once the 
old lease has been terminated. In order to terminate a lease, the landlord must take the following 
steps (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(f)): 
1. Landlord must give the tenant proper written notice, which informs the tenant that the current 
lease is terminated, and the tenant can remain in the premises by signing a new lease at an 
increased rent. 
2. Written notice must also state that  end of the current lease, tenant has the right to continue 
renting the premises at the increased rent.

Notice requirements for rent increases are contained in the Anti -Eviction Act ( N.J.S.A. 
2A:18-61.1 et seq.). This law provides that before an owner can evict a tenant for nonpayment of 
an increased rent, they must first serve the tenant with a valid notice to quit and notice of rent 
increase. This notice does not mean that the tenant must actually leave; the tenant has the right to 
remain as long as they pay any legal increase in rent. The increase in rent must not be 
unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest 
person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.

Property Tax Rebate for Tenants 
 The Tenants’ Property Tax Rebate Act (N.J.S.A. 54:4-6.2 to – 6.13; N.J.A.C. 5:33-3.1 et 
seq.), as amended in 1998, may require owners of properties with five (5) or more rental units to 
pass on to their tenants as a rent credit or cash rebate, the full amount of any current property tax 
reduction. Reductions are calculated by comparing the current year’s taxes with a previous year 
(beginning with 1998) that shows a larger tax amount. The difference is the amount to be rebated 
to tenants. Municip alities with rent control ordinances that do not permit landlords to pass tax 
increases along to tenants are not subject to the law. The law also contains exceptions for certain 
types of rental properties. See N.J.S.A. 54:4-6.3 for the list of the types of  properties that are 
exempt. 
 In each municipality, where a rebate is due, a notice of property tax reduction ( N.J.S.A. 
54:4-6.7) is sent from the local tax collector to the building owners within 30 days after tax bills 
are issued to the building owner. Generally, rebates are to be distributed in monthly installments 
at rent payment dates, beginning within 30 days after receipt of Notice of Tax Reduction. The first 
rebate is to be cumulative from January and all are to be completed by December 31. However, if 
the notice is received after November 1, the rebate is to be completed by June 30 of the following 
year.  
 Under the law, in  eligible municipalities, a property rebate is due to tenants only when 
property taxes are reduced because of: 1) a municipal wide revaluation of all real estate and only 
in the first year the revaluation takes effect, 2) generally, when the property tax rate in the current 
year is lower than the base year (usually 1998), 3) taxpayers in the municipality receive tax rate 
credit through the Regional Efficiency Aid Program (REAP)  (N.J.S.A. 54:4-8.76 et seq .). The 
entire amount of the REAP credit must be passed through to tenants.

year is lower than the base year (usually 1998), 3) taxpayers in the municipality receive tax rate 
credit through the Regional Efficiency Aid Program (REAP)  (N.J.S.A. 54:4-8.76 et seq .). The 
entire amount of the REAP credit must be passed through to tenants.

rules.title: Five-percent annual general adjustment cap with banking preserved
rules.requirement: The Rent Board's annual general adjustment for fully covered rental units may not exceed 5%, even if the ordinance's CPI-linked formula produces a larger amount. A landlord may implement banked unused AGAs from earlier years to raise rent to the rent ceiling even when the resulting increase exceeds 5%.
rules.key_value: Maximum annual AGA: 5%; banked AGAs may produce an increase above 5%
rules.coverage_conditions: Fully covered rental units; the cap limits the annual AGA approved by the Board. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. This rent-amount regulation requires FULL coverage; partially covered units retain other protections but not this rent cap.
rules.exemptions: The 5% AGA cap is not an absolute cap on a tenant's implemented increase when unused prior AGAs are banked and used to reach the rent ceiling. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.
rules.quoted_span: The maximum AGA is 5%. This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%. This cap does not prevent a landlord who has “banked” (unused) AGAs from previous years from implementing a rent increase that is greater than 5% in order to raise the rent to the rent ceiling.
rules.interaction:
Distinguishes the annual formula cap from accumulated banked adjustments and the unit's rent ceiling.
r-0071 coexists r-0266 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.
rules.temporal_notes: No operative date for the 5% cap is specified.
limitations: The CPI percentage, rounding method, and detailed banking eligibility rules are not supplied in this chunk.

evidence.quote: The AGA is the amount by which the landlord of a fully-covered rental unit may raise the rent each year. The elected Rent Board sets the AGA by following a formula in the Rent Ordinance that ties the AGA to the Consumer Price Index.

The maximum AGA is 5%. This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%. This cap does not prevent a landlord who has “banked” (unused) AGAs from previous years from implementing a rent increase that is greater than 5% in order to raise the rent to the rent ceiling.

(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.

security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

rules.title: Minimum rental debt for nonpayment eviction
rules.requirement: A nonpayment eviction requires rental debt at least equal to one month's HUD Fair Market Rent for a unit of equivalent size in the Oakland-Fremont, CA HUD Metro FMR area, using the fiscal year in which rent is demanded.
rules.key_value: Rental debt ≥ one month of applicable HUD Fair Market Rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Nonpayment evictions under Berkeley's Rent Ordinance for fully or partially covered units. The benchmark depends on equivalent unit size, the specified metropolitan area, and the fiscal year of the rent demand. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.
rules.exemptions: Ordinance-exempt units are outside the coverage stated in this section. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.
rules.quoted_span: For a landlord to evict a tenant for nonpayment of rent, the tenant must owe an amount of rental debt equal to or greater than one month of the Fair Market Rent (FMR) value for a unit of equivalent size in the metro area Oakland-Fremont, CA HUD Metro FMR as determined by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development for the fiscal year in which the rent is demanded.
rules.interaction: This limits the nonpayment just cause; it does not establish rent forgiveness or eliminate other eviction requirements.

evidence.quote:
Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.

Protected Units: (1) Residential dwelling units that are or were subject to a recorded covenant, ordinance, or law that restricts 
rents to levels affordable to persons and families of lower or very low income within the past five years. (2) Residential 
dwelling units that are or were subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police 
power within the past five years.  This includes all RSO units. (3) Residential dwelling units that are or were rented by lower or 
very low income households within the past five years. (4) Residential dwelling units that were withdrawn from rent or lease in 
accordance the Ellis Act within the past 10 years.

Owners who demolish a Protected Unit for the purpose of new construction within 5 years after the 
filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD are required to 
comply with relocation requirements under the RPO.

*Single Family Dwellings that are not lower income may be entitled to one month’s equivalent
of rent for relocation payment depending on various factors. See page 5.

For Option 2, the owner must provide a letter from the LAHD Housing Development Bureau 
approving the comparable replacement unit in compliance with State law at the time of filing with 
LAHD. If the owner does not have the approval letter, then they may choose Option 1 or 3 to 
proceed with the filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or the Declaration of Intent to Evict. 
Additionally, the owner must comply with the RSO or JCO relocation requirements in Chart A.

CHART A: RSO or JCO Amounts  
Effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 (Increases July 1st)

Requirements for Landlords 
To terminate tenancy for the purpose of demolition of a Protected Unit1, a landlord must: 
1. File with LAHD a Declaration of Intent to Evict for units regulated by the JCO per the Los Angeles
Municipal Code (LAMC) Section 165.03.I(1) or file with LAHD a  Notice of Intent to Withdraw Units
From Rental Housing Use for units regulated by the RSO.  Only RSO units are subject to the Ellis
Act provisions (LAMC 151.22-151.28).  All RSO units are Protected Units.
2. Serve tenants with a written notice to move out and file a copy of it with LAHD within 3 business
days online at https://lahd.service-now.com/efs. For more information go to
housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices
3. Pay relocation assistance to tenants in compliance with the State law’s Housing Crisis Act
(California Government Code Section 66300 et seq.) or the City laws, whichever is higher.  City
laws require all tenants be paid relocation assistance in the amounts required by the RSO or JCO
within 15 days of serving a notice to terminate tenancy, which must be enhanced for lower income
tenants if the project is subject to the Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.  The RSO and JCO amounts must also be enhanced for
lower income tenants under the HCA regardless of the RPO applicability.  Parties are encouraged
to seek legal advice to understand the HCA State law if the RPO does not apply to them.
*The regular RSO or JCO relocation rules apply as described in the A. Relocation Assistance
Bulletin: No-Fault Evictions Under the RSO & JCO if the units to be demolished are not Protected
Units or are not occupied by a lower income tenant.

rents to levels affordable to persons and families of lower or very low income within the past five years. (2) Residential 
dwelling units that are or were subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police 
power within the past five years.  This includes all RSO units. (3) Residential dwelling units that are or were rented by lower or 
very low income households within the past five years. (4) Residential dwelling units that were withdrawn from rent or lease in 
accordance the Ellis Act within the past 10 years.

Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) 
The Housing Crisis Act of 2019 (HCA) originally introduced replacement requirements and occupant 
protections through Senate Bill (SB) 330 and has since been updated by SB 8 and Assembly Bill (AB) 1218. 
On February 11, 2025, the Los Angeles City Council adopted the RPO which codified and expanded upon 
replacement requirements and occupant protections of the HCA, and enhanced requirements for 
Restricted Affordable Units.  The RPO only applies to Protected Units that will be demolished for the 
purpose of new construction.  
The RPO’s occupant protections include: 1) Right to Relocation, 2) Right to Remain in the unit up to 6 
months prior to start of construction activities, which includes a 6-month notice to move out, 3) Right 
to Return to the same unit if the demolition does not proceed, 4) Right of First Refusal to the new 
building for some tenants and 5) Tenant Notification Requirements.  For more details, please go the Los 
Angeles City Planning Department’s website https://planning.lacity.gov/ and review the Fact Sheet: 
Replacement Unit Requirements and Occupant Protections.

Relocation Options Under the RPO 
Owners who demolish a Protected Unit for the purpose of new construction within 5 years after the 
filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD are required to 
comply with relocation requirements under the RPO. Failure to comply with the RPO may result in 
financial penalties starting at $250,000 per displaced unit and withholding of LAHD permit clearances.  
Owners have 3 relocation options to comply with the RPO relocation rules. The owner chooses one of 
the options. The owner must pay the highest of the applicable relocation amounts to comply with State 
and City laws.

3. Pay relocation assistance to tenants in compliance with the State law’s Housing Crisis Act
(California Government Code Section 66300 et seq.) or the City laws, whichever is higher.  City
laws require all tenants be paid relocation assistance in the amounts required by the RSO or JCO
within 15 days of serving a notice to terminate tenancy, which must be enhanced for lower income
tenants if the project is subject to the Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.  The RSO and JCO amounts must also be enhanced for
lower income tenants under the HCA regardless of the RPO applicability.  Parties are encouraged
to seek legal advice to understand the HCA State law if the RPO does not apply to them.
*The regular RSO or JCO relocation rules apply as described in the A. Relocation Assistance
Bulletin: No-Fault Evictions Under the RSO & JCO if the units to be demolished are not Protected
Units or are not occupied by a lower income tenant.

Option 2: Comparable Replacement Unit & RSO/JCO Relocation 
For Option 2, the owner must provide a letter from the LAHD Housing Development Bureau 
approving the comparable replacement unit in compliance with State law at the time of filing with 
LAHD. If the owner does not have the approval letter, then they may choose Option 1 or 3 to 
proceed with the filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or the Declaration of Intent to Evict. 
Additionally, the owner must comply with the RSO or JCO relocation requirements in Chart A. 
Option 2 has unpredictable relocation consultant services fees to find a comparable replacement

evidence.quote:
Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) 
The Housing Crisis Act of 2019 (HCA) originally introduced replacement requirements and occupant 
protections through Senate Bill (SB) 330 and has since been updated by SB 8 and Assembly Bill (AB) 1218. 
On February 11, 2025, the Los Angeles City Council adopted the RPO which codified and expanded upon 
replacement requirements and occupant protections of the HCA, and enhanced requirements for 
Restricted Affordable Units.  The RPO only applies to Protected Units that will be demolished for the 
purpose of new construction.  
The RPO’s occupant protections include: 1) Right to Relocation, 2) Right to Remain in the unit up to 6 
months prior to start of construction activities, which includes a 6-month notice to move out, 3) Right 
to Return to the same unit if the demolition does not proceed, 4) Right of First Refusal to the new 
building for some tenants and 5) Tenant Notification Requirements.  For more details, please go the Los 
Angeles City Planning Department’s website https://planning.lacity.gov/ and review the Fact Sheet: 
Replacement Unit Requirements and Occupant Protections.

rules.title: Charging requires one of two alternative screening processes
rules.requirement: At collection, a landlord or agent may charge an application screening fee only if offering either the ordered-consideration process in subdivision (c)(2)(A), meeting all its conditions, or the refund-to-every-unselected-applicant process in (c)(2)(B). These are alternative routes, not cumulative requirements.
rules.key_value: Process (A) OR process (B), offered at fee collection
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential application screening fees charged by owners or their agents to applicants, including guarantors or cosignors. Process (A) requires considering completed applications in receipt order under established criteria, providing criteria in writing with the application, approving the first qualifying applicant, and charging only when an application is considered. Process (B) instead requires returning the entire fee to every unselected applicant regardless of reason, by the earlier of seven days after tenant selection or 30 days after submission. Fee amount and unit availability are independently governed by (b) and (c)(1).
rules.exemptions: Under process (A), inadvertent charges from concurrent submissions do not violate the consideration-before-charge condition if unconsidered applicants receive a refund within seven days; the landlord may offer application of the fee to another unit at the applicant's discretion. Process (A) does not require a refund to an applicant rejected after consideration for failing established criteria, but the unused-fee rule in (e) remains separately relevant. The section does not preempt housing-assistance-program deposit or fee rules.
rules.interaction: The detailed route-specific duties are separately identified for review; route (A)'s criteria and processing requirements must not be asserted as universal tenant-selection duties outside this fee-authorizing route.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The original onset of the two-route scheme is not separately stated; footer identifies the supplied version as amended effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: The seven-day refund wording in (A)(iv) does not expressly name its clock-start event; this draft preserves that uncertainty rather than inventing one.

(2) A landlord or their agent may charge an applicant an application screening fee only if the landlord or their agent, at the time the application screening fee is collected, offers any of the following:
(A) An application screening process that complies with all of the following:
(i) Completed applications are considered, as provided for in the landlord’s established screening criteria, in the order in which the completed applications were received. The landlord’s screening criteria shall be provided to the applicant in writing together with the application form.

charged an application screening fee unless or until their application is actually considered.

The landlord may offer, as an alternative to refunding the screening fee, the option, at the applicant’s discretion, for the screening fee paid by the applicant to be applied to an application for another rental unit offered by the landlord. A landlord or their agent shall not be required to refund an application screening fee to an applicant whose application is denied, after consideration, because the applicant does not meet the landlord’s established screening criteria.
(B) An application screening process in which the landlord or their agent returns the entire screening fee to any applicant who is not selected for tenancy, regardless of the reason, within 7 days of selecting an applicant for tenancy or 30 days of when the application was submitted, whichever occurs first.

In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.
(c) (1) A landlord or their agent shall not charge an applicant an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available at that time or will be available within a reasonable period of time.

rules.coverage_conditions: Termination notices addressed by the Rent Ordinance's eviction-notice provisions. rules.title: No owner retaliation for protected fair-housing activity
rules.requirement: A housing owner must not harass, evict, or otherwise discriminate in rental housing when the dominant purpose is retaliation for the protected opposition, reporting, participation, or assistance described in subdivision (f). The provision is not intended to cause or permit delay of an unlawful-detainer action.
rules.key_value: Dominant retaliatory purpose
rules.coverage_conditions: Owners of rental housing acting against a person who opposed practices unlawful under this section; informed law enforcement about practices believed unlawful under this section; testified or assisted in a proceeding under this part; or aided or encouraged another person to exercise or enjoy rights secured by this part. The supplied clause also covers sale-related retaliation, not separately extracted here.
rules.exemptions: Subdivision (f) expressly preserves the no-delay qualification for unlawful-detainer actions; it is not a general stay or a requirement that every eviction have an enumerated just cause.
rules.interaction: This is a prohibition on retaliation including eviction, not a general list of permissible eviction grounds.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset unknown from the supplied text; version amended effective 2024-01-01.
limitations: The referenced rights and proceedings under this part may extend beyond the provisions reproduced in D027.

Nothing herein is intended to cause or permit the delay of an unlawful detainer action.

(f) For any owner of housing accommodations to harass, evict, or otherwise discriminate against any person in the sale or rental of housing accommodations when the owner’s dominant purpose is retaliation against a person who has opposed practices unlawful under this section, informed law enforcement agencies of practices believed unlawful under this section, has testified or assisted in any proceeding under this part, or has aided or encouraged a person to exercise or enjoy the rights secured by this part. Nothing herein is intended to cause or permit the delay of an unlawful detainer action.
(Amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 776, Sec. 1.   (SB 267)   Effective January 1, 2024.)

It shall be unlawful:
(a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
(b) For the owner of any housing accommodation to make or to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry concerning the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of any person
seeking to purchase, rent, or lease any housing accommodation.
(c) For any person to make, print, or publish, or cause to be made, printed, or published any notice, statement, or advertisement, with respect to the sale or rental of a housing accommodation that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information or an intention to make that preference, limitation, or discrimination.
(d) For any person subject to the provisions of Section 51 of the Civil Code, as that section applies to housing accommodations, to discriminate against any person on the basis of sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, color, race,
religion, ancestry, national origin, familial status, marital status, disability, genetic information, source of income, veteran or military status, or on any other basis prohibited by that section. Selection preferences based on age, imposed in connection with a federally approved housing program, do not constitute age discrimination in housing.

(f) For any owner of housing accommodations to harass, evict, or otherwise discriminate against any person in the sale or rental of housing accommodations when the owner’s dominant purpose is retaliation against a person who has opposed practices unlawful under this section, informed law enforcement agencies of practices believed unlawful under this section, has testified or assisted in any proceeding under this part, or has aided or encouraged a person to exercise or enjoy the rights secured by this part. Nothing herein is intended to cause or permit the delay of an unlawful detainer action.

Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) 
The Housing Crisis Act of 2019 (HCA) originally introduced replacement requirements and occupant 
protections through Senate Bill (SB) 330 and has since been updated by SB 8 and Assembly Bill (AB) 1218. 
On February 11, 2025, the Los Angeles City Council adopted the RPO which codified and expanded upon 
replacement requirements and occupant protections of the HCA, and enhanced requirements for 
Restricted Affordable Units.  The RPO only applies to Protected Units that will be demolished for the 
purpose of new construction.  
The RPO’s occupant protections include: 1) Right to Relocation, 2) Right to Remain in the unit up to 6 
months prior to start of construction activities, which includes a 6-month notice to move out, 3) Right 
to Return to the same unit if the demolition does not proceed, 4) Right of First Refusal to the new 
building for some tenants and 5) Tenant Notification Requirements.  For more details, please go the Los 
Angeles City Planning Department’s website https://planning.lacity.gov/ and review the Fact Sheet: 
Replacement Unit Requirements and Occupant Protections.

Relocation Options Under the RPO 
Owners who demolish a Protected Unit for the purpose of new construction within 5 years after the 
filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD are required to 
comply with relocation requirements under the RPO. Failure to comply with the RPO may result in 
financial penalties starting at $250,000 per displaced unit and withholding of LAHD permit clearances.  
Owners have 3 relocation options to comply with the RPO relocation rules. The owner chooses one of 
the options. The owner must pay the highest of the applicable relocation amounts to comply with State 
and City laws.

rules.title: Disclosure before a buyout offer and tenant refusal rights
rules.requirement: Before any buyout offer, the landlord must give each tenant written disclosure of the right to refuse an agreement, consult an attorney, and be free from retaliation for refusing or declining negotiations; the ability of all tenants of the property to stop future offers for six months by written notice and rescind that refusal in writing; relocation eligibility and the required amount under §98.0706(c); and all persons authorized to discuss and enter the buyout for the landlord. The form must provide tenant and landlord signature/date spaces. These regulate voluntary displacement negotiations rather than supplying an eviction ground.
rules.key_value: Disclosure before any offer; collective written refusal effective for 6 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. The separately defined Tenant and this rule's trigger govern the initial scope inquiry. Applicability of the narrower Tenancy duration/fixed-term definition to this independent Tenant right is unresolved in the supplied text; do not use it as an automatic exclusion. Rule-specific applicability: Before making any buyout offer, landlord gives each tenant written disclosure. All tenants can jointly refuse future offers by written notice effective 6 months; written rescission restores willingness. Tenant counteroffer does not end bargaining. Additional event and branch tests: Landlord pays money or other consideration for tenant to vacate; offer includes oral/written discussion or bargaining and tenant counteroffer does not end it. An agreement settling a PENDING unlawful-detainer action is excluded from the buyout-agreement definition. Before making any buyout offer, landlord gives each tenant written disclosure.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles. The Section 98.0702 Tenancy duration/fixed-term definition is not established here as an additional blanket Division-wide exemption from this independent Tenant right.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

A San Diego tenant filed Keller v. UDR Inc. in the Southern District of California under San Diego Municipal Code § 98.1103, alleging that UDR improperly used RealPage products. San Diego similarly authorizes tenant suits for damages, injunctive relief and penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, with each month and affected rental property potentially constituting a separate violation. San Diego Mun. Code §§ 98.1103(b) & 98.1104(a).
Seattle has now generated at least two similar cases. In Nicolas v. Essex Management Corp., plaintiffs allege that Essex Management, Essex Property Trust, RealPage, and Yardi violated Seattle Municipal Code Chapter 7.34 by using prohibited “coordinating services” in connection with Seattle multifamily properties. And, in Romano v. UDR Inc., plaintiffs assert a similar theory against UDR and RealPage. Seattle’s ordinance expressly prohibits specified algorithmic coordinating services and provides penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. Seattle Mun. Code ch. 7.34.040.
In Liu v. Willow Bridge Property Company LLC and RealPage Inc., a class of Philadelphia tenants allege that Willow Bridge subscribed to and used RealPage services in violation of Philadelphia Code § 9-813. And, in Jahanbakhsh v. Greystar., a different Philadelphia tenant class alleges similar claims against Greystar. Philadelphia’s ordinance permits an aggrieved person to elect statutory damages of $2,000 per violation or treble actual damages, together with equitable relief, interest and attorney fees and costs. Phila. Code § 9-813(2)(c)(i).
In a public enforcement action, the City of Providence filed claims against Audubon Capital Partners, LLC in Providence Municipal Court under Providence Code § 13-70, alleging that Audubon used a dynamic pricing system to coordinate rental prices at 95 Lofts in violation of the city’s ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices. The ordinance authorizes the city solicitor to bring enforcement actions and provides for civil penalties of up to $500 per day per violation, as well as costs and attorney fees in a successful enforcement action. Providence Code §§ 13-71 & 13-72.
LOCAL REGULATION IS QUICKLY EXPANDING
Municipal regulation relating to the use of algorithmic pricing tools to set rental prices in multifamily housing has developed quickly, but not uniformly. Some regulations supplement existing antitrust law, while others create landlord-specific prohibitions and direct tenant remedies. Definitions of prohibited data and services also differ, as do the availability of private actions, statutory damages, and fee shifting.

rules.title: Separate disclosure of gross monthly rent and concessions
rules.requirement: The lease, rental agreement, or amendment must separately list and identify the gross per-month rental rate and any owner-offered discounts, incentives, concessions, or credits.
rules.key_value: Separate identification of monthly gross rent and owner-offered concessions
rules.coverage_conditions: Agreements for property subject to section 1947.12(a). The requirement is part of the gross-rent calculation framework, rather than a separate rent percentage.
rules.exemptions: Section-wide exclusions apply: qualifying recorded/subsidized affordable housing; institutional dormitories; valid stricter public rent/price controls consistent with Chapter 2.7; certificates of occupancy within 15 years except mobilehomes; qualifying continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures without ADU/JADU units and with owner occupancy at tenancy inception; mobilehome homeowners; and separately alienable property meeting both owner-type restrictions and prescribed exemption-notice conditions. Subdivision (b) excepts initial rent establishment for a new tenancy with no prior tenant remaining from subdivision (a).
rules.quoted_span:
The gross per-month rental rate and any owner-offered discounts, incentives, concessions, or credits shall be separately listed and identified in the lease or rental agreement or any
amendments to an existing lease or rental agreement.
rules.interaction: Supports the gross-rent baseline used by the maximum-increase formula.
rules.temporal_notes: Current section operative April 1, 2024 and repealed January 1, 2030.
limitations: The passage does not specify a separate fixed penalty for deficient itemization.

The gross per-month rental rate and any owner-offered discounts, incentives, concessions, or credits shall be separately listed and identified in the lease or rental agreement or any
amendments to an existing lease or rental agreement.
(2) If the same tenant remains in occupancy of a unit of residential real property over any 12-month period, the gross rental rate for the unit of residential real property shall not be increased in more than two increments over that 12-month period, subject to the other restrictions of this subdivision governing gross rental rate increase.
(b) For a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession of the residential real property, the owner may establish the initial rental rate not subject to subdivision (a). Subdivision (a) is only applicable to subsequent increases after that initial rental rate has been established.

rules.title: Tenant remedies and prevailing-party attorney-fee protection
rules.requirement: A tenant may bring a civil action against a landlord for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; a prevailing landlord or tenant shall recover costs and reasonable attorney fees, and a tenant granted injunctive relief counts as prevailing. Lease terms limiting either party's attorney-fee recovery for Division 11 claims are unenforceable; remedies are cumulative, and the City may enforce under Chapter 1, Article 2.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation; costs and reasonable attorney fees for a prevailing landlord OR tenant
rules.coverage_conditions: A covered software or product calculates nonpublic competitor data of TWO OR MORE landlords to advise or recommend rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property in San Diego. Nonpublic data includes attributable, anonymized, derived or other-person data about rent, changes, supply, occupancy, or lease dates. Incorporated landlord, residential-rental-property, lease and tenant definitions come from section 98.0702; do not import section 98.0703 eviction exemptions into Division 11. Rule-specific trigger: Tenant sues landlord for a violation of Division 11; prevailing-party fee recovery depends on the action outcome.
rules.exemptions: Exclude reporting software using aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old OR information available to the public, ONLY IF it does not recommend rates or occupancy for future leases or renewals. Also exclude products establishing rents or income limits under local, state or federal affordable-housing guidelines. Separately exclude appraisal software or products that do not recommend rental rates during runtime operation.
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code §98.1104, added by Ordinance O-21955
rules.quoted_span:
(a) A tenant may seek injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation of this Division, in a civil action against a landlord. In an action brought under this Division, a prevailing landlord or tenant shall recover costs and reasonable attorney’s fees. A prevailing tenant includes a tenant granted an order for injunctive relief. A lease provision that limits a landlord or tenant from recovering attorney’s fees shall not be enforceable against a landlord’s or tenant’s claim for attorney’s fees that arise under this Division.
(b) The remedies under section 98.1104 are cumulative and are in addition to any other remedies in this Division or at law, statute, or ordinance.
(c) The City may enforce this Division under Chapter 1, Article 2 of this Code, including civil and criminal remedies.

§98.1104  Remedies
( a ) A tenant may seek injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to
$1,000 per violation of this Division, in a civil action against a landlord.
In an action brought under this Division, a prevailing tenant shall recover
costs and reasonable attorney’s fees. A prevailing tenant includes a tenant
granted an order for injunctive relief. A lease provision that limits a tenant
from recovering attorney’s fees shall not be enforceable against a tenant’s
claim for attorney’s fees that arise under this Division.
(b) The remedies under section 98.1104 are cumulative and are in addition to
any other remedies in this Division or at law, statute, or ordinance.

rules.title: Screening standards and disclosure for a returning displaced tenant
rules.requirement: When making the new-tenancy offer required by §98.0706(d), a landlord may screen the displaced tenant using industry-accepted methods and must communicate minimum screening criteria in the written offer.
rules.key_value: Industry-accepted methods; minimum criteria disclosed in the written offer
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: Landlord makes the new-tenancy offer required by §98.0706(d) to a qualifying displaced tenant; minimum screening criteria must be communicated in the written offer. If the landlord screens the tenant, the permitted methods are industry-accepted methods. Additional event and branch tests: Property offered again for residential rent/lease within 5 years after eviction under 98.0704(b)(1),(3), OR(4) AND displaced tenant requested offer in writing within 30 days of termination notice AND supplied mailing/email address including changes. Market-withdrawal(b)(2) is not listed. Tenant has 30 days after offer receipt to accept; landlord may screen with industry-accepted methods and must state minimum criteria in written offer. Landlord makes the new-tenancy offer required by §98.0706(d) to a qualifying displaced tenant; minimum screening criteria must be communicated in the written offer. If the landlord screens the tenant, the permitted methods are industry-accepted methods.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. §98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

evidence.quote:
(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:

(A) (i) Subject to subparagraph (C), and except as provided by clause (ii), the landlord shall return the remainder of the security by personal delivery or by a check made payable to the tenant and mailed by first-class mail, postage prepaid.
(ii) (I) If the landlord received the security or rental payments from the tenant electronically, the landlord shall return the remainder of the security electronically to a bank account or other financial
institution designated by the tenant in writing, or by any electronic or virtual method available to the landlord if agreed to in writing by the tenant. Alternatively, the landlord and tenant may, by written agreement, designate another method of return, including, but not limited to, by personal delivery or by a check made payable to the tenant and mailed by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to an address provided by the tenant. Upon the termination of a landlord’s interest in the premises and the transfer of the security to the landlord’s successor in interest as provided in subdivision (i), the landlord’s successor in interest shall return the remainder of the security electronically to a bank account or other financial institution designated by the tenant in writing or by any electronic or virtual method available to the landlord’s successor
in interest if agreed to in writing by the tenant only if the landlord’s successor in interest received rental payments electronically from the tenant.
(II) Pursuant to subclause (I), if the landlord received the security or rental payments from the tenant electronically or the landlord’s successor in interest received rental payments from the tenant electronically, the landlord or the landlord’s successor in interest shall, within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s right to receive the security electronically to a bank account or other financial institution designated by the
tenant, or by any electronic or virtual method available to the landlord or the landlord’s successor in interest, if agreed to in writing by the tenant, pursuant to subclause (I). The requirements of this subclause do not apply when the landlord or the landlord’s successor in interest and tenant have previously entered into a written agreement designating another method of return of the security pursuant to subclause (I) or when the tenancy is terminated pursuant to subdivision (2), (3), or (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
(B) (i) Subject to subparagraph (C), and except as provided by clause (ii), the landlord shall
furnish the itemized statement by personal delivery or first-class mail, postage prepaid.
(ii) Upon mutual agreement between the landlord and tenant entered into at the commencement of the tenancy or at any time during or after the tenancy, the itemized statement may be furnished by either of the following:
(I) Emailed to an account provided by the tenant.
(II) Mailed to an address provided by the tenant by first-class mail, postage prepaid.
(C) (i) Except as provided in clause (iii) and unless the landlord and all adult tenants residing in the unit enter into a written mutual agreement pursuant to clause (ii), if multiple adult tenants reside
in the unit, the landlord shall return the remainder of the security by a check made payable to all adult tenants on the rental or lease agreement at the time the tenancy terminates and furnish the itemized statement by personal delivery or first-class mail, postage prepaid, to any one of the adult tenants chosen by the landlord.
(ii) If multiple adult tenants reside in the unit, the landlord may
enter into a mutual written agreement between the landlord and all adult tenants, at the commencement of the tenancy or at any time during or after the tenancy, that specifies both of the following:
(I) How any remaining portion of the security will be returned, including whether it will be returned to a specific adult tenant or divided among multiple tenants, with the allocation percentages. If any remaining portion of the security is to be returned to multiple adult tenants, the landlord may return the security by either a check by first-class mail, postage prepaid, or an electronic deposit to a bank account or other financial institution designated by each adult tenant, as specified in the written agreement.
(II) For each adult tenant, whether the landlord will
furnish the itemized statement by email or first-class mail, postage prepaid, along with a forwarding address or email account.
(iii) If multiple adult tenants reside in a unit and a tenant terminates the lease pursuant to Section 1946.7 and no written mutual agreement was entered into by the landlord and all adult tenants pursuant to clause (ii), and the tenant who terminated the lease pursuant to Section 1946.7 requests that the security be disbursed in a manner other than by check made payable to all adult tenants, the landlord may return the security in a manner other than by check made payable to all adult tenants.
(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340, Sec. 1.   (AB 414)   Effective January 1, 2026.)

(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.
(b) Any lessor or his agent who receives a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give said tenant or prospective tenant at the time of receiving such security deposit a receipt indicating the amount of such security deposit, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom such security deposit is received, the date on which it is received, and a description of the premises leased or rented.  Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit.

rules.title: Reasonable disability modifications and allocation of costs
rules.requirement: For housing covered by subsections 6 and 7, refusing to permit or make a reasonable modification necessary for a handicapped person's full enjoyment of existing premises is discrimination. The handicapped person generally pays. The owner or other person with ownership rights pays for publicly assisted housing, multiple-dwelling housing of ten or more units, or contiguously located housing of ten or more units, subject to the stated limits. Examples include accessible numbers, flashing doorbells, lowered cabinets, ramps for front entrances of five or fewer vertical steps, widened doorways, and grab bars.
rules.key_value: Owner-payment trigger: publicly assisted housing OR qualifying multiple-dwelling or contiguously located housing with at least 10 units; maximum 10% of units for owner-paid modifications making units fully wheelchair accessible
rules.coverage_conditions: Existing premises occupied or to be occupied by a handicapped person, under subsections 6 and 7 and their applicable coverage restrictions. The ten-unit thresholds concern the specified housing configurations, not a stated aggregate threshold across the owner's whole portfolio.
rules.exemptions: Publicly owned housing modification costs are subject to appropriation. For a tenant-paid modification materially altering marketability, a landlord may require agreement to restore or pay to restore the interior to its prior condition, excluding reasonable wear and tear. An owner need not pay for ramping a front entrance with more than five steps or installing a wheelchair lift. Owner-paid modifications imposing undue hardship are not required. Required owner-paid modifications making units fully wheelchair accessible are limited to 10% of units; the text does not specify the denominator's property-versus-portfolio scope. The subsection 7 owner-occupied two-family exemption remains relevant to housing covered through subsection 7.
rules.quoted_span: (1) a refusal to permit or to make, at the expense of the handicapped person, reasonable modification of existing premises occupied or to be occupied by such person if such modification is necessary to afford such person full enjoyment of such premises;
rules.interaction:
Defines handicap discrimination for subsections 6 and 7. Overall housing-business size is an undue-hardship factor, distinct from the ten-unit owner-payment triggers.

7A. For purposes of subsections 6 and 7 discrimination on the basis of handicap shall include but not be limited to:

(1) a refusal to permit or to make, at the expense of the handicapped person, reasonable modification of existing premises occupied or to be occupied by such person if such modification is necessary to afford such person full enjoyment of such premises;

provided, however, that, in the case of publicly assisted housing, multiple dwelling housing consisting of ten or more units, or contiguously located housing consisting of ten or more units, reasonable modification shall be at the expense of the owner or other person having the right of ownership;

provided, further, that, in the case of public ownership of such housing units the cost of such reasonable modification shall be subject to appropriation; and provided, further, that, in the case of a rental, the landlord may, where the modification to be paid for by the handicapped person will materially alter the marketability of the housing, condition permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore or pay for the cost of restoring, the interior of the premises to the condition that existed prior to such modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted;

Reasonable modification shall include, but not be limited to, making the housing accessible to mobility-impaired, hearing-impaired and sight-impaired persons including installing raised numbers which may be read by a sight-impaired person, installing a door bell which flashes a light for a hearing-impaired person, lowering a cabinet, ramping a front entrance of five or fewer vertical steps, widening a doorway, and installing a grab bar;

provided, however, that for purposes of this subsection, the owner or other person having the right of ownership shall not be required to pay for ramping a front entrance of more than five steps or for installing a wheelchair lift.

Notwithstanding any other provisions of this subsection, an accommodation or modification which is paid for by the owner or other person having the right of ownership is not considered to be reasonable if it would impose an undue hardship upon the owner or other person having the right of ownership and shall therefore not be required. Factors to be considered shall include, but not be limited to, the nature and cost of the accommodation or modification needed, the extent to which the accommodation or modification would materially alter the marketability of the housing, the overall size of the housing business of the owner or other person having the right of ownership, including but not limited to, the number and type of housing units, size of budget and available assets, and the ability of the owner or other person having the right of ownership to recover the cost of the accommodation or modification through a federal tax deduction.

Ten percent shall be the maximum number of units for which an owner or other person having the right of ownership shall be required to pay for a modification in order to make units fully accessible to persons using a wheelchair pursuant to the requirements of this subsection.

New law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
October 16, 2024
Legislation
adding Section 37.10C to the Rent Ordinance went into effect on October 14, 2024. The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
The term “algorithmic device” means a device such as a software program that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data for the purposes of providing a landlord recommendations on what rent to charge for a vacant unit. The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.
