Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) 
The Housing Crisis Act of 2019 (HCA) originally introduced replacement requirements and occupant 
protections through Senate Bill (SB) 330 and has since been updated by SB 8 and Assembly Bill (AB) 1218. 
On February 11, 2025, the Los Angeles City Council adopted the RPO which codified and expanded upon 
replacement requirements and occupant protections of the HCA, and enhanced requirements for 
Restricted Affordable Units.  The RPO only applies to Protected Units that will be demolished for the 
purpose of new construction.  
The RPO’s occupant protections include: 1) Right to Relocation, 2) Right to Remain in the unit up to 6 
months prior to start of construction activities, which includes a 6-month notice to move out, 3) Right 
to Return to the same unit if the demolition does not proceed, 4) Right of First Refusal to the new 
building for some tenants and 5) Tenant Notification Requirements.  For more details, please go the Los 
Angeles City Planning Department’s website https://planning.lacity.gov/ and review the Fact Sheet: 
Replacement Unit Requirements and Occupant Protections.

rules.title: Coercing adoption of common-pricing-algorithm recommendations
rules.requirement: A person may not use or distribute a common pricing algorithm while coercing another person to set or adopt its recommended price or commercial term for the same or similar products or services within California.
rules.key_value: Coercion to adopt an algorithm-recommended price or commercial term
rules.coverage_conditions: The algorithm must be a methodology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to influence a price or commercial term. The coercion must concern the same or similar products or services in California. Distribution includes selling, licensing, access, subscriptions, and other means of making the algorithm available. Commercial terms include service level, availability, and output; price includes money or other tangible or intangible value for a product or service. Rental pricing falls within this record only if these general statutory conditions are met.
rules.exemptions: End consumers are excluded from the definition of person. The balance of that definition is incorporated from Section 16702 and is not supplied.
rules.citation: Business and Professions Code § 16729(b), (c), (d), added by AB 325, Chapter 338

rules.interaction: The prohibition coexists with other antitrust provisions; Section 16729 expressly preserves their applicability. Subsection (b) states a coercion trigger separately from subsection (a)'s unlawful-restraint trigger.

conditions.description: At least two persons must use the methodology.

rules.title: Tenant civil enforcement, possession defense, and cumulative remedies
rules.requirement: A tenant claiming a Division violation may sue the landlord in a court of competent jurisdiction and seek injunctive relief, equitable relief, and money damages including punitive damages. A tenant may assert any Division violation or noncompliance as an affirmative defense to a landlord's possession action. Remedies are cumulative with other remedies under the Division or law. The City may enforce through the Code's civil and criminal remedies. These are enforcement and procedural rights.
rules.key_value: Civil action; affirmative defense; cumulative relief
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. The separately defined Tenant and this rule's trigger govern the initial scope inquiry. Applicability of the narrower Tenancy duration/fixed-term definition to this independent Tenant right is unresolved in the supplied text; do not use it as an automatic exclusion. Rule-specific applicability: Tenant claims applicable Division violation in civil action OR raises noncompliance as defense to landlord possession action. Tenant remedies cumulative; City enforcement is separate public authority. Additional event and branch tests: Tenant claims applicable Division violation in civil action OR raises noncompliance as defense to landlord possession action. Remedies cumulative with other law; City may enforce through Code Chapter 1 Article 2.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. §98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

rules.title: No-fault termination notice, relocation disclosures, and return-right instructions
rules.requirement: A landlord issuing a covered no-fault termination must give written notice at least 30 or 60 days before the proposed termination date as required by Civil Code §1946.1, in at least 12-point font. The notice must describe the termination basis and the right to relocation assistance by direct payment or rent waiver. A direct-payment election requires disclosure of the amount and payment within 15 days of the notice; a waiver election requires disclosure of the waived amount and that no rent is due for the corresponding final months. For the return right associated with owner occupancy, government/order vacancy, or demolition/remodel, the notice must explain the five-year re-rental condition, 30-day acceptance period, and tenant's need to opt in in writing within 30 days of the termination notice, provide a mailing or email address, and update it. These are procedural obligations, not independent just-cause grounds.
rules.key_value: 30 or 60 days' notice; 12-point font; direct payment within 15 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: Landlord issues no-fault termination notice; 30 OR 60-day lead time determined by Civil Code 1946.1, minimum 12-point font. Payment election changes disclosure: direct amount/payment within 15 days OR rent-waiver amount/final months. Return-right instructions refer to(b)(1),(3),(4), not withdrawal. Reporting is separately portal-activated. Additional event and branch tests: Landlord issues no-fault termination notice; 30 OR 60-day lead time determined by Civil Code 1946.1, minimum 12-point font. Return-right notice must explain 5 year re-rental, 30 day opt-in, contact/updates and 30 day acceptance for listed grounds. No-fault Commission reporting activates 30 days after portal establishment and public announcement.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles.

for the condition or conditions triggering the order or need to vacate 
under section 98.0704(b)(3), the tenant shall not be entitled to any

The landlord shall give written notice to the tenant 
at least 30 or 60 days prior to the proposed date of termination as 
required by California Civil Code section 1946.1, as may be amended, 
in no less than 12-point font.

(A) The landlord shall provide a description of the basis for the 
termination. 
(B) The notice shall state the tenant’s right to relocation assistance 
established in section 98.0706(c) by a direct payment to the 
tenant or rent waiver.

(i) If the landlord elects to provide relocation assistance by 
a direct payment to the tenant, the notice shall state the 
amount of relocation assistance available to the tenant 
and that the landlord shall provide the payment within 
15 days from the date of the notice.  
(ii) If the landlord elects to provide relocation assistance by 
rent waiver, the notice shall state the amount of rent 
waived and that no rent is due for the final 
corresponding months of the tenancy.

(C) The notice shall state the tenant’s right to receive an offer to 
renew the tenancy established in section 98.0706(d) and 
30 days to accept the offer in the event the residential rental 
property is offered again for rent or lease for residential 
purposes within five years of the date the tenant was evicted 
under sections 98.0704(b)(1), (3), or (4), and that to exercise 
such right, the tenant:   
(i) shall notify the landlord in writing within 30 days of 
the termination notice of tenant’s desire to receive an 
offer to renew the tenancy;

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0703 Exemptions 
This Division shall not apply to the following types of residential rental properties or 
residential circumstances: 
(a) transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in California Civil Code 
section 1940(b), as may be amended; 
(b) short-term residential occupancy, as defined in and subject to Chapter 5, 
Article 10, Division 1 of this Code, as may be amended;  
 
(c) housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement 
with a government agency, or other document as affordable housing for 
persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be amended;  
(d)  housing subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable 
housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as 
defined in California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be 
amended, or comparable federal statutes. This exemption shall not include 
Section 8;

(3-2024)

Code sections 798-799.11), as may be amended;  
 
(f) housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended 
care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 1569.2, as may be amended, an 
adult residential facility, as defined in Title 22, Division 6, Chapter 6 of the 
Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the California Department of 
Social Services, as may be amended, or non- profit transitional housing; 
(g) dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or an 
institution offering instruction to any grade from kindergarten through 12;

Non-profit transitional housing means temporary housing operated by a non-profit 
organization for up to 24 months with supportive services to individuals and families 
with the goal of interim stability and support to successfully move to and maintain 
permanent housing, which may cover housing costs and accompanying supportive 
services for program participants.

rules.title: Itemized receipt for screening fees
rules.requirement: The landlord or agent must personally deliver or mail a receipt itemizing the out-of-pocket expenses and time spent obtaining and processing applicant information for the fee paid. The parties may agree to email a copy to an account provided by the applicant.
rules.key_value: Receipt itemizing expenses and processing time
rules.coverage_conditions: An application screening fee paid by a residential rental applicant, including a guarantor or cosignor, to the residential owner or agent as defined by the section.
rules.exemptions: Email delivery is available by agreement; this section does not preempt federal or state housing-assistance-program deposit and fee provisions.
rules.interaction: The receipt duty is not limited to only one of the alternative screening processes.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The source provides no original onset; supplied version amended effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: Subdivision (d) does not state a numerical receipt-delivery deadline.
rules.quoted_span: (d) The landlord or their agent shall provide, personally, or by mail, the applicant with a receipt for the fee paid by the applicant, which receipt shall itemize the out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord or their agent to obtain and process the information about the applicant. The landlord or their agent and the applicant may agree to have the landlord provide a copy of the receipt for the fee paid by the applicant to an email account provided by the applicant.

rules.title: Assault or terrorist-threat conviction ground
rules.requirement: A conviction, guilty plea or juvenile adjudication involving assault or terrorist threats against the landlord, the landlord's family or employee may support eviction. Knowingly allowing a person convicted of or pleading guilty to those offenses to reside continuously or occasionally may also qualify. Give at least three days' Notice to Quit and file within two years of adjudication, conviction or release, whichever is later.
rules.key_value: 3-day Notice to Quit; 2-year filing limit
rules.coverage_conditions: Covered tenancy and the stated offenses or knowingly permitted occupants.
rules.exemptions: The guide says the Act may not apply to owner-occupied two- or three-unit premises with no more than two rental units. Transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house occupants are excluded. However, hotel or motel occupants who reside continually and have no alternate residence remain covered under the guide. A unit held in trust for an immediate family member who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies it is excluded.

(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.
(b) Any lessor or his agent who receives a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give said tenant or prospective tenant at the time of receiving such security deposit a receipt indicating the amount of such security deposit, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom such security deposit is received, the date on which it is received, and a description of the premises leased or rented.  Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit.

rules.title: Delayed public payments require a hearing continuance and conditional preservation of the tenancy
rules.requirement: If nonpayment resulted from failure or delay in mailing or delivering a qualifying public subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the possession hearing for at least seven days to give notice to the appropriate agency. If all rent due, interest, and suit costs are tendered to the landlord within that time, the court must treat the tenancy as not terminated.
rules.key_value: Hearing continuance of at least 7 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Rent due under a written lease; delay or failure by the federal government, the commonwealth, a municipality, or their departments, agencies, or authorities in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, check, or voucher to either tenant or landlord, causing the nonpayment.
rules.exemptions: Salary payments are excluded; preserving the tenancy requires tender of all rent due with interest and suit costs within the continuance.
rules.interaction: Provides an additional payment-delay protection in a possession action; the continuance and conditional nontermination are separate consequences of the same qualifying circumstances.

limitations: The organizer eviction category is used for termination and possession procedures; this provision does not itself establish a general just-cause requirement.

rules.title: Accelerated deposit return after displacement
rules.requirement: Return the deposit within five business days after qualifying fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation displacement. Within three business days after notice of displacement, tell the tenant where to collect it. The municipal clerk may hold it. After 30 days uncollected, it may be redeposited with the former institution. If the tenant returns after collecting it, repayment is due in thirds immediately, after 30 days and after 60 days.
rules.key_value: 5 business days return; 3 business days collection notice; thirds at 0/30/60 days
rules.coverage_conditions: An authorized official has posted a notice prohibiting occupancy OR certified expected displacement longer than seven days; Security Deposit Law coverage applies.
rules.exemptions: Displacement alone without either stated official action does not establish this accelerated trigger. Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings unless the tenant opts in as described.
rules.quoted_span:
Within five (5) business days after a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or 
evacuation, the landlord must return the security deposit. The law requires the return when either 
an authorized public official has posted a notice prohibiting occupancy or has certified that the 
displacement is expected to continue longer than seven (7) days.
rules.interaction:
Special deadline instead of the ordinary post-termination return period.
r-0156 coexists r-0295 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.

evidence.quote:
Within five (5) business days after a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or 
evacuation, the landlord must return the security deposit. The law requires the return when either 
an authorized public official has posted a notice prohibiting occupancy or has certified that the 
displacement is expected to continue longer than seven (7) days.

Within three (3) business days of 
having received notice of the displacement, the landlord must let the tenant know where the 
security deposit can be collected.

The landlord may arrange to have the municipal clerk hold the 
security deposit so that the tenant may collect it at the clerk’s office. If the tenant has not collected 
the deposit within 30 days, the landlord can redeposit it with the banking institution or investment 
company with which it was deposited before the displacement.

If the tenant is later  able to move 
back into the dwelling unit but has already collected the deposit, the tenant must again pay the 
landlord a security deposit (one -third will be due immediately, another one -third in 30 days, and 
the last one-third in 60 days)

The Security Deposit Law applies to most  residential rental properties, including mobile 
homes. The exception is an owner-occupied two-, or three-family dwelling. A tenant in an owner-
occupied two-, or three-family dwelling may, however, make this provision applicable to their 
tenancy 30 days  after sending a  written  request  to the landlord  that  the landlord  fulfill  the 
requirements of the Security Deposit Law. In New Jersey, the landlord is not required to collect a 
security deposit from  the tenant,  however, if they do, they must  follow prescribed rules and 
regulations (N.J.S.A. 46:8-26).

rules.title: Limits on criminal records considered for eviction
rules.requirement: Covered developers or agents agree not to consider non-conviction arrests, convictions subject to judicial relief, juvenile records, or convictions more than five years old when considering eviction, subject to the policy's criminal-history exceptions. This restricts eviction decision criteria; it does not establish a comprehensive just-cause eviction requirement.

rules.coverage_conditions: Providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; the policy also applies to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.

rules.title: Written notice of initial-inspection and attendance rights
rules.requirement: Within a reasonable time after notification of either party's intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the lease term ends, the landlord must notify the tenant in writing of the option to request an initial inspection and the right to be present.
rules.key_value: Reasonable time after termination-intent notification, or before lease end
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security inspections under subdivision (f), following notice of either party's intention to terminate or before the lease term ends.
rules.exemptions: Subdivision (f) does not apply when the tenancy is terminated under Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(2), (3), or (4). If the tenant chooses not to request an initial inspection, the landlord's duties under the subdivision are discharged; this does not erase the preceding duty to notify the tenant of that choice.
rules.interaction: The tenant's request determines the subsequent inspection duties.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Subdivision (r) characterizes specified 2003 amendments to (f)(1) as declaratory of existing law; original onset is not inferred from the footer's 2026-01-01 amendment date.
limitations: The referenced grounds in Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 are not reproduced in D025.
rules.quoted_span:
(f) (1) Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before
the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. The purpose of the initial inspection shall be to allow the tenant an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies, in a manner consistent with the rights and obligations of the parties under the rental agreement, in order to avoid deductions from the security. If a tenant chooses not to request an initial inspection, the duties of the landlord under this subdivision are discharged. If an inspection is requested, the parties shall attempt to schedule the inspection at a mutually acceptable date and time. The landlord shall give at least 48 hours’ prior written notice of the date and time of the inspection if either a mutual time is
agreed upon, or if a mutually agreed time cannot be scheduled but the tenant still wishes an inspection. The tenant and landlord may agree to forgo the 48-hour prior written notice by both signing a written waiver. The landlord shall proceed with the inspection whether the tenant is present or not, unless the tenant previously withdrew their request for the inspection. rules.title: Discrimination against households with children prohibited, with specified exceptions
rules.requirement: Covered housing actors may not deny rental housing or discriminate in housing terms, privileges, facilities, or services because a person has children who occupy or will occupy the premises with that person.
rules.key_value: Hardship exception: dwelling with no more than 3 apartments; elderly means at least 65; temporary-leasing exception: absence no longer than 1 year
rules.coverage_conditions: Publicly assisted, multiple-dwelling, contiguously located, or other covered housing; applies to the owners, sublessees, brokers, assignees, managing agents, rights holders, agents or employees, and condominium or cooperative unit-owner organizations listed in subsection 11.
rules.exemptions: Local, state, and federal maximum-occupancy restrictions remain applicable. Subsection 11 excludes: (1) dwellings with three or fewer apartments where one apartment is occupied by an elderly or infirm person for whom children would constitute a hardship; elderly means 65 or older, and infirm means disabled or chronically ill; (2) temporary leasing or subleasing of a single-family dwelling, single apartment, or single condominium or cooperative unit by an owner or sublessor who ordinarily uses it as a principal residence, during an absence not exceeding one year; and (3) leasing one unit in a two-family dwelling where the owner resides in the other unit.
rules.quoted_span: to refuse to rent or lease or sell or otherwise to deny to or withhold from any person such accommodations because such person has a child or children who shall occupy the premises with such person or to discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of such accommodations or the acquisition thereof, or in the furnishing of facilities and services in connection therewith, because such person has a child or children who occupy or shall occupy the premises with such person;
rules.interaction: Expressly preserves applicable maximum-occupancy restrictions without specifying their numerical limits.

rules.title: The accompanying form must prominently display the prescribed eviction warning
rules.requirement: The form must prominently display the prescribed statement explaining that a notice to quit is not an eviction, immediate departure is not required, the tenant is entitled to a legal proceeding to defend against eviction, and only a court order can force departure.
rules.key_value: Prominent display of the source-prescribed statement
rules.coverage_conditions: A written landlord notice to quit for nonpayment of rent given to a residential tenant pursuant to chapter 186. This requirement concerns the form accompanying that notice, and the source provides the required wording.
rules.interaction: The exact statement is supplied by the original evidence span; this summary is not replacement notice language.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot presents the provision without a pending or future-version label; the original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The eviction category covers notice and filing procedure; this provision does not itself establish a general just-cause requirement.
rules.quoted_span:
Section 31. (a) A notice to quit for nonpayment of rent given in writing by a landlord to a residential tenant pursuant to this chapter shall be accompanied by a form that shall include, but not be limited to: (i) documentation of any agreements between the tenant and landlord for the tenant to repay the landlord for nonpayment of rent; and (ii) information on: (1) rental assistance programs including, but not limited to, the residential assistance for families in transition program; (2) applicable trial court rules, standing orders or emergency administrative orders pertaining to actions for summary process; and (3) any relevant federal or state legal restrictions on residential evictions. The form shall also prominently display the following statement:
''THIS NOTICE TO QUIT IS NOT AN EVICTION. YOU DO NOT NEED TO IMMEDIATELY LEAVE YOUR UNIT. YOU ARE ENTITLED TO A LEGAL PROCEEDING IN WHICH YOU CAN DEFEND AGAINST THE EVICTION. ONLY A COURT ORDER CAN FORCE YOU TO LEAVE YOUR UNIT.''

rules.title: Limits on sharing and using applicant criminal records
rules.requirement: Unless otherwise required by law, do not share an applicant's criminal record with anyone not expected to use it to evaluate the applicant consistently with the Act, or use it for an inconsistent purpose.
rules.coverage_conditions: Covered housing providers handling residential rental applicants' criminal records.
rules.exemptions: Disclosures or uses otherwise required by law are excepted. Units in owner-occupied premises with no more than four dwelling units are excluded.

rules.title: Upfront-payment protections cannot be waived by lease or tenant agreement
rules.requirement: A lease term conflicting with section 15B's upfront-payment protections, or a tenant's or prospective tenant's waiver of them, is void and unenforceable.
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenants and prospective tenants covered by the section's allowed-upfront-charge, prepaid-last-month-rent receipt, interest, and successor-credit protections. The current subsection (1)(b) actor-inclusive introductory restriction on required payments is expressly effective August 1, 2025.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: This applies the section-wide antiwaiver clause to the fee-restriction category; it is not an additional amount or a separate fee exception.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).

[ Introductory paragraph of clause (b) of subsection (1) as amended by 2025, 9, Secs. 54 and 55 effective August 1, 2025.  See 2025, 9, Sec. 136.  For text effective until August 1, 2025, see above.]
(b) At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, no lessor or agent of the lessor may require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay, to the lessor or to an agent of the lessor, any amount in excess of the following:
(i) rent for the first full month of occupancy;  and,
(ii) rent for the last full month of occupancy calculated at the same rate as the first month;  and,
(iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2);  provided, however, that the executive office of housing and livable communities may promulgate regulations to authorize a lessor and a tenant or prospective tenant to agree to the payment of a fee in lieu of payment of a security deposit;  provided further, that any such regulations shall:  (A) require the lessor to utilize a fee collected to waive a security deposit to cover for unpaid rent or unit damage that applies to the tenant's lease;  (B) require that a fee so collected be:  (I) entirely or partially non-refundable;  provided, however, that the lessor shall disclose that the fee is non-refundable in the lease;  provided further, that the tenant shall agree to the fee and acknowledge that the tenant understand that it is entirely or partially non-refundable, as the case may be, in writing;  and (II) a recurring monthly fee, or payable upon any schedule and in an amount that the lessor and tenant agree upon, as authorized by the executive office;  (C) limit the total sum of the fee or recurring payments, regardless of the duration of the lease and any extensions thereto, to an amount not to exceed 1 month's rent;  (D) require that the fee be made optional for both the tenant and the lessor and that the tenant be permitted to choose to pay a full security deposit rather than the fee;  (E) require a lessor who offers such a fee in lieu of security deposit:  (I) to offer the option of a fee in lieu of a security deposit to every prospective tenant whose application for occupancy has been approved, regardless of income, race, gender, gender identity, disability, sexual orientation, immigration status, size of household or credit score;  and (II) not to consider such factors and categories when setting the amount of the fee;  and (F) allow a tenant who agrees to pay a fee to waive a security deposit to opt-out of the obligation to pay such fee if such tenant pays the security deposit that would otherwise be in effect for the tenant's apartment on the day the tenant chooses to opt-out of such fee;  provided further, that the sum of fees paid to waive a security deposit and the payment of the security deposit shall not exceed, in total, the amount of 1 month's rent;  and provided further, that the executive office shall consult with the office of the attorney general prior to promulgating regulations authorizing a fee in lieu of a security deposit under this section;  and,
(iv) the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.

(7A) Whenever a lessor who receives rent in advance for the last month of tenancy transfers his interest in the dwelling unit for which the rental advance was received, whether by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or trustee in bankruptcy, or otherwise, the lessor shall credit an amount equal to such rental advance together with any interest which has accrued thereon for the benefit of the tenant who made such rental advance, to the successor in interest of such lessor, and said successor in interest shall be liable for crediting the tenant with such rental advance, and for paying all interest accrued thereon in accordance with the provisions of this section from the date upon which said transfer is made;  provided, however, that the granting of a mortgage on such premises shall not be deemed a transfer of interest.  The successor in interest shall, within forty-five days from the date of said transfer, notify the tenant who made such rental advance that such rental advance was so credited, and that such successor has assumed responsibility therefor pursuant to the foregoing provision.  Such notice shall also contain the lessor's name, business address, and business telephone number, and the name, business address, and business telephone number of his agent, if any.  Said notice shall be in writing.
Upon such transfer, the lessor or his agent shall continue to be liable with respect to the provisions of this section until:--(a) there has been a credit of the amount of the rental advance so held to the lessor's successor in interest and the tenant has been notified in writing of the transfer and of the successor in interest's name, business address, and business telephone number;  (b) there has been compliance with this clause by the successor in interest;  or (c) the rental advance has been credited to the tenant and all accrued interest has been paid thereon.
In the event that the lessor fails to credit said rental advance to his successor in interest as required by this subsection, the successor in interest shall, without regard to the nature of the transfer, assume liability for crediting of the rental advance, and payment of all interest thereon to the tenant in accordance with the provisions of this section;  provided, however, that if the tenant still occupies the dwelling unit for which the rental advance was given, said successor in interest may satisfy such obligation by granting the tenant free use and occupancy of the dwelling unit for a period of time equivalent to the period of time covered by the rental advance.  The liability imposed by this subsection shall not apply to a city or town which acquires title to property pursuant to chapter sixty or to a foreclosing mortgagee or a mortgagee in possession which is a financial institution chartered by the commonwealth or by the United States.

rules.title: JCO just-cause requirement and permitted eviction grounds
rules.requirement: Covered tenancies cannot be terminated without just cause. Listed at-fault grounds are failure to pay rent; failure to cure a rental-agreement violation; nuisance or property damage; illegal use; failure to renew a similar rental agreement; denial of reasonable access; and an unapproved subtenant remaining at lease end. Listed no-fault grounds are owner or immediate-family occupancy; resident-manager occupancy when required by law or an affordable-housing covenant or regulatory agreement; demolition, permanent market withdrawal, or nonresidential conversion; a government vacate order; HUD ownership and sale; residential-hotel conversion or demolition; and conversion to affordable housing.

rules.title: Utility charges for newer fully covered tenancies
rules.requirement: For fully covered tenancies starting on or after February 6, 2024, utility costs must be included as a set amount in base rent unless the service is separately metered and the lease requires the tenant to place it in the tenant's name. A landlord charging utilities separately on or after that date may petition to add average utility costs to the rent ceiling. A ceiling increase requires the petition process; a hearing waiver may be requested if the parties agree and the submitted agreement and proof meet the stated but unspecified standards.
rules.key_value: Base-rent inclusion OR separately metered service in tenant's name; petition required for ceiling increase
rules.coverage_conditions: The charging restriction applies to fully covered units with tenancies beginning on or after February 6, 2024. The petition option is described for landlords charging separately for utilities on or after that date. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. This rent-amount regulation requires FULL coverage; partially covered units retain other protections but not this rent cap.
rules.exemptions: Separate utility charges are permitted when the utility is separately metered and the lease requires the account in the tenant's name. Agreement alone does not bypass the petition process. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.
rules.quoted_span: For tenancies starting on or after February 6, 2024, a landlord may charge a tenant in a fully covered unit for utilities only if either: the cost of the  utilities are part of the base rent, or the utility service is separately-metered and the lease requires the tenant to place the utility in the tenant’s name.
rules.interaction: A utility-cost ceiling adjustment is petition-based and distinct from the annual general adjustment.

Rent ceiling increases must be made through the petition process, but the parties can ask to waive the hearing if they agree on the increase, and the agreement and proof submitted with the petition meet certain standards. See our
Rent Adjustment Petitions page
for details.

The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

rules.requirement: For a materials or supplies deduction, the landlord must supply a copy of the bill, invoice, or receipt with the security accounting. rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security deductions for materials or supplies used in repairs or cleaning, with documentation delivered under subdivision (h)(1)-(2).
rules.exemptions: Paragraphs (h)(2)-(3) are excused when combined repair and cleaning deductions are at most $125 or the tenant signs a waiver substantially containing paragraph (2)'s text at or after notice under section 1946 or 1946.1 or Code of Civil Procedure section 1161, or no earlier than 60 days before fixed-term expiration. A tenant request within 14 calendar days after statement receipt reinstates compliance within 14 calendar days after the landlord receives the tenant's request. If outside documents are not possessed within 21 days after vacancy, paragraph (3)'s good-faith estimate and 14-day later-completion procedure may apply.
rules.interaction: The evidentiary alternative for routinely purchased items does not remove the reasonable-restoration amount limit in (e)(2)(B).

(2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.

rules.title: Pre-fee screening-rights and maximum-fee disclosure
rules.requirement: When an owner or agent receives a request to rent Berkeley residential property and charges the described credit-report/application-processing fee, provide a clear and conspicuous Tenant Screening Fee Rights Statement, or a substantially similar statement, and the state-law maximum fee. Provide it in the application or a separate disclosure before receiving the fee. Contrary lease provisions are unenforceable.

rules.title: Capital-improvement rent petitions require completed work
rules.requirement: Landlords may petition for capital-improvement rent increases only for completed improvements; preliminary authorization of increases for planned improvements is no longer available.
rules.key_value: Completed improvements only
rules.coverage_conditions: Capital-improvement rent-increase petitions under Berkeley's Rent Ordinance. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. This rent-amount regulation requires FULL coverage; partially covered units retain other protections but not this rent cap.
rules.exemptions: Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.

rules.title: Owner or qualifying relative occupancy as no-fault just cause
rules.requirement: An owner may recover possession in good faith for the owner, spouse, domestic partner, child or grandchild by blood or adoption, parent, or grandparent to use the property as a primary residence for at least 12 continuous months. The intended occupant must move in within 90 days after the tenant vacates. This ground is unavailable if the intended occupant already occupies a rental unit on the property or a similar unit is vacant there. For leases entered into on or after June 24, 2023, the tenant must agree to termination in writing or the lease must expressly permit the specified owner-occupancy termination. For tenancies already in effect before that date, adding such a clause to a new, renewed, or fixed-term lease counts as substantially similar for the renewal-refusal ground. The termination notice must identify intended occupants and their relationships to the owner, inform the tenant of the right to request proof, and the owner must supply that proof on request.
rules.key_value: Move in within 90 days; primary residence for at least 12 continuous months
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: Owner invokes owner/qualifying-relative occupancy ground and gives notice naming occupants/relationships plus right to request proof; supply proof on request. Do not omit conjunctive ownership, consent, vacancy and actual-occupancy tests. Additional event and branch tests: Owner means a natural person with at least 25% recorded ownership; OR a natural person with any recorded interest when 100% of recorded ownership is divided among the specified related family members; OR a natural person whose recorded interest is owned through an LLC or partnership. Natural person includes a settlor or beneficiary of a family trust, or for LLC/partnership ownership a natural person with 25% ownership in the property. Family trust is a revocable living or irrevocable trust whose settlors and beneficiaries are related as sibling, spouse, domestic partner, child by blood/adoption, parent, grandparent, or grandchild by blood/adoption. These are source definitions, not permission for any property manager to claim owner occupancy. Good-faith owner/spouse/domestic partner/child or grandchild by blood or adoption/parent/grandparent primary residence for>=12 continuous months. Intended occupant must move in within 90 days after tenant vacancy. For lease entered>=2023-06-24, tenant written agreement to termination OR express lease owner-occupancy termination clause required. For older tenancy adding clause to new/renewed/fixed lease counts as substantially similar. Owner-occupancy ground unavailable if intended occupant already occupies rental unit on property OR similar unit is already vacant there. Occupant must move-in within 90 days and occupy 12 continuous months; moving in time then dying before 12 months is not noncompliance. Owner invokes owner/qualifying-relative occupancy ground and gives notice naming occupants/relationships plus right to request proof; supply proof on request.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for

circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

Annual increases for owner move-in and Ellis Act eviction relocation assistance payments go into effect January 1, 2026.
Published:
October 27, 2025
Last Updated:
October 27, 2025
The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction. The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same relocation assistance payments for tenants evicted so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market. Both ordinances index the relocation payments to inflation, and provide that the Rent Board shall publish the yearly inflationary increases.
At its October 16, 2025 Special Meeting, the Rent Board approved relocation assistance payment increases that will go into effect on January 1, 2026.
The standard relocation assistance payment will increase to
$19,413
.
The additional relocation assistance payment for qualifying households will increase to
$6,471
.
These increases represent a 1.5% upward adjustment in the previous amounts, which is the 12-month increase in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers in the San Francisco-Oakland-San Jose region. These annual increases are required by the terms set forth in the Rent and Ellis Implementation Ordinances.
The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same relocation assistance payments for tenants evicted so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market.

rules.title: Annual bank and interest statement, payment option, and tenant deduction
rules.requirement: At each tenancy year's end, the landlord must send or give a statement identifying the bank's name and address, deposit amount, account number, and interest payable, and pay the interest or include notice permitting deduction from the next rent payment. rules.title: Governmental order to vacate ground
rules.requirement: The bulletin identifies compliance with a governmental agency's Order to Vacate as a no-fault eviction ground. The landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict before giving notice to tenants.
rules.key_value: Declaration before tenant notice
rules.coverage_conditions: RSO- or JCO-covered units subject to a governmental agency's Order to Vacate. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Eviction-related procedure is stated for ALL Los Angeles RSO OR JCO rental properties; verify relevant program property classification and keep disputed scope unknown. Substantive program scope: For these substantive no-fault grounds, require EITHER verified RSO property/tenancy coverage OR verified JCO property coverage AND (tenant has lived in the same unit for at least six months OR the original lease has expired, whichever occurs first). Apply the elapsed/original-lease test only to the JCO branch. Verify the particular ground and its other conditions separately. The all-properties filing rule in D040 lines 73-75 does not establish substantive JCO tenancy coverage.

The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.

Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

All tenant not- at-fault evictions require payment of relocation assistance and the filing of a 
Declaration of Intent to Evict form with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) before 
evicting tenants from units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause 
Ordinance (JCO). Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices. 
 Not-At-Fault Reasons for Eviction
1. The landlord evicts for the occupancy of her/himself, spouse, grandchildren, children,  
parents or grandparents, or a resident manager (Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC)  
151.09.A.8, 165.03.H.). Evictions for the purpose of resident manager occupancy are 
allowed only if required by law or an affordable housing covenant, or a regulatory  
agreement. Landlords must comply with the restrictions and requirements of LAMC Section  
151.30.
2. The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.
3. The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.
4. The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both the owner and plaintiff and seeks 
to recover possession to vacate the property prior to sale (LAMC 151.09.A.12, 165.03.K.).
5. Residential Hotel Unit conversion or demolition (LAMC 151.09.A.13, 165.03.L.).
6. The landlord seeks to recover possession of the rental unit to convert the subject property 
to an affordable housing accommodation (LAMC 151.09.A.14, 165.03.M.).
7. The landlord demolishes the property or converts the use of the property to condominiums, 
stock cooperatives, community apartment projects, hotels, and commercial uses, regardless 
of whether the property is subject to the RSO OR JCO (LAMC 47.06 & 47.07).

3. The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.

rules.title: Habitual late payment after warnings
rules.requirement: Continuous nonpayment or habitual late payment after written Notice to Cease may support eviction with at least one month's Notice to Quit. Habitual lateness means more than one late payment after the warning. A landlord accepting later late payments must continue reasonably warning that further lateness will lead to eviction or the original warning may be treated as waived.

rules.exemptions: Acceptance without continued reasonable warning may waive the original Notice to Cease.

If the tenant continuously fails to pay rent or habitually pays late, after written Notice to

criteria.condition: Continuous nonpayment OR more than one late payment AFTER written cease notice.

evidence.quote:
J. Tenant Continuously Fails to Pay Rent or Habitually Pays Late 
If the tenant continuously fails to pay rent or habitually pays late, after written Notice to 
Cease, the landlord may file a suit for eviction. A Notice to Quit must be served on the 
tenant at least one month before filing a suit for eviction (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(j)). 
 
Note: The Courts have ruled that habitual late payments means more than one (1) late 
payment following the Notice to Cease. Also, the N.J. Supreme Court ruled that a 
landlord, after giving a tenant a notice to cease late payments, must continue to give the 
tenant reasonable and sufficient notice when accepting further late payments, that 
continued late payments from the tenant would result in an eviction action. If the 
landlord does not give this continued notice, the original Notice to Cease given to the 
tenant may be considered to be waived by the Court.

rules.title: Notice and opportunity to cure before a curable at-fault termination
rules.requirement: Before terminating for an at-fault curable lease violation, the landlord must give written notice describing the violation and an opportunity to cure under Code of Civil Procedure §1161(3). If the violation remains uncured within the notice period, the landlord may serve a three-day notice to quit without another cure opportunity. This is a procedural protection accompanying the just-cause requirement.
rules.key_value: Initial cure opportunity; subsequent 3-day notice to quit if uncured

This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. §98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0703 Exemptions 
This Division shall not apply to the following types of residential rental properties or 
residential circumstances: 
(a) transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in California Civil Code 
section 1940(b), as may be amended;

Article 10, Division 1 of this Code, as may be amended;

with a government agency, or other document as affordable housing for 
persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be amended;

housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as 
defined in California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be 
amended, or comparable federal statutes. This exemption shall not include

notice, the landlord may terminate the tenancy without another 
opportunity to cure by serving a three-day notice to quit.

rules.title: RPO demolition relocation coverage, option choice, and enforcement
rules.requirement: Owners demolishing a Protected Unit for new construction within five years after filing a withdrawal notice or eviction declaration must comply with RPO relocation requirements. The owner selects one of three relocation options and must satisfy the highest applicable state or city relocation amount. Lower-income households require enhanced relocation when the project is subject to the RPO.
rules.key_value: Demolition within 5 years after filing; three owner-selected relocation options
rules.coverage_conditions: Protected Units demolished for new construction. Protected status includes affordability restrictions, public rent/price control, or occupancy by lower/very-low-income households within the past five years, OR Ellis Act withdrawal within the past ten years. All RSO units are Protected Units. Enhanced payments concern lower-income households at or below 80% AMI, adjusted for household size. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Protected Unit intended for demolition for new construction: current/past 5 year restricted affordability OR public rent/price control OR lower/very low income occupancy, OR Ellis withdrawal past 10 years; all RSO units protected. RPO applies only to Protected Units demolished for new construction; occupant protections listed include rights beyond income-based enhanced cash payments. Owner demolishes Protected Unit for new construction within 5 years after Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict filing; owner selects one of 3 options and must pay highest applicable State/City amount.
rules.exemptions: If the units are not Protected Units or are not occupied by a lower-income tenant, the bulletin directs use of ordinary RSO/JCO relocation rules. HCA requirements may still apply even if the RPO does not.
rules.quoted_span:
Owners who demolish a Protected Unit for the purpose of new construction within 5 years after the 
filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD are required to 
comply with relocation requirements under the RPO. Failure to comply with the RPO may result in 
financial penalties starting at $250,000 per displaced unit and withholding of LAHD permit clearances.
rules.interaction:
RPO codifies and expands HCA protections; applicable state and city amounts are compared rather than automatically added.
r-0182 coexists r-0179 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.
rules.temporal_notes: The text expressly calls the RPO effective February 11, 2025. The five-year post-filing demolition condition is distinct from Protected Unit lookbacks.
