evidence.quote:
City
laws require all tenants be paid relocation assistance in the amounts required by the RSO or JCO
within 15 days of serving a notice to terminate tenancy, which must be enhanced for lower income
tenants if the project is subject to the Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.

The RSO and JCO amounts must also be enhanced for
lower income tenants under the HCA regardless of the RPO applicability.

*The regular RSO or JCO relocation rules apply as described in the A. Relocation Assistance
Bulletin: No-Fault Evictions Under the RSO & JCO if the units to be demolished are not Protected
Units or are not occupied by a lower income tenant.

Protected Units: (1) Residential dwelling units that are or were subject to a recorded covenant, ordinance, or law that restricts 
rents to levels affordable to persons and families of lower or very low income within the past five years. (2) Residential 
dwelling units that are or were subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police 
power within the past five years.  This includes all RSO units. (3) Residential dwelling units that are or were rented by lower or 
very low income households within the past five years. (4) Residential dwelling units that were withdrawn from rent or lease in 
accordance the Ellis Act within the past 10 years.

Owners who demolish a Protected Unit for the purpose of new construction within 5 years after the 
filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD are required to 
comply with relocation requirements under the RPO. Failure to comply with the RPO may result in 
financial penalties starting at $250,000 per displaced unit and withholding of LAHD permit clearances.

Owners have 3 relocation options to comply with the RPO relocation rules. The owner chooses one of 
the options. The owner must pay the highest of the applicable relocation amounts to comply with State 
and City laws.

Requirements for Landlords 
To terminate tenancy for the purpose of demolition of a Protected Unit1, a landlord must: 
1. File with LAHD a Declaration of Intent to Evict for units regulated by the JCO per the Los Angeles
Municipal Code (LAMC) Section 165.03.I(1) or file with LAHD a  Notice of Intent to Withdraw Units
From Rental Housing Use for units regulated by the RSO.  Only RSO units are subject to the Ellis
Act provisions (LAMC 151.22-151.28).  All RSO units are Protected Units.
2. Serve tenants with a written notice to move out and file a copy of it with LAHD within 3 business
days online at https://lahd.service-now.com/efs. For more information go to
housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices
3. Pay relocation assistance to tenants in compliance with the State law’s Housing Crisis Act
(California Government Code Section 66300 et seq.) or the City laws, whichever is higher.  City
laws require all tenants be paid relocation assistance in the amounts required by the RSO or JCO
within 15 days of serving a notice to terminate tenancy, which must be enhanced for lower income
tenants if the project is subject to the Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.  The RSO and JCO amounts must also be enhanced for
lower income tenants under the HCA regardless of the RPO applicability.  Parties are encouraged
to seek legal advice to understand the HCA State law if the RPO does not apply to them.
*The regular RSO or JCO relocation rules apply as described in the A. Relocation Assistance
Bulletin: No-Fault Evictions Under the RSO & JCO if the units to be demolished are not Protected
Units or are not occupied by a lower income tenant.
1 Protected Units: (1) Residential dwelling units that are or were subject to a recorded covenant, ordinance, or law that restricts 
rents to levels affordable to persons and families of lower or very low income within the past five years. (2) Residential 
dwelling units that are or were subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police 
power within the past five years.  This includes all RSO units. (3) Residential dwelling units that are or were rented by lower or 
very low income households within the past five years. (4) Residential dwelling units that were withdrawn from rent or lease in 
accordance the Ellis Act within the past 10 years.

Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) 
The Housing Crisis Act of 2019 (HCA) originally introduced replacement requirements and occupant 
protections through Senate Bill (SB) 330 and has since been updated by SB 8 and Assembly Bill (AB) 1218. 
On February 11, 2025, the Los Angeles City Council adopted the RPO which codified and expanded upon 
replacement requirements and occupant protections of the HCA, and enhanced requirements for 
Restricted Affordable Units.  The RPO only applies to Protected Units that will be demolished for the 
purpose of new construction.  
The RPO’s occupant protections include: 1) Right to Relocation, 2) Right to Remain in the unit up to 6 
months prior to start of construction activities, which includes a 6-month notice to move out, 3) Right 
to Return to the same unit if the demolition does not proceed, 4) Right of First Refusal to the new 
building for some tenants and 5) Tenant Notification Requirements.  For more details, please go the Los 
Angeles City Planning Department’s website https://planning.lacity.gov/ and review the Fact Sheet: 
Replacement Unit Requirements and Occupant Protections.

Relocation Options Under the RPO 
Owners who demolish a Protected Unit for the purpose of new construction within 5 years after the 
filing of the Notice of Intent to Withdraw or Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD are required to 
comply with relocation requirements under the RPO. Failure to comply with the RPO may result in 
financial penalties starting at $250,000 per displaced unit and withholding of LAHD permit clearances.  
Owners have 3 relocation options to comply with the RPO relocation rules. The owner chooses one of 
the options. The owner must pay the highest of the applicable relocation amounts to comply with State 
and City laws.

3. Pay relocation assistance to tenants in compliance with the State law’s Housing Crisis Act
(California Government Code Section 66300 et seq.) or the City laws, whichever is higher.  City
laws require all tenants be paid relocation assistance in the amounts required by the RSO or JCO
within 15 days of serving a notice to terminate tenancy, which must be enhanced for lower income
tenants if the project is subject to the Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.  The RSO and JCO amounts must also be enhanced for
lower income tenants under the HCA regardless of the RPO applicability.  Parties are encouraged
to seek legal advice to understand the HCA State law if the RPO does not apply to them.
*The regular RSO or JCO relocation rules apply as described in the A. Relocation Assistance
Bulletin: No-Fault Evictions Under the RSO & JCO if the units to be demolished are not Protected
Units or are not occupied by a lower income tenant.

The RSO and JCO amounts must also be enhanced for
lower income tenants under the HCA regardless of the RPO applicability.

rules.title: Individualized criminal-history screening
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers agree not to deny housing through a blanket arrest-or-conviction policy and must consider applicants individually. Recommended considerations include disability and domestic-violence circumstances; seriousness, safety relationship, frequency, age and recency of criminal activity; subsequent rental history, sentence completion, substance-abuse treatment, employment, education, community involvement and family support; and the effects of denial on the household and community. Providers should give applicants examples of mitigating evidence.
rules.key_value: Case-by-case review; no blanket arrest-or-conviction exclusion
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy. The policy also applies to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.
rules.exemptions: The text states that the arrest-and-conviction policy does not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety. It also excludes current criminal behavior. Conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements prevail.
rules.citation: BOSTON FAIR CHANCE TENANT SELECTION POLICY
rules.quoted_span:
will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions. Housing providers will consider applicants on 
a case-by-case basis.
rules.interaction: The policy expressly yields to conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements and identifies disability protections and VAWA as relevant to individualized review.
rules.temporal_notes: The supplied policy is the February 2017 version; no operative date or sunset is stated.
limitations: This is a policy commitment for the identified providers and program, not a general prohibition applicable to every Boston landlord.
The listed individualized-review factors and provision of mitigating-evidence examples are recommendations.
The text does not define the direct-relationship or substantial-harm exception.
No statutory section, enforcement penalty, or subsequent policy history is supplied.

 A direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and or unreasonable

rules.title: Good-faith withdrawal from the rental market
rules.requirement: A landlord's good-faith recovery of possession to withdraw the residential rental property from the rental market is a permitted no-fault just-cause ground.
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: Landlord in good faith seeks withdrawal of residential rental property from rental market. No five-year first-offer rule under 98.0706(d) is expressly attached to this(b)(2)ground. Additional event and branch tests: Landlord in good faith seeks withdrawal of residential rental property from rental market. No-fault ground requires honest intent without ulterior motives.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0703 Exemptions 
This Division shall not apply to the following types of residential rental properties or 
residential circumstances: 
(a) transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in California Civil Code 
section 1940(b), as may be amended; 
(b) short-term residential occupancy, as defined in and subject to Chapter 5, 
Article 10, Division 1 of this Code, as may be amended;  
 
(c) housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement 
with a government agency, or other document as affordable housing for 
persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be amended;  
(d)  housing subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable 
housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as 
defined in California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be 
amended, or comparable federal statutes. This exemption shall not include 
Section 8;  
Ch. Art. Div.

(3-2024) 
 
 
 
(e) mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law (California Civil 
Code sections 798-799.11), as may be amended;  
 
(f) housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended 
care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 1569.2, as may be amended, an 
adult residential facility, as defined in Title 22, Division 6, Chapter 6 of the 
Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the California Department of 
Social Services, as may be amended, or non- profit transitional housing; 
(g) dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or an 
institution offering instruction to any grade from kindergarten through 12;

Non-profit transitional housing means temporary housing operated by a non-profit 
organization for up to 24 months with supportive services to individuals and families 
with the goal of interim stability and support to successfully move to and maintain 
permanent housing, which may cover housing costs and accompanying supportive 
services for program participants.

(i) single-family residence occupied by the landlord as the landlord’s principal 
place of residence, including both of the following:  
 
(1) a residence in which the landlord-occupant rents or leases no more 
than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior 
accessory dwelling units, as defined in section 113.0103; and  
 
(2) a mobilehome.

(j) a property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in 
which the landlord occupies one of the dwelling units as the landlord’s 
principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the 
landlord continues in occupancy;

(k) housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 
15 years, unless the housing is a mobilehome; and

(l) residential rental property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate 
from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following 
apply:

corporation; or

Civil Code section 798.2, as may be amended. 
(2) The tenants have been provided written notice that the residential 
rental property is exempt from this Division using the following

rules.title: Annual positive-CPI adjustment of the application-fee cap
rules.requirement: Beginning January 1 of the year after enactment and annually thereafter, adjust the application-fee ceiling in direct proportion to a positive percentage change in the specified CPI over the 12 months ending the previous October 31. The Treasurer determines the adjustment by December 1, and the adjusted ceiling applies to fees charged during the following calendar year beginning January 1. Make no adjustment when the CPI change is zero or negative.
rules.key_value: Annual positive-CPI adjustment; first adjusted-fee period begins January 1, 2027
rules.coverage_conditions: The fee limitation under C.46:8-18.1(a). CPI means All Urban Consumers, New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island Metropolitan Area, All Items (1982-84=100), published by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics. The Consumer Affairs director adjusts and annually publishes the applicable ceiling; the Treasurer determines the adjustment amount.
rules.exemptions: The cap's one-family/two-family dwelling exemption and exemption for Real Estate Commission licensees who are not the property's landlord continue to apply. No adjustment is made unless the specified CPI change is greater than zero.
rules.quoted_span:
Beginning on
January 1 of the year next following enactment of P.L.2025, c.405 (C.46:8-18.1
et seq.) and each year thereafter, the amount of the fee limitation established
pursuant to subsection a. of this section shall be adjusted by the Director of
the Division of Consumer Affairs in the Department of Law and Public Safety in
direct proportion to the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over a
12-month period ending October 31 of the previous year.
rules.interaction:
Adjusts the subsection (a) cap; it is not a separate surcharge or additional fee permission.
r-0185 coexists r-0265 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.

conditions.description: Only a positive change triggers an adjustment; the calendar-year fee ceiling follows the December 1 determination.

rules.temporal_notes: The preserved 2027-01-01 date describes first adjusted-fee use. The act became effective May 1, 2026; Treasurer determination by December 1 precedes the following January 1 fee-use year, and anticipatory implementation is authorized. The combined agency/fee-use record needs temporal branch review rather than blanket exclusion of every 2026 agency duty.
limitations: No CPI change, published adjusted ceiling, or rounding method is supplied.
The not-yet-effective status refers to the first adjusted-fee period, not to the Act as a whole.

rules.title: Criminal-history records that housing providers cannot consider
rules.requirement: When screening rental applicants, housing providers cannot consider arrests that did not lead to conviction, sealed or expunged records, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system.
rules.key_value: Nonconviction arrests; sealed or expunged records; juvenile-justice records or matters
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies when a housing provider considers an applicant's criminal history.

Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system.

evidence.quote: Generally, a housing provider may check the criminal history of an applicant, but there are some limitations. Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system.

FEHA also provides protections for people and circumstances related to protected characteristics, including:
the right to operate a licensed family childcare in a provider’s home

What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

Can a housing provider consider an applicant’s criminal history in deciding whether or not to rent to them?
Yes.  Generally, a housing provider may check the criminal history of an applicant, but there are some limitations. Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system. Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.

rules.title: Subsidized applicants must be offered alternative evidence before credit-history screening
rules.requirement: Where there is a government rent subsidy, credit history must not be used in a rental application without offering the applicant the option, at the applicant's discretion, to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of reasonable ability to pay the tenant's share of rent.
rules.key_value: Applicant-elected alternative evidence of ability to pay tenant rent share
rules.coverage_conditions: Government-subsidized rental applications in which a housing provider proposes to use credit history. Examples of lawful, verifiable alternatives include government benefit payments, pay records, and bank statements, and are nonexclusive.
rules.exemptions: Subdivision (o) preserves the housing owner's ability to verify employment, request landlord references, and verify identity. The clause does not ban all credit-history screening outside the stated government-subsidy and alternative-evidence conditions.
rules.interaction: If the applicant chooses the alternative-evidence option, the reasonable-response-time and in-lieu consideration duties in (o)(1)(B)(ii) follow.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Footer states the supplied version amendment effective 2024-01-01; it does not independently identify this clause's original onset in the source text.

rules.title: Access to deposit records and remedy for wrongful denial
rules.requirement: On request, the tenant or prospective tenant must be allowed to inspect the deposit records during normal business hours at the landlord's or agent's office. Wrongful failure to provide access entitles the requester to immediate return of security paid plus accrued interest.
rules.key_value: Immediate deposit return with accrued interest for wrongful denial
rules.coverage_conditions: A tenant or prospective tenant requests access to the deposit record required under subsection (2)(d).
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required. The return remedy requires wrongful failure to make the record available.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
rules.quoted_span: Said record shall be available for inspection upon request of a tenant or prospective tenant during normal business hours in the office of the lessor or his agent.  Upon a wrongful failure by the lessor or his agent to make such record available for inspection by a tenant or prospective tenant, said tenant or prospective tenant shall be entitled to the immediate return of any amount paid in the form of a security deposit together with any interest which has accrued thereon.

Section 15B. (1) (a) No lease relating to residential real property shall contain a provision that a lessor may, except to inspect the premises, to make repairs thereto or to show the same to a prospective tenant, purchaser, mortgagee or its agents, enter the premises before the termination date of such lease.  A lessor may, however, enter such premises:
(9) The provisions of this section shall not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of one hundred days or less in duration which lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose.

(e) A security deposit shall continue to be the property of the tenant making such deposit, shall not be commingled with the assets of the lessor, and shall not be subject to the claims of any creditor of the lessor or of the lessor's successor in interest, including a foreclosing mortgagee or trustee in bankruptcy;  provided, however, that the tenant shall be entitled to only such interest as is provided for in subsection (3)(b).
(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.
(b) Any lessor or his agent who receives a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give said tenant or prospective tenant at the time of receiving such security deposit a receipt indicating the amount of such security deposit, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom such security deposit is received, the date on which it is received, and a description of the premises leased or rented.  Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit.

Said record shall be available for inspection upon request of a tenant or prospective tenant during normal business hours in the office of the lessor or his agent.  Upon a wrongful failure by the lessor or his agent to make such record available for inspection by a tenant or prospective tenant, said tenant or prospective tenant shall be entitled to the immediate return of any amount paid in the form of a security deposit together with any interest which has accrued thereon.

rules.key_value: 30 years after completion of construction
rules.coverage_conditions: A newly constructed multiple dwelling satisfying the cited statute's omitted definition and procedural prerequisites, during the thirty years following completion of building construction. Building age alone does not establish the exemption.

newly

rules.interaction: Exemption from municipal rent control, not an express exemption from statewide notice or unconscionability protections.
rules.temporal_notes: A building-specific period measured from construction completion; no certificate-of-occupancy trigger is supplied.
limitations: The guide does not supply the statute's full eligibility definitions or procedural prerequisites.

rules.title: Nonpayment notices must state the cure right and omission extends the cure deadline
rules.requirement: Every nonpayment notice terminating an estate at will must include the prescribed notification explaining the prior-twelve-month condition, full-rent tender, permitted recipients, and ten-day cure right. If that notification is omitted, the tenant's applicable cure period extends to the answer due date in the landlord's possession action, but the omission does not otherwise invalidate the notice.
rules.key_value: Mandatory cure-right notification; omission extends cure to the answer due date
rules.coverage_conditions: Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment; the source supplies mandatory notification wording. The cure right described in that wording applies when no nonpayment notice was received within the preceding twelve months.
rules.exemptions: Omission does not otherwise affect notice validity; the source extends the period within which the tenant would be entitled to pay or tender under this section.
rules.interaction: The source's prescribed wording is preserved by the original evidence span; a paraphrase is not a replacement notice form.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot contains this provision with no pending or future-version label; its original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The organizer eviction category is used for termination and possession procedures; this provision does not itself establish a general just-cause requirement.
rules.quoted_span: Section 12. Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing for that purpose given to the other party; and, if the rent reserved is payable at periods of less than three months, the time of such notice shall be sufficient if it is equal to the interval between the days of payment or thirty days, whichever is longer. Such written notice may include an offer to establish a new tenancy for the same premises on terms different from that of the tenancy being terminated and the validity of such written notice shall not be affected by the inclusion of such offer. In case of neglect or refusal to pay the rent due from a tenant at will, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the tenancy; provided, that the tenancy of a tenant who has not received a similar notice from the landlord within the twelve months next preceding the receipt of such notice shall not be determined if the tenant, within ten days after the receipt thereof, pays or tenders to the landlord, the landlord's attorney, or the person to whom the tenant customarily pays rent, the full amount of any rent due. Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent shall contain the following notification to the tenant: ''If you have not received a notice to quit for nonpayment of rent within the last twelve months, you have a right to prevent termination of your tenancy by paying or tendering to your landlord, your landlord's attorney or the person to whom you customarily pay your rent the full amount of rent due within ten days after your receipt of this notice.'' If any notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent shall fail to contain such notification, the time within which the tenant receiving the notice would be entitled to pay or tender rent pursuant to this section shall be extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises. Failure to include such notice shall not otherwise affect the validity of the said notice. If the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due was caused by a failure or delay of the federal government, the commonwealth or any municipality, or any departments, agencies or authorities thereof, in the mailing or delivery of any subsistence or rental payment, check or voucher other than a salary payment to either the tenant or the landlord, the court in any action for possession shall continue the hearing not less than seven days in order to furnish notice of such action to the appropriate agency and shall, if all rent due with interest and costs of suit has been tendered to the landlord within such time, treat the tenancy as not having been terminated.

(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:
(1) The compensation of a landlord for a
tenant’s default in the payment of rent.
(2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.
(3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. The amendments to this paragraph enacted by the act adding this sentence shall apply only to tenancies for which the tenant’s right to occupy begins after January 1, 2003.
(4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the
security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

(h) As used in this section, “landlord” means an owner of residential rental property.
(i) As used in
this section, “application screening fee” means any nonrefundable payment of money charged by a landlord or their agent to an applicant, the purpose of which is to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application for the rent or lease of residential rental property.
(j) As used in this section, “applicant” means any entity or individual who makes a request to a landlord or their agent to rent a residential housing unit, or an entity or individual who agrees to act as a guarantor or cosignor on a rental agreement.
(k) The application screening fee shall not be considered an “advance fee” as that term is used in Section 10026 of the Business and Professions Code, and shall not be considered “security” as that term is used in Section 1950.5.

If deductions were made, the landlord must give the tenant a written statement itemizing the amount of and and purpose for any security deposit deductions, accompanied by copies of documents showing charges incurred and deducted by the landlord to repair or clean the premises, including a copy of any bill, invoice, or receipt for materials or supplies deductions. The landlord must also return any remaining portion of the security deposit. Starting January 1, 2025, landlords must provide proof that necessary repairs were completed.

(2) The landlord shall also include, along with and at the same time the itemized statement is sent, copies of documents showing charges incurred and deducted by
the landlord to repair or clean the premises, as follows:
(A) If the landlord or landlord’s employee did the work, the itemized statement shall reasonably describe the work performed. The itemized statement shall include the time spent and the reasonable hourly rate charged.
(B) If the landlord or landlord’s employee did not do the work, the landlord shall provide the tenant a copy of the bill, invoice, or receipt supplied by the person or entity performing the work. The itemized statement shall provide the tenant with the name, address, and telephone number of the person or entity, if the bill, invoice, or receipt does not include that information.
(C) If a deduction is made for materials or supplies, the landlord shall
provide a copy of the bill, invoice, or receipt. If a particular material or supply item is purchased by the landlord on an ongoing basis, the landlord may document the cost of the item by providing a copy of a bill, invoice, receipt, vendor price list, or other vendor document that reasonably documents the cost of the item used in the repair or cleaning of the unit.
(D) If a deduction is made for repairs or cleanings allowed by this section, the landlord shall provide photographs taken pursuant to subdivision (g), along with a written explanation of the cost of the allowable repairs or cleanings, as described in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive. The landlord may provide such photographs to the tenant by mail, email, computer flash drive, or by providing a link where the tenant may view the photographs online.
(3) If a repair to be done by the landlord or the landlord’s employee cannot reasonably be completed within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, or if the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord’s possession within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord may deduct the amount of a good faith estimate of the charges that will be incurred and provide that estimate with the itemized statement. If the reason for the estimate is because the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord’s possession, the itemized statement shall include the name, address, and telephone number of the person or entity. Within 14 calendar days of completing the repair or receiving the documentation,
the landlord shall complete the requirements in paragraphs (1) and (2) in the manner specified.
(4) The landlord need not comply with paragraph (2) or (3) if either of the following applies:
(A) The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).
(B) The tenant waived the rights specified in paragraphs (2) and (3). The waiver shall only be effective if it is signed by the tenant at the same time or after a notice to terminate a tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1 has been given, a notice under Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been given, or no earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease. The waiver shall
substantially include the text of paragraph (2).
(5) Notwithstanding paragraph (4), the landlord shall comply with paragraphs (2) and (3) when a tenant makes a request for documentation within 14 calendar days after receiving the itemized statement specified in paragraph (1). The landlord shall comply within 14 calendar days after receiving the request from the tenant.

rules.title: Fee-paying applicant receives the consumer credit report within seven days
rules.requirement: If the applicant paid a screening fee, the landlord or agent must provide that applicant a copy of the consumer credit report about them by personal delivery, mail, or email within seven days after receiving the report.
rules.key_value: 7 days after the landlord or agent receives the report
rules.coverage_conditions: A fee-paying residential rental applicant who is the subject of the consumer credit report received by the residential owner or agent; applicant includes the persons or entities, guarantors, and cosignors defined in (j). Under (a), the landlord or agent may but need not accept and rely on an applicant-presented consumer credit report; under (g), this section does not prevent accepting a reusable report pursuant to section 1950.1.
rules.exemptions: This section does not preempt deposit and fee provisions under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.conflict_note: Merge review: D005 expressly says a landlord MUST use a tenant-provided reusable screening report. D026 section 1950.6(a) expressly says a landlord MAY, but is NOT REQUIRED to, accept an applicant-presented consumer credit report, and subdivision (g) preserves accepting reusable reports under section 1950.1. Reusable screening reports may be a distinct qualified subset; section 1950.1 is not reproduced. This is an unresolved relationship requiring that missing definition/provision, not an established legal contradiction or authorization to override either claim. Keep both statements and their source boundaries.
rules.interaction: The right to a copy is conditioned on payment of a screening fee and receipt of the report; it does not itself require accepting an applicant-provided report or purchasing a new report.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset is not stated; the supplied version was amended effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: Section 1950.1 and the external consumer-credit-reporting-agency definition are not reproduced in D026.

What Falls Under RSO
If you own rental property in the City of Los Angeles, it may be subject to the
city’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO)
.
Find out
if your property falls under this ordinance and what you need to know to be in compliance.
Generally, the RSO applies to rental properties that were first built on or before October 1, 1978, as well as replacement units under
LAMC Section 151.28

Apartment
Condominium (Rent amount is not regulated for tenancies that commenced after December 31, 1995)

Duplex

Residential unit(s) attached to a commercial building
Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU)
Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit (JADU)
Mobile homes
and recreational vehicles in mobile home parks are also covered under the RSO.

rules.title: Treble unpaid-interest award for last-month rent advances
rules.requirement: If the landlord fails to pay interest due on prepaid last-month rent within thirty days after tenancy termination, a tenant who proves the failure in an action must receive three times the unpaid interest, court costs, and reasonable attorney fees.
rules.key_value: 3 times unpaid advance-rent interest, plus costs and reasonable attorney fees
rules.coverage_conditions: Interest owed under subsection (2)(a) on residential last-month rent paid in advance, remaining unpaid thirty days after termination and proved in an action against the landlord.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: This award is measured by interest owed, unlike the subsection (7) award measured by the security deposit or balance due.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
limitations: The organizer category includes allowed upfront charges and their receipts/refunds. This rule concerns prepaid last-month rent, not a security deposit; its amounts, interest and remedies must remain distinct from deposit provisions.

Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.

rules.title: Security held for the tenant with priority over landlord creditors
rules.requirement: The landlord must hold security for the tenant who is party to the lease or agreement. The tenant's claim to that security has priority over claims of the landlord's creditors.
rules.coverage_conditions: Security for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling, within the subdivision (b) definition, held for the tenant who is party to the lease or agreement.

evidence.quote:
(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:
(1) The compensation of a landlord for a
tenant’s default in the payment of rent.
(2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.
(3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. The amendments to this paragraph enacted by the act adding this sentence shall apply only to tenancies for which the tenant’s right to occupy begins after January 1, 2003.
(4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the
security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

(6) This subdivision shall not apply to a security collected or demanded by the landlord before July 1, 2024.
(d) Any security shall be held by the landlord for the tenant who is party to the lease or agreement. The claim of a tenant to the security shall be prior to the claim of any creditor of the landlord.
(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340, Sec. 1.   (AB 414)   Effective January 1, 2026.)

rules.title: Default method for returning remaining security
rules.requirement: Subject to the electronic-payment and multiple-adult-tenant provisions, the landlord must return remaining security by personal delivery or a check payable to the tenant sent by prepaid first-class mail.
rules.key_value: Personal delivery or prepaid first-class mailed check
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security remaining after lawful deductions, returned under subdivision (h)(1) no later than 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates and no earlier than the specified termination-notice or fixed-term timing. Mailed items go to the tenant-provided address, or the vacated unit if no address is provided.
rules.exemptions: Electronic payment receipt triggers (h)(1)(A)(ii), subject to written alternative arrangements; multiple adult tenants trigger (h)(1)(C), including its written-agreement and section 1946.7 exceptions.
rules.interaction: The default yields to the expressly referenced electronic and multiple-tenant arrangements.

(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:

(h) (1) No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, but not earlier than the time that either the landlord or the tenant provides a notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1, Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or not earlier than 60 calendar days prior to
the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant as follows:

(ii) (I) If the landlord received the security or rental payments from the tenant electronically, the landlord shall return the remainder of the security electronically to a bank account or other financial
institution designated by the tenant in writing, or by any electronic or virtual method available to the landlord if agreed to in writing by the tenant. Alternatively, the landlord and tenant may, by written agreement, designate another method of return, including, but not limited to, by personal delivery or by a check made payable to the tenant and mailed by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to an address provided by the tenant. Upon the termination of a landlord’s interest in the premises and the transfer of the security to the landlord’s successor in interest as provided in subdivision (i), the landlord’s successor in interest shall return the remainder of the security electronically to a bank account or other financial institution designated by the tenant in writing or by any electronic or virtual method available to the landlord’s successor
in interest if agreed to in writing by the tenant only if the landlord’s successor in interest received rental payments electronically from the tenant.

(C) (i) Except as provided in clause (iii) and unless the landlord and all adult tenants residing in the unit enter into a written mutual agreement pursuant to clause (ii), if multiple adult tenants reside
in the unit, the landlord shall return the remainder of the security by a check made payable to all adult tenants on the rental or lease agreement at the time the tenancy terminates and furnish the itemized statement by personal delivery or first-class mail, postage prepaid, to any one of the adult tenants chosen by the landlord.
(ii) If multiple adult tenants reside in the unit, the landlord may
enter into a mutual written agreement between the landlord and all adult tenants, at the commencement of the tenancy or at any time during or after the tenancy, that specifies both of the following:
(I) How any remaining portion of the security will be returned, including whether it will be returned to a specific adult tenant or divided among multiple tenants, with the allocation percentages. If any remaining portion of the security is to be returned to multiple adult tenants, the landlord may return the security by either a check by first-class mail, postage prepaid, or an electronic deposit to a bank account or other financial institution designated by each adult tenant, as specified in the written agreement.
(II) For each adult tenant, whether the landlord will
furnish the itemized statement by email or first-class mail, postage prepaid, along with a forwarding address or email account.
(iii) If multiple adult tenants reside in a unit and a tenant terminates the lease pursuant to Section 1946.7 and no written mutual agreement was entered into by the landlord and all adult tenants pursuant to clause (ii), and the tenant who terminated the lease pursuant to Section 1946.7 requests that the security be disbursed in a manner other than by check made payable to all adult tenants, the landlord may return the security in a manner other than by check made payable to all adult tenants.

(6) Any mailings to the tenant pursuant to this subdivision shall be sent to the address provided by the tenant. If the tenant does not provide an address, mailings pursuant to this subdivision shall be sent to the unit that has been vacated.
(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340, Sec. 1.   (AB 414)   Effective January 1, 2026.)

the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant as follows:

furnish the itemized statement by personal delivery or first-class mail, postage prepaid.
(ii) Upon mutual agreement between the landlord and tenant entered into at the commencement of the tenancy or at any time during or after the tenancy, the itemized statement may be furnished by either of the following:
(I) Emailed to an account provided by the tenant.
(II) Mailed to an address provided by the tenant by first-class mail, postage prepaid.
(C) (i) Except as provided in clause (iii) and unless the landlord and all adult tenants residing in the unit enter into a written mutual agreement pursuant to clause (ii), if multiple adult tenants reside

rules.title: Retaliation prohibited
rules.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for exercising rights under the Division or seeking its enforcement. Retaliation includes a threat or other adverse action for exercising or attempting to exercise a guaranteed right. This is an anti-retaliation protection, distinct from the requirement to establish a permissible termination ground.
rules.key_value: Threats and other adverse actions prohibited when retaliatory
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. The separately defined Tenant and this rule's trigger govern the initial scope inquiry. Applicability of the narrower Tenancy duration/fixed-term definition to this independent Tenant right is unresolved in the supplied text; do not use it as an automatic exclusion. Rule-specific applicability: Landlord threatens/adversely acts because tenant exercises, attempts to exercise or seeks enforcement of Division right. Causal connection to protected conduct required; threat alone can be adverse conduct. Additional event and branch tests: Landlord threatens/adversely acts because tenant exercises, attempts to exercise or seeks enforcement of Division right. Retaliation includes threat or other adverse action for exercise or attempted exercise of guaranteed right.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles. The Section 98.0702 Tenancy duration/fixed-term definition is not established here as an additional blanket Division-wide exemption from this independent Tenant right.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0703 Exemptions

residential circumstances: 
(a) transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in California Civil Code 
section 1940(b), as may be amended;

Article 10, Division 1 of this Code, as may be amended;

with a government agency, or other document as affordable housing for 
persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be amended;  
(d)  housing subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable 
housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as 
defined in California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be 
amended, or comparable federal statutes. This exemption shall not include 
Section 8;

(e) No Waiver. The provisions of section 98.0707 may not be waived by a buyout

§98.0709 Remedies 
(a) A tenant claiming a violation of this Division may file an action against a

(c) A tenant may raise, as an affirmative defense, any violation or noncompliance 
with this Division in any action by a landlord to recover possession of a 
residential rental property. 
 
(d) Any attempt by a landlord to recover possession of a residential rental 
property or any actual recovery of possession of a residential rental property 
in violation of this Division shall render the landlord liable to the tenant in a 
civil action for wrongful eviction for damages of not less than three times the 
actual economic damages. 
 
(e) Any landlord who fails to provide relocation assistance as required by 
section 98.0706(c) shall be liable to the tenant in a civil action for not less 
than three times the required relocation assistance and actual economic 
damages. 
 
(f) In the court's discretion, a landlord who attempts to recover possession of a 
residential rental property in material violation of this Division shall be liable 
to the tenant in a civil action for reasonable attorney’s fees and costs. 
 
(g) The remedies under section 98.0709 are cumulative and may be used in 
addition to any other remedies in this Division or at law, statute, or ordinance. 
 
(h) The City may enforce this Division under Chapter 1, Article 2 of this Code, 
including civil and criminal remedies. 
(“Remedies” added 5-25-2023 by O-21647 N.S.; effective 6-24-2023.)

rules.title: Coordinator facilitation of anticompetitive agreements
rules.requirement: A coordinator may not facilitate a tacit or express agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition regarding residential dwelling units, including by performing a coordinating function.
rules.coverage_conditions: A coordinator operates algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device performing a coordinating function for an owner, including an owner acting for itself. A coordinating function consists of collecting two or more owners' competitively sensitive information for algorithmic or automated analysis or training used to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, or occupancy; setting those matters using another owner's competitively sensitive information through algorithmic or automated analysis, processing, or training; OR setting or recommending those matters for two or more owners through the same or substantially similar algorithm or automated process facilitating parallel pricing coordination. Competitively sensitive information includes nonpublic prices, supply, security deposits, ideal occupancy, termination, renewal dates, and other material terms. Nonpublic information is not publicly available at no cost; a public/nonpublic combination is entirely nonpublic. Owners include direct and indirect owners of one or more residential rental units; a controlling person and the controlled owning entity count as one owner. Units must be intended as primary residences in New Jersey. Tacit consent requires no verbal or written communication and need not be shown through a conduct pattern.
rules.exemptions: Covered units exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. An algorithmic device excludes a spreadsheet both operating without artificial intelligence and requiring human analysis, and a database whose only algorithmic use is querying stored unprocessed data. Coordinating-function exclusions cover solely research, statistical analysis, or testing with no use to set or recommend rents, material lease terms, fees, occupancy, or other current or future lease terms; publicly available free rent estimates; equally available subscriber brokerage databases that list properties but neither recommend or set rent, material terms, or occupancy nor collect competitively sensitive information for those purposes; and lawful government affordability controls. A government entity lawfully imposing such controls is not a coordinator. Parallel pricing coordination excludes actions required by affordability controls. Those controls are government-program rent restrictions, including the specified federal Section 8 homeownership program, State housing programs, NJ Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency programs, local rent control or leveling, and other government housing programs.

shared_scope_logic.logic: First evaluate temporal gate: as-of2026-10-01 not operative regardless address/facts. For future/historical conduct on or after2027-07-01, apply relevant primary-residence, institutional and independent-owner definitions. Other antitrust laws remain separate.

Any one function branch suffices unless a stated function exclusion applies. The>=2owners threshold belongs branches1/3; branch2 uses another owner's information. No blanket property unit minimum. Evaluate parallel agreement definition only where branch3 requires it.

Identify the alleged coordinator separately from the actor whose conduct is assessed. Apply software/device/function and government exceptions to that coordinator. Section 4(a) separately tests the owner-side acquisition conduct; section 4(d) separately tests the actor relationship and parallel-pricing conduct. The purchaser or agent need not personally operate software merely because its provider/principal must qualify as a coordinator. Device exclusion does not defeat a separate software route or section 4(e) any-person function prohibition.

The Department does not have jurisdiction over the administratio n of the courts, nor can 
the Department render legal advice. This publication is based on existing New Jersey statutes, 
regulations, and court cases that concern landlord-tenant relations; however, this publication is not 
a complete summary of all laws, regulations, and court cases that concern landlord-tenant relations 
in New Jersey. Any person who plans to initiate a legal action resulting from a landlord -tenant 
dispute may wish to consult the appropriate enforcing agency, a county legal services agency, 
private counsel, or an owner’s, tenant’s, or mobile home organization. A list of additional agencies 
and organizations that may be available to provide assistance is located in the appendix section of 
this publication.  Please be advised that this guide may be amended by the Department as required, 
and will be posted on the Department’s website accordingly.

Rent Control/Rent Increases 
 The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling. Locally created boards enforce 
these ordinances. Rent control ordinances have been upheld as a val id exercise of the municipal 
police power where there is a housing shortage (Iganamort v. Borough of Fort Lee , 120 N.J. 
Super. 286 (1973); Helmsley v. Borough of Fort Lee, 78 N.J. 200 (1978); Orange Taxpayers 
Council, Inc. v. City of Orange, 83 N.J. 246 (1980)) 
 Under the Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law ( N.J.S.A. 2A:42 -84.5), newly 
constructed multiple dwellings shall be exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period 
of 30 years following completion of construction of the building. Rent s that are subsidized by 
governmental funding may also be exempt from local rent control ordinances. A tenant may 
contact the Rent Control Board or municipal clerk in their town to find out if their rental unit is 
covered by a rent control or rent leveling ordinance.

Public Financed and Subsidized Housing 
 Housing developments owned or subsidized by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban 
Development (HUD), as well as unsubsidized developments with HUD -insured mortgages 
determined by HUD to have certain economic problems, are not subject to municipal rent control. 
For further information on the proper notice of a rent increase (the allowable amount of each rent 
increase in HUD buildings), contact the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, 
New Jersey State Office, 1 Newark Center, Newark, New Jerse y 07102-5260, (973) 622 -7900. 
Likewise, rents fixed and controlled by the New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency 
(NJHMFA) in projects it finances are not subject to municipal rent control ordinances. For further 
information on the proper notice of a rent increase or the allowable amount of rent increase in a 
NJHMFA project, contact the New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency, 637 South 
Clinton Ave., Post Office Box 18550, Trenton, New Jersey 08650-2085, (609) 278-7400.

rules.title: No higher security deposit because a household includes children
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers may not charge a higher security deposit because a household includes children.
rules.key_value: No discriminatory deposit surcharge for households with children
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to households with children in housing subject to the familial-status protections described by the guidance.
rules.exemptions: Qualifying senior housing may exclude applicants based on age, including families with children. This is an admission exception; the source does not authorize a deposit surcharge for admitted families. The source's owner-occupied, one-additional-person exception expressly concerns applicant exclusion and does not explain deposit treatment.
rules.quoted_span: Prohibiting housing providers from having conditions or rules that discriminate against households with children, such as charging a higher security deposit to households with children or excluding children from playing in common areas open to other tenants.

conditions.description: The prohibited higher deposit is based on the household including children.

rules.temporal_notes: No operative date is stated.
limitations: This is an antidiscrimination requirement, not a general dollar or monthly-rent deposit cap.
No statutory section is supplied.

evidence.quote: When an owner is occupying a home and is renting to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics.

Prohibiting housing providers from having conditions or rules that discriminate against households with children, such as charging a higher security deposit to households with children or excluding children from playing in common areas open to other tenants.

However, housing that has been specifically designed for senior citizens (persons 55 and older in some cases or 62 and older in others) can exclude people based on age, including families with children.

What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

Can a housing provider refuse to rent to families with children?
Generally, housing providers cannot discriminate against families with children. This is called “familial status” discrimination and protections include:
Prohibiting landlords and other types of housing providers from refusing to rent to someone because their household includes children.
Requiring that admission and occupancy requirements  be enforced the same for everyone, including families with children. For example, if a housing provider allows up to four people to live in a one-bedroom unit, they must allow a family of two parents and two children, or a mother or father with three children, to reside in the unit.
Prohibiting housing providers from having conditions or rules that discriminate against households with children, such as charging a higher security deposit to households with children or excluding children from playing in common areas open to other tenants.
However, housing that has been specifically designed for senior citizens (persons 55 and older in some cases or 62 and older in others) can exclude people based on age, including families with children. To qualify as “senior housing,” a housing accommodation must meet specific legally defined requirements, which may include a minimum number of units, age-based residency limits, and design features.

However, housing that has been specifically designed for senior citizens (persons 55 and older in some cases or 62 and older in others) can exclude people based on age, including families with children. To qualify as “senior housing,” a housing accommodation must meet specific legally defined requirements, which may include a minimum number of units, age-based residency limits, and design features.
Is it legal to develop and market housing for seniors?
Yes, but only when the facility or community is:
Provided under any state or federal program that the Federal Department of Housing and Urban Development has determined to be specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons
Designed to meet the physical and social needs of senior citizens; or
A mobile home park that:
Is intended for, and solely occupied by, people aged 62 years or older; or
Is intended and operated for occupancy by people aged 55 years or older and that meets a set of requirements including: at least 80% of the occupied units are intended to be occupied by at least one person who is 55 or older, the park publishes and adheres to policies and procedures demonstrating the intent for occupancy by people 55 or older, and the park complies with HUD’s rules for verification of occupancy.

rules.title: Senior housing pet rights and pet-related nonrenewal
rules.requirement: A senior citizen in a covered housing project may keep or care for a pet after written notice. Pet-related nonrenewal is permitted for code violations, improper care, failure to control the pet when taking it to or from the building, failure to take prompt action to remove pet waste when requested by the landlord, or failure to confine waste functions to areas that do not interfere with common areas or anyone's entrance to or exit from the project.
rules.key_value: Written notice by tenant
rules.coverage_conditions: Senior citizens residing in a senior citizen housing project, defined here as a building or structure having at least three rental dwelling units.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises with no more than three rental dwelling units and health care facilities are excluded.
rules.quoted_span:
Any senior citizen residing in a senior citizen housing project and 
providing written notice to the landlord is allowed to own or care for a pet.
rules.interaction: A protection against pet-based nonrenewal, subject to the stated grounds.
limitations: The excerpt does not define senior citizen age for this particular law.

The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same relocation assistance payments for tenants evicted so the owner can remove a property from the rental housing market. Both ordinances index the relocation payments to inflation, and provide that the Rent Board shall publish the yearly inflationary increases.

$19,413

$6,471
.

These annual increases are required by the terms set forth in the Rent and Ellis Implementation Ordinances.
