rules.title: Common pricing algorithms used in unlawful restraints of trade
rules.requirement: A person may not use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, trust combination, or conspiracy restraining trade or commerce in violation of the chapter. The provision is not a blanket prohibition on pricing software.
rules.key_value: Use or distribution as part of a prohibited restraint of trade
rules.coverage_conditions: A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. Distribution includes selling, licensing, providing access, or otherwise making available by any means, including subscription or sale of a service. Commercial terms include service level, availability, and output. Price encompasses money or other tangible or intangible value expected, required, or given for a product or service. Rental pricing is covered only insofar as it falls within these general definitions and the prohibited conduct.
rules.exemptions: An end consumer of a product or service is excluded from the definition of person. Other aspects of the person definition are incorporated from Section 16702, whose text is not supplied.
rules.citation: Business and Professions Code § 16729(a), (c), (d), added by AB 325, Chapter 338
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.interaction: Coexists with the antitrust laws defined as the provisions of the same part; the section expressly does not impair or limit their applicability.

conditions.description: The methodology must be used by at least two persons.
This requirement applies together with the multiple-user requirement.
Either use or distribution must occur as part of the prohibited restraint.

rules.title: Nondiscriminatory rental screening and access
rules.requirement: Rental decisions may not discriminate based on race, color, religion, disability, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, marital status, rental assistance, family status or military status. The guidance identifies refusal of rental assistance, protected-characteristic steering, falsely claiming unavailability, denying a family because of lead paint, and discriminatory rental terms or fees as examples of housing discrimination.

rules.title: One-month relocation for qualifying JCO single-family dwellings
rules.requirement: For a qualifying JCO single-family dwelling owned by a natural person, relocation is one month's rent at the rate in effect when the termination notice was served, payable as money or a credit. Qualifying ownership includes a trust or registered legal entity controlled by that natural person. The owner must own no more than four dwelling units and a single-family home on a separate lot in Los Angeles. LAMC 151.30(E) does not apply.
rules.key_value: One month's rent at notice service, as payment or credit
rules.coverage_conditions: Single-family dwelling subject to JCO AND qualifying natural-person ownership AND the stated Los Angeles portfolio limit. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Bulletin A covers RSO/JCO no-fault displacements and separately listed demolitions/conversions under 47.06/47.07 even outside RSO/JCO; establish the applicable entitlement branch. Payment calculation: For the Bulletin A relocation payment, a landlord may offset the tenant's accumulated rent against relocation assistance, EXCEPT when payment is owed because termination is required by a governmental agency order to vacate or to comply with an issued order for an unpermitted dwelling. This is a payment-amount modifier, not a complete exemption. Do not assume the same offset is authorized against distinct state HCA/RPO replacement-housing or enhanced benefits without establishing that entitlement's governing law.
rules.exemptions: For demolition for new construction, the bulletin limits its one-month chart footnotes to households above low income; lower-income households may require enhanced HCA/RPO benefits. LAMC 151.30(E) is expressly inapplicable. Exempt manager replacement with another resident manager, BUT manager-tenant compensated only by free/reduced rent may be entitled; exempt required natural-disaster hazard eviction ONLY if hazard not caused by landlord negligence. Resolve manager exception from missing RAC 920. Accumulated-rent offset is unavailable for the specified governmental-order terminations; it is otherwise a conditional amount modifier rather than an exemption from entitlement.

natural person, who owns no more than four dwelling units and a single-family home on a
separate lot  in the City of Los Angeles: one month’s rent that was in effect when   the
landlord served the written notice to terminate the tenancy, as either a monetary payment
or credit. The Los Angeles Municipal Code Section 151.30(E) shall not apply. (LAMC
165.06.A.(6)).

All tenant not- at-fault evictions require payment of relocation assistance and the filing of a 
Declaration of Intent to Evict form with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) before 
evicting tenants from units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause 
Ordinance (JCO). Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices. 
 Not-At-Fault Reasons for Eviction
1. The landlord evicts for the occupancy of her/himself, spouse, grandchildren, children,  
parents or grandparents, or a resident manager (Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC)  
151.09.A.8, 165.03.H.). Evictions for the purpose of resident manager occupancy are 
allowed only if required by law or an affordable housing covenant, or a regulatory  
agreement. Landlords must comply with the restrictions and requirements of LAMC Section  
151.30.
2. The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.
3. The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.
4. The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both the owner and plaintiff and seeks 
to recover possession to vacate the property prior to sale (LAMC 151.09.A.12, 165.03.K.).
5. Residential Hotel Unit conversion or demolition (LAMC 151.09.A.13, 165.03.L.).
6. The landlord seeks to recover possession of the rental unit to convert the subject property 
to an affordable housing accommodation (LAMC 151.09.A.14, 165.03.M.).
7. The landlord demolishes the property or converts the use of the property to condominiums, 
stock cooperatives, community apartment projects, hotels, and commercial uses, regardless 
of whether the property is subject to the RSO OR JCO (LAMC 47.06 & 47.07).

Exemptions from Relocation Assistance Payments 
Landlords are exempt from paying relocation assistance when: 
1. Evicting a resident manager to replace him/her with another resident manager. If the
resident manager is a Manager -Tenant receiving free or reduced rent with no other
compensation, he/she may be entitled to relocation assistance. (See RAC Regulations
920.00, Managers as Tenants.)
2. They are required to evict due to hazardous conditions caused by a natural disaster ,
which is not caused by the landlord's negligence.

3. Relocation Offset: A landlord may offset the tenant's accumulated rent against any
relocation assistance, unless the relocation assistance is owed because a termination of
tenancy is required by a governmental agency order to vacate or comply with an issued
order for an unpermitted dwelling. (LAMC 151.09.G,5., 165.06.J.).

● Single Family Dwellings Owned by Natural Persons  When the residential real property  is
a single-family dwelling subject to the JCO and the owner is a natural person, including
natural  persons who hold properties in a trust or registered legal entity controlled by   that
natural person, who owns no more than four dwelling units and a single-family home on a
separate lot  in the City of Los Angeles: one month’s rent that was in effect when   the
landlord served the written notice to terminate the tenancy, as either a monetary payment
or credit. The Los Angeles Municipal Code Section 151.30(E) shall not apply. (LAMC
165.06.A.(6)).

*Single Family Dwellings that are not lower income may be entitled to one month’s equivalent
of rent for relocation payment depending on various factors. See page 5.

rules.title: Rent restriction for a new tenancy during owner-occupancy periods
rules.requirement: A new tenancy commencing during the periods specified in §98.0704(b)(1)(E) must be offered and rented or leased at the lawful rent in effect when the termination notice was served.
rules.key_value: Lawful rent at service of the termination notice
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: New tenancy begins during referenced 90-day move-in or 12 continuous-month periods following owner-occupancy termination. Offer AND rent at lawful rent in effect when termination notice served; do not use vacancy-date rent selector here. Additional event and branch tests: New tenancy begins during referenced 90-day move-in or 12 continuous-month periods following owner-occupancy termination.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles.

(“Just Cause Required for Termination of Tenancy” added 5-25-2023 by

(Amended 2-27-2024 by O-21769 N.S.; effective 3-28-2024.)

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find

rules.title: Opportunity to cure before termination for a curable lease violation
rules.requirement: Before issuing a just-cause termination notice for a curable lease violation, the owner must first notify the tenant of the violation and provide an opportunity to cure under Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(3). Only if the violation remains uncured within the notice period may the owner then serve a three-day notice to quit without another opportunity to cure.
rules.key_value: Prior cure opportunity; subsequent three-day notice to quit if uncured
rules.coverage_conditions: Curable lease violations in residential tenancies subject to section 1946.2 and its occupancy-duration requirements. This is a procedural prerequisite, not a separate just-cause ground.
rules.exemptions: Section-wide exclusions apply: transient/tourist occupancy; specified hospital/religious/care facilities; institution-owned-and-operated dormitories; resident-owner shared kitchen/bathroom housing; qualifying single-family owner-occupied housing and mobilehomes; qualifying owner-occupied two-unit structures without ADU/JADU units; non-mobilehome housing with a certificate of occupancy within 15 years; qualifying recorded/subsidized affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners; and separately alienable property meeting both owner-type restrictions and prescribed exemption-notice requirements. Qualifying local ordinances displace the section.
rules.quoted_span:
Before an owner of residential real property issues a notice to terminate a tenancy for just cause that is a curable lease violation, the
owner shall first give notice of the violation to the tenant with an opportunity to cure the violation pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

evidence.quote:
Before an owner of residential real property issues a notice to terminate a tenancy for just cause that is a curable lease violation, the
owner shall first give notice of the violation to the tenant with an opportunity to cure the violation pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
If the violation is not cured within the time period set forth in the notice, a three-day notice to quit without an opportunity to cure may thereafter be served to terminate the tenancy.

(k) For the purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply:
(1) “Owner” includes any person, acting as principal or through an agent, having the right to offer residential real property for rent, and includes a predecessor in interest to the owner.
(2) “Residential real property” means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.
(3) “Tenancy” means the lawful occupation of residential real
property and includes a lease or sublease.

(e) This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties or residential circumstances:
(1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940.

(2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in Section 1569.2 of the Health and Safety Code, or an adult residential facility, as defined in Chapter 6 of Division 6 of Title 22 of the Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the State Department of Social Services.
(3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school.
(4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property.

(5) Single-family owner-occupied residences, including both of the following:
(A) A residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms, including, but not limited to, an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.
(B) A mobilehome.

(6) A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner’s principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.

(7) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15
years, unless the housing is a mobilehome.

(8) Residential real property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following apply:
(A) The owner is not any of the following:
(i) A real estate investment trust, as defined in Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code.
(ii) A corporation.
(iii) A limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.
(iv) Management of a mobilehome park, as defined in Section 798.2.
(B) (i) The tenants have been
provided written notice that the residential property is exempt from this section using the following statement:

This property meets the requirements of Sections 1947.12 (d)(5) and 1946.2 (e)(8) of the Civil Code and the owner is not any of the following: (1) a real estate investment trust, as defined by Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code; (2) a corporation; or (3) a limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.”
(ii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for a tenancy existing before July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the
rental agreement.
(II) For a tenancy in a mobilehome existing before July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the rental agreement.
(iii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for any tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) must be provided in the rental agreement.
(II) For any tenancy in a mobilehome commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) shall be provided in the rental agreement.
(iv) Addition of a provision containing the notice required under clause (i) to any new or renewed rental agreement or fixed-term lease constitutes a similar provision for the purposes of subparagraph
(E) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (b).

(9) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement with a government agency, or other recorded document as affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code, or subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code or comparable federal statutes.

(i) (1) This section does not apply to the following residential real property:
(A) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted on or before September 1, 2019, in which case the local ordinance shall apply.
(B) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted or amended after September 1, 2019, that is more protective than this section, in which case the local ordinance shall apply. For purposes of this subparagraph, an ordinance is “more protective” if it meets all of the following criteria:
(i) The just cause for termination of a residential tenancy under the local ordinance is consistent with this section.
(ii) The ordinance further limits the reasons for termination of a residential tenancy, provides for higher relocation assistance amounts, or provides additional tenant protections that are not prohibited by any other provision of law.
(iii) The local government has made a binding finding within their local ordinance that the ordinance is more protective than the provisions of this section.
(2) A residential real property shall not be subject to both a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy and this section.
(3) A local ordinance adopted
after September 1, 2019, that is less protective than this section shall not be enforced unless this section is repealed.

rules.title: Criminal-history inquiries and housing discrimination prohibited
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not inquire into criminal history; require its disclosure or authorization for its release; advertise or state that people with criminal backgrounds will not be considered; refuse to rent, demand higher rent, or otherwise treat applicants or tenants differently because of criminal history; refuse an immediate family member's addition because of that member's history; or disqualify tenants from rental assistance on that basis, subject to the listed exceptions.
rules.key_value: Criminal-history screening and discrimination prohibited, subject to exemptions
rules.coverage_conditions: Current and prospective tenants of Berkeley rental housing; advertising, application materials, verbal statements, tenant selection, and housing decision-making. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Berkeley current/prospective rental tenants and provider decisions involving criminal history. Investigate listed exemptions rather than treating them as fully specified: lifetime sex offenders; limited public/Section 8 cases; owner-occupied 1–3-unit property with owner of record residing as primary residence; BMC 13.76.130 A.9 owner-return agreement; existing tenants subletting or adding/replacing roommates. Obtain specific requirements before deciding a claimed exemption.

The guide directs readers to the ordinance for each exemption's specific requirements.

When a tenant vacates a dwelling unit after having been given notice that the  landlord 
wishes to personally occupy the unit the landlord must occupy the unit for at least six (6) months. 
If instead the landlord permits personal occupancy of the unit by another tenant or registration of 
conversion of the property to a condominium or cooperative, the landlord is liable to the former

rules.title: Delayed public subsistence or rental payments protect a tenancy at will during a continuance
rules.requirement: If nonpayment was caused by failure or delay in mailing or delivering a qualifying public subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue a possession hearing for at least seven days to notify the appropriate agency. If all rent due, interest, and suit costs are tendered to the landlord within that time, the court must treat the tenancy as not terminated.
rules.key_value: Hearing continuance of at least 7 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenancy at will; causative failure or delay by the federal government, the commonwealth, a municipality, or their departments, agencies, or authorities in mailing or delivering a subsistence or rental payment, check, or voucher to tenant or landlord.
rules.exemptions: Salary payments are excluded; nontermination requires tender of all rent due with interest and costs of suit within the continuance.
rules.interaction: This is an additional conditional protection for delayed public payments, not a replacement of the ordinary notice and cure provisions.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot contains this provision with no pending or future-version label; its original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The organizer eviction category is used for termination and possession procedures; this provision does not itself establish a general just-cause requirement.
rules.quoted_span: Section 12. Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing for that purpose given to the other party; and, if the rent reserved is payable at periods of less than three months, the time of such notice shall be sufficient if it is equal to the interval between the days of payment or thirty days, whichever is longer. Such written notice may include an offer to establish a new tenancy for the same premises on terms different from that of the tenancy being terminated and the validity of such written notice shall not be affected by the inclusion of such offer. In case of neglect or refusal to pay the rent due from a tenant at will, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the tenancy; provided, that the tenancy of a tenant who has not received a similar notice from the landlord within the twelve months next preceding the receipt of such notice shall not be determined if the tenant, within ten days after the receipt thereof, pays or tenders to the landlord, the landlord's attorney, or the person to whom the tenant customarily pays rent, the full amount of any rent due. Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent shall contain the following notification to the tenant: ''If you have not received a notice to quit for nonpayment of rent within the last twelve months, you have a right to prevent termination of your tenancy by paying or tendering to your landlord, your landlord's attorney or the person to whom you customarily pay your rent the full amount of rent due within ten days after your receipt of this notice.'' If any notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent shall fail to contain such notification, the time within which the tenant receiving the notice would be entitled to pay or tender rent pursuant to this section shall be extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises. Failure to include such notice shall not otherwise affect the validity of the said notice. If the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due was caused by a failure or delay of the federal government, the commonwealth or any municipality, or any departments, agencies or authorities thereof, in the mailing or delivery of any subsistence or rental payment, check or voucher other than a salary payment to either the tenant or the landlord, the court in any action for possession shall continue the hearing not less than seven days in order to furnish notice of such action to the appropriate agency and shall, if all rent due with interest and costs of suit has been tendered to the landlord within such time, treat the tenancy as not having been terminated.

evidence.quote: Jersey City Code § 218-12 (effective June 2025)
Prohibits a landlord’s use of algorithmic rent coordination services; includes public and private enforcement; fines up to $2,000 per day.

Jersey City, NJ
Jersey City Code § 218-12 (effective June 2025)
Prohibits a landlord’s use of algorithmic rent coordination services; includes public and private enforcement; fines up to $2,000 per day.

WHAT THE NEW MUNICIPAL LAWS MEAN FOR EXISTING COMPLIANCE MEASURES
The new municipal cases and new regulations arise against an important backdrop: the multifamily housing industry and revenue-management vendors have already made significant changes in response to the various investigations and related legislation. Government settlements with several major property managers restrict the use of revenue-management software that relies on competitors' nonpublic information to generate rent recommendations, and various software providers have modified products to eliminate or restrict the use of competitors' nonpublic data in generating pricing recommendations. The federal government's resolution with RealPage likewise requires significant restrictions on the use of competitors' nonpublic, competitively sensitive information.
Those changes may materially reduce prospective risk under many of the new municipal ordinances, but they do not necessarily eliminate litigation over past conduct. Several local laws became effective, many prohibiting use of coordination services or software even if secured prior to the effective date of the law, while landlords and software providers were still modifying their practices, and some ordinances treat each affected unit and each month of prohibited use as a separate violation. The date on which a particular product or property ceased using prohibited data therefore becomes a critical issue in determining both liability and the scope of any putative class.
The municipal laws also place a premium on property-level documentation of software functionality. Owners and managers should be able to identify, for each covered jurisdiction, which revenue-management products were used, when relevant functionality was enabled or disabled, what data sources generated recommendations, and whether recommendations continued to rely on competitors' nonpublic information after a local prohibition became effective. Vendor representations that a product has been modified should be documented and tested against the definitions in the applicable ordinance rather than assumed to resolve compliance across jurisdictions.
These issues may also provide important defenses. A plaintiff's allegation that a landlord subscribed to RealPage, Yardi, or another revenue-management platform does not necessarily establish that every property used prohibited functionality throughout the proposed class period. Product versions, configuration changes, data sources, and effective dates may determine whether—and for how long—a particular local prohibition was implicated.
WHAT OWNERS AND PROPERTY MANAGERS SHOULD BE DOING
Owners and property managers should consider several immediate steps to understand and mitigate municipal regulation risk:
Create an ordinance-effective-date matrix: For every affected property, match the ordinance's effective date against the dates the pricing product and particular data functionality were used.
Test the ordinance's exclusions rather than relying on an “antitrust compliant” label: A product may satisfy a federal consent decree but still need to be assessed separately against a city's definition of “algorithmic device,” “coordinating service,” prohibited data, or permitted historical/public-data reporting.

rules.title: No blanket exclusion of applicants with criminal histories
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not maintain a blanket ban on all people with a criminal history.
rules.key_value: Blanket criminal-history bans prohibited
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing-provider rental screening policies.
rules.exemptions: The guidance permits criminal-history checks and qualifying conviction-based decisions subject to its separate restrictions.
rules.quoted_span: Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.
rules.temporal_notes: No operative date is stated.
limitations: No statutory section or criminal-history-specific coverage exceptions are supplied.

evidence.quote: Generally, a housing provider may check the criminal history of an applicant, but there are some limitations.
Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.

If a housing provider intends to deny someone’s application based on a criminal conviction, it must be directly-related to someone’s ability to be a good tenant and to not be a threat to the health and safety of others and the property.

What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

Can a housing provider consider an applicant’s criminal history in deciding whether or not to rent to them?
Yes.  Generally, a housing provider may check the criminal history of an applicant, but there are some limitations. Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system. Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.
If a housing provider intends to deny someone’s application based on a criminal conviction, it must be directly-related to someone’s ability to be a good tenant and to not be a threat to the health and safety of others and the property. In determining whether a criminal conviction is directly-related, a housing provider should consider the nature and severity of the crime and the amount of time that has passed since the criminal conduct occurred.

rules.title: Clear and convincing proof is required to rebut the reprisal presumption
rules.requirement: The presumption may be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that the action was not a reprisal, had sufficient independent justification, and would have occurred in the same manner and at the same time regardless of protected tenant activity or the belief that tenants engaged in it.
rules.key_value: Clear and convincing evidence; all specified rebuttal elements
rules.coverage_conditions: Receipt of a tenancy-termination notice other than for nonpayment, a rent-increase notice, or notice of a substantial alteration of tenancy terms within six months after the tenant commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in the described action, exercised the described rights, made the described report or complaint, or organized or joined a tenants' union. The paragraph also covers the six months after another person takes such action for the tenant or in or relating to the tenant's building.
rules.exemptions: The presumption's termination-notice branch excludes nonpayment of rent.
rules.interaction: Applies when the preceding six-month presumption arises, including its rent-increase branch; it is not described as the burden governing every retaliation claim.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot presents the provision without a pending or future-version label; the original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The presumption paragraph does not expressly repeat the unit-owner rent-payment activity listed in the underlying liability paragraph.
rules.quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities. Such presumption shall be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that such person's action was not a reprisal against the tenant and that such person had sufficient independent justification for taking such action, and would have in fact taken such action, in the same manner and at the same time the action was taken, regardless of tenants engaging in, or the belief that tenants had engaged in, activities protected under this section.

rules.title: Higher security deposits based on criminal history prohibited
rules.requirement: Do not demand a higher security deposit from a current or prospective tenant based on criminal history, subject to the listed exemptions.
rules.key_value: No criminal-history-based deposit surcharge
rules.coverage_conditions: Current and prospective tenants in covered Berkeley rental housing. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Berkeley current/prospective rental tenants and provider decisions involving criminal history. Investigate listed exemptions rather than treating them as fully specified: lifetime sex offenders; limited public/Section 8 cases; owner-occupied 1–3-unit property with owner of record residing as primary residence; BMC 13.76.130 A.9 owner-return agreement; existing tenants subletting or adding/replacing roommates. Obtain specific requirements before deciding a claimed exemption.
rules.exemptions: Listed exemptions concern lifetime sex offenders; limited public housing/Section 8 circumstances; owner-occupied properties of 1–3 units with an owner of record residing in one unit as a primary residence; owner-return agreements under BMC 13.76.130 A.9; and existing tenants seeking to sublet or add/replace roommates. The guide does not supply each exemption's requirements.

rules.penalty: Administrative fines of $1,000–$10,000 per violation; civil damages including actual damages or three times one month's rent; punitive damages; attorney’s fees and costs; and injunctive relief.
limitations: This rule does not establish a general numerical deposit cap.

rules.title: No deposit demand exceeding the statutory amount after commencement
rules.requirement: After tenancy commencement, neither the landlord nor its successor may demand a security deposit exceeding the amount allowed by section 15B.
rules.key_value: Statutory deposit amount remains controlling after commencement
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenancies after commencement, including demands by a successor in interest; the allowed deposit amount and prerequisites are set out in subsection (1)(b)(iii).
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: The same paragraph separately regulates advance rent and binds successors to advance occupancy payments; those independent upfront-payment duties are extracted under application_screening_fees rather than relabeled as deposits.

Landlords may use screening fees to obtain information about a prospective tenant like a consumer credit report. Prospective tenants should expect to receive a copy of their credit report within 7 days of receipt by the landlord, a receipt for the fee paid and an itemized list of any out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord on the screening, and a refund of any unused portion of the fee. If the tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.

(d) The landlord or their agent shall provide, personally, or by mail, the applicant with a receipt for the fee paid by the applicant, which receipt shall itemize the out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord or their agent to obtain and process the information about the applicant. The landlord or their agent and the applicant may agree to have the landlord provide a copy of the receipt for the fee paid by the applicant to an email account provided by the applicant.
(e) If the landlord or their agent does
not perform a personal reference check or does not obtain a consumer credit report, the landlord or their agent shall return any amount of the screening fee that is not used for the purposes authorized by this section to the applicant.

rules.title: Permitted upfront payments restrict additional landlord or agent fees
rules.requirement: Before or at tenancy commencement, a landlord or its agent may not require payments to the landlord or its agent beyond the enumerated first-month rent, last-month rent at the same rate, allowed security deposit, and key-and-lock purchase and installation cost. The exhaustive list limits additional required application or screening charges by these actors.
rules.key_value: Only the enumerated upfront payments
rules.coverage_conditions: Payments required from a tenant or prospective tenant at or before tenancy commencement to the lessor or an agent of the lessor. The deposit item is bounded by subsection (1)(b)(iii) and its required account and condition statement.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required. The list permits first full month rent; last full month rent at the first-month rate; a deposit up to first-month rent with the statutory conditions; and actual purchase and installation cost for a key and lock. The separate fee-in-lieu language authorizes regulations rather than proving an implemented fee program.
rules.interaction: The current introductory paragraph expressly includes agents and payment recipients; the deposit-specific conditions remain attached to the deposit rules.
rules.temporal_notes: The introductory paragraph at lines 29-30 expressly takes effect August 1, 2025. The prior introductory text at lines 27-28 is historical as of 2026-10-01 and is retained in the review queue rather than exported as concurrently in force.
limitations: This record addresses fees required by the landlord or its agent; it does not resolve independently hired brokers or the contents of other statutes.
Application and screening fees are classified through the restriction on additional required upfront amounts, not because those fee names appear in this paragraph.
rules.quoted_span:
(b) At or prior to the commencement of any tenancy, no lessor or agent of the lessor may require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay, to the lessor or to an agent of the lessor, any amount in excess of the following:
(i) rent for the first full month of occupancy;  and,
(ii) rent for the last full month of occupancy calculated at the same rate as the first month;  and,
(iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2);  provided, however, that the executive office of housing and livable communities may promulgate regulations to authorize a lessor and a tenant or prospective tenant to agree to the payment of a fee in lieu of payment of a security deposit;  provided further, that any such regulations shall:  (A) require the lessor to utilize a fee collected to waive a security deposit to cover for unpaid rent or unit damage that applies to the tenant's lease;  (B) require that a fee so collected be:  (I) entirely or partially non-refundable;  provided, however, that the lessor shall disclose that the fee is non-refundable in the lease;  provided further, that the tenant shall agree to the fee and acknowledge that the tenant understand that it is entirely or partially non-refundable, as the case may be, in writing;  and (II) a recurring monthly fee, or payable upon any schedule and in an amount that the lessor and tenant agree upon, as authorized by the executive office;  (C) limit the total sum of the fee or recurring payments, regardless of the duration of the lease and any extensions thereto, to an amount not to exceed 1 month's rent;  (D) require that the fee be made optional for both the tenant and the lessor and that the tenant be permitted to choose to pay a full security deposit rather than the fee;  (E) require a lessor who offers such a fee in lieu of security deposit:  (I) to offer the option of a fee in lieu of a security deposit to every prospective tenant whose application for occupancy has been approved, regardless of income, race, gender, gender identity, disability, sexual orientation, immigration status, size of household or credit score;  and (II) not to consider such factors and categories when setting the amount of the fee;  and (F) allow a tenant who agrees to pay a fee to waive a security deposit to opt-out of the obligation to pay such fee if such tenant pays the security deposit that would otherwise be in effect for the tenant's apartment on the day the tenant chooses to opt-out of such fee;  provided further, that the sum of fees paid to waive a security deposit and the payment of the security deposit shall not exceed, in total, the amount of 1 month's rent;  and provided further, that the executive office shall consult with the office of the attorney general prior to promulgating regulations authorizing a fee in lieu of a security deposit under this section;  and,
(iv) the purchase and installation cost for a key and lock.

rules.title: Conditional-offer or housing remedy for a repeat violation
rules.requirement: Upon finding a violation and at least one other violation within the preceding five years, the director may require a good-faith effort to remedy the applicant's injury when possible: issue a conditional offer if the violation prevented one, or provide the same or a similar unit on the prior offer's terms if the violation caused withdrawal and such a unit is or will become available.
rules.key_value: At least one other violation within the preceding 5 years
rules.coverage_conditions: Covered housing providers with the specified repeat-violation history; relief depends on a director's order, possibility of a remedy, the type of violation, and, for provision of housing, present or future availability of the same or a similar unit.
rules.exemptions: Units in owner-occupied premises with no more than four dwelling units are excluded. The remedy is discretionary and requires good-faith effort when possible, not unconditional provision of unavailable housing.
rules.quoted_span:
If a housing provider has committed at least one
other violation of this act within the preceding five-year period, the director
may require the housing provider to make a good faith effort to remedy the
violation with respect to the applicant when a remedy is possible, by issuing a
conditional offer, if the violation has resulted in a failure to issue a
conditional offer, or by providing the same or a similar rental dwelling unit
to the applicant on the same terms as the prior conditional offer if the same
or a similar rental dwelling unit is currently or will become available, if the
violation has resulted in the withdrawal of a conditional offer.
rules.interaction:
A successful appeal reversing the underlying finding can trigger the distinct eviction provision in the same paragraph.

rules.title: Illegal-occupancy relocation payment and collection rights
rules.requirement: A tenant removed for illegal occupancy is entitled to landlord-paid relocation assistance equal to six times monthly rent. If not paid at least five days before removal, payment may come from an established municipal revolving fund, repayable by the landlord. If no fund exists and the landlord misses payment, 18% annual interest accrues until full payment; the debt is a property lien enforceable by filing a lien statement.

rules.title: Rental agreements may not characterize security as nonrefundable
rules.requirement: A lease or rental agreement must not contain a provision characterizing any security as nonrefundable.
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential leases and rental agreements within the section's scope, using the statutory definition of security in subdivision (b), including its exception cross-reference to section 1950.6.
rules.interaction: The prohibition applies to statutory security; it does not reclassify every separately governed fee as security.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset is unspecified; supplied version amendment effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: The referenced treatment of fees under section 1950.6 is not independently resolved by D025.
rules.quoted_span: (n) A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security as “nonrefundable.”

quoted_span_location.quote: (n) A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security as “nonrefundable.”

evidence.quote:
(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:
(1) The compensation of a landlord for a
tenant’s default in the payment of rent.
(2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.
(3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. The amendments to this paragraph enacted by the act adding this sentence shall apply only to tenancies for which the tenant’s right to occupy begins after January 1, 2003.
(4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the
security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.
(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340, Sec. 1.   (AB 414)   Effective January 1, 2026.)

(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:
(1) The compensation of a landlord for a
tenant’s default in the payment of rent.
(2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.
(3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. The amendments to this paragraph enacted by the act adding this sentence shall apply only to tenancies for which the tenant’s right to occupy begins after January 1, 2003.
(4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the
security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

(h) As used in this section, “landlord” means an owner of residential rental property.
(i) As used in
this section, “application screening fee” means any nonrefundable payment of money charged by a landlord or their agent to an applicant, the purpose of which is to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application for the rent or lease of residential rental property.
(j) As used in this section, “applicant” means any entity or individual who makes a request to a landlord or their agent to rent a residential housing unit, or an entity or individual who agrees to act as a guarantor or cosignor on a rental agreement.
(k) The application screening fee shall not be considered an “advance fee” as that term is used in Section 10026 of the Business and Professions Code, and shall not be considered “security” as that term is used in Section 1950.5.
(n) A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security as “nonrefundable.”

rules.title: Timely tenant documentation request overrides small-charge and waiver exceptions
rules.requirement: If the tenant requests documentation within 14 calendar days after receiving the paragraph (h)(1) itemized statement, the landlord must comply with paragraphs (h)(2)-(3) within 14 calendar days after receiving that request despite the paragraph (4) exceptions.
rules.key_value: Tenant request within 14 calendar days; landlord compliance within 14 calendar days
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenants who received the paragraph (h)(1) statement and timely request supporting documentation, including where the repair and cleaning deductions total $125 or less or the tenant previously signed the qualifying waiver. Compliance concerns supporting work, cost, and photograph documentation and the paragraph (3) accounting requirements.
rules.interaction: Expressly overrides paragraph (h)(4)'s exception for small deductions and its signed-waiver exception.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset not stated; supplied version amendment effective 2026-01-01.

(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:

(h) (1) No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, but not earlier than the time that either the landlord or the tenant provides a notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1, Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or not earlier than 60 calendar days prior to
the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant as follows:

(2) The landlord shall also include, along with and at the same time the itemized statement is sent, copies of documents showing charges incurred and deducted by
the landlord to repair or clean the premises, as follows:
(A) If the landlord or landlord’s employee did the work, the itemized statement shall reasonably describe the work performed. The itemized statement shall include the time spent and the reasonable hourly rate charged.
(B) If the landlord or landlord’s employee did not do the work, the landlord shall provide the tenant a copy of the bill, invoice, or receipt supplied by the person or entity performing the work. The itemized statement shall provide the tenant with the name, address, and telephone number of the person or entity, if the bill, invoice, or receipt does not include that information.
(C) If a deduction is made for materials or supplies, the landlord shall
provide a copy of the bill, invoice, or receipt. If a particular material or supply item is purchased by the landlord on an ongoing basis, the landlord may document the cost of the item by providing a copy of a bill, invoice, receipt, vendor price list, or other vendor document that reasonably documents the cost of the item used in the repair or cleaning of the unit.
(D) If a deduction is made for repairs or cleanings allowed by this section, the landlord shall provide photographs taken pursuant to subdivision (g), along with a written explanation of the cost of the allowable repairs or cleanings, as described in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive. The landlord may provide such photographs to the tenant by mail, email, computer flash drive, or by providing a link where the tenant may view the photographs online.
(3) If a repair to be done by the landlord or the landlord’s employee cannot reasonably be completed within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, or if the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord’s possession within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord may deduct the amount of a good faith estimate of the charges that will be incurred and provide that estimate with the itemized statement. If the reason for the estimate is because the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord’s possession, the itemized statement shall include the name, address, and telephone number of the person or entity. Within 14 calendar days of completing the repair or receiving the documentation,
the landlord shall complete the requirements in paragraphs (1) and (2) in the manner specified.
(4) The landlord need not comply with paragraph (2) or (3) if either of the following applies:
(A) The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).
(B) The tenant waived the rights specified in paragraphs (2) and (3). The waiver shall only be effective if it is signed by the tenant at the same time or after a notice to terminate a tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1 has been given, a notice under Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been given, or no earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease. The waiver shall
substantially include the text of paragraph (2).

rules.title: Permissible deposit deductions and cleaning restrictions
rules.requirement: Deduct only amounts reasonably necessary for rent default; tenant- or guest-caused damage beyond normal wear and tear; cleaning to the initial cleanliness level for tenancies beginning after January 1, 2003; or, if the lease allows it, restoring or replacing personal property, keys, or furniture beyond ordinary wear and tear. Do not require payment or assert claims against the tenant or deposit for professional carpet or other professional cleaning unless reasonably necessary to restore the initial condition minus ordinary wear and tear.
rules.key_value: Reasonably necessary amounts only
rules.coverage_conditions: Security-deposit deductions and professional-cleaning claims. The listed cleaning-to-initial-cleanliness purpose expressly concerns tenancies beginning after January 1, 2003. Personal-property or furniture restoration/replacement additionally requires lease authorization.
rules.exemptions: Normal or ordinary wear and tear is excluded from the specified damage, personal-property, and professional-cleaning charges. Professional cleaning is permitted only under the stated reasonable-necessity standard.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord may deduct only the amount that is reasonably necessary to:
Cover rent default
Repair damages caused by a tenant or a tenant's guest other than normal wear and tear
Clean the unit to return it to the same level of cleanliness as at the start of the tenancy (for tenancies beginning after January 1, 2003)
If allowed by the lease, cover the cost of restoring or replacing personal property (including keys) or furniture, excluding ordinary wear and tear
rules.interaction: The professional-cleaning restriction also limits direct claims against the tenant, not only withholding from the deposit.
rules.temporal_notes: The cleaning deduction's tenancy-start condition is strictly 'after January 1, 2003'; it is not treated as the operative date of every deduction restriction.
limitations: No statutory section is supplied; citation uses the official guidance title.
Treatment of the listed cleaning deduction for earlier tenancies is not explained.

rules.title: Prohibition on obtaining a coordinator's services
rules.requirement: A rental property owner, or its agent, representative, or subcontractor, may not receive, subscribe to, contract for, or otherwise exchange any form of consideration for use of a coordinator's services.
rules.coverage_conditions: A rental property owner directly or indirectly owns one or more residential rental units; a person with a controlling interest and the entity owning a unit count as one owner. Covered units are houses, apartments, accessory units, or other units intended as primary residences in New Jersey. A coordinator operates algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function, including an owner acting for its own benefit. A coordinating function means: collecting two or more owners' competitively sensitive information for algorithmic or automated analysis or training used to set or recommend rent, material lease terms, or occupancy; setting those matters through analysis, processing, or training using another owner's competitively sensitive information; OR setting or recommending those matters for two or more owners through the same or substantially similar algorithm or automated process facilitating parallel pricing coordination. Competitively sensitive information is nonpublic and includes prices, supply, security deposits, ideal occupancy, lease termination, renewal dates, and other material lease terms. Information unavailable publicly at no cost is nonpublic; combining it with public information makes the entire combination nonpublic. Parallel pricing coordination requires a tacit or express agreement to raise, change, maintain, or manipulate leasing prices of reasonably interchangeable residential units, including coordinator agreements with multiple owners. Tacit consent can exist without verbal or written communication and need not be demonstrated by a conduct pattern.
rules.exemptions: Residential units exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. Algorithmic devices exclude spreadsheets that both operate without artificial intelligence and require human analysis to process or calculate data, and databases using an algorithm only to query stored unprocessed data. Coordinating functions exclude: use, provision, or collection of competitively sensitive information solely for research, statistical analysis, or testing when it is not used to set or recommend prices, material lease terms, fees, occupancy rates or levels, or other current or future lease terms; rent estimates publicly available at no cost; real estate brokerage databases equally available to subscribers that list properties but neither set or recommend rent, material lease terms, or occupancy nor collect competitively sensitive information for those purposes; and lawful government affordability controls. Government entities lawfully setting or limiting residential rents or sale prices through affordability controls are not coordinators. Parallel pricing coordination excludes action required by affordability controls. Affordability controls are government-program rent restrictions, including the specified federal Section 8 homeownership program, State housing programs, NJ Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency programs, local rent control or leveling, and other government housing programs.
rules.citation: P.L. 2026, c.43, §4(a) (Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act)
rules.interaction: Section 4 violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; section 5 preserves application of C.56:9-6 through 9-17. Section 6 makes the Act additional to existing law and does not authorize already unlawful conduct. Municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances, subject to ordinances explicitly authorized or required by other law. No particular municipal ordinance is identified as conflicting or repealed.

rules.title: Return screening fees unused for authorized purposes
rules.requirement: If the landlord or agent does not perform a personal reference check or does not obtain a consumer credit report, they must return to the applicant any screening-fee amount not used for purposes authorized by the section.

rules.coverage_conditions: Residential owners or agents holding application screening fees paid by an applicant, including a guarantor or cosignor. rules.exemptions: This section does not preempt provisions on deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.

rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset is unspecified; footer amendment effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: The supplied subsection states no separate numerical deadline for returning the unused amount.

evidence.quote:
(a) Notwithstanding Section 1950.5, when a landlord or their agent receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant, the landlord or their agent may charge, pursuant to subdivision (c), that applicant an application screening fee to cover the costs of obtaining information about the applicant. The information requested and obtained by the landlord or their agent may include, but is not limited to, personal reference checks and consumer credit reports produced by consumer credit reporting agencies as defined in Section 1785.3. A landlord or their agent may, but is not required to, accept and rely upon a consumer credit report presented by an applicant.
(b) The amount of the application screening fee shall not be greater than the actual
out-of-pocket costs of gathering information concerning the applicant, including, but not limited to, the cost of using a tenant screening service or a consumer credit reporting service, and the reasonable value of time spent by the landlord or their agent in obtaining information on the applicant. In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

(h) As used in this section, “landlord” means an owner of residential rental property.
(i) As used in
this section, “application screening fee” means any nonrefundable payment of money charged by a landlord or their agent to an applicant, the purpose of which is to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application for the rent or lease of residential rental property.
(j) As used in this section, “applicant” means any entity or individual who makes a request to a landlord or their agent to rent a residential housing unit, or an entity or individual who agrees to act as a guarantor or cosignor on a rental agreement.

(iv) Clause (iii) shall not be considered violated if a landlord or their agent inadvertently collects an application screening fee from an applicant as the result of multiple concurrent application submissions, provided that the landlord or their agent issues a refund of the application screening fee within seven days to any applicant whose application is not considered. The landlord may offer, as an alternative to refunding the screening fee, the option, at the applicant’s discretion, for the screening fee paid by the applicant to be applied to an application for another rental unit offered by the landlord. A landlord or their agent shall not be required to refund an application screening fee to an applicant whose application is denied, after consideration, because the applicant does not meet the landlord’s established screening criteria.

(l) This section is not intended
to preempt any provisions or regulations that govern the collection of deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67, Sec. 29.   (AB 1170)   Effective January 1, 2026.)

rules.title: Required relationship between a criminal conviction and rental suitability
rules.requirement: A conviction used to deny a rental application must be directly related to the applicant's ability to be a good tenant and not threaten others' health and safety or property. In assessing that relationship, the guidance says providers should consider the crime's nature and severity and the time since the conduct.
rules.key_value: Direct relationship to tenancy suitability and safety
rules.coverage_conditions: Triggered when a housing provider intends to deny an application based on a criminal conviction.
rules.exemptions: The separate prohibitions on considering sealed, expunged, and juvenile-justice records still limit which records may be used.
rules.quoted_span: If a housing provider intends to deny someone’s application based on a criminal conviction, it must be directly-related to someone’s ability to be a good tenant and to not be a threat to the health and safety of others and the property. In determining whether a criminal conviction is directly-related, a housing provider should consider the nature and severity of the crime and the amount of time that has passed since the criminal conduct occurred.

conditions.description: The direct-relationship requirement governs conviction-based application denials.

If a housing provider intends to deny someone’s application based on a criminal conviction, it must be directly-related to someone’s ability to be a good tenant and to not be a threat to the health and safety of others and the property. In determining whether a criminal conviction is directly-related, a housing provider should consider the nature and severity of the crime and the amount of time that has passed since the criminal conduct occurred.

What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

If a housing provider intends to deny someone’s application based on a criminal conviction, it must be directly-related to someone’s ability to be a good tenant and to not be a threat to the health and safety of others and the property. In determining whether a criminal conviction is directly-related, a housing provider should consider the nature and severity of the crime and the amount of time that has passed since the criminal conduct occurred.

Yes.  Generally, a housing provider may check the criminal history of an applicant, but there are some limitations. Housing  providers cannot consider some types of criminal history including arrests that did not lead to a conviction, records that are sealed or expunged, or records or matters processed in the juvenile justice system. Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.

sources.title: California Civil Rights Department: Housing
sources.quote: California law protects individuals from illegal discrimination and harassment by housing providers based on certain protected characteristics

rules.title: Criminal-record inquiries before a conditional offer
rules.requirement: A housing provider must not require a housing application containing criminal-record inquiries before a conditional offer and must not make oral or written criminal-record inquiries before that offer. Section 4(a)(1) expressly permits consideration of specified methamphetamine convictions and lifetime sex-offender registration. Apply the application-process standards nondiscriminatorily.
rules.key_value: Conditional offer before criminal-record inquiry, subject to specified exceptions
rules.coverage_conditions: Applicants for residential rental dwelling units. Housing providers include landlords, owners, lessors, sublessors, assignees, agents, and others receiving or entitled to rents or occupancy benefits. A conditional offer may depend on a subsequent criminal-record inquiry or other lawful eligibility criteria.
rules.exemptions: Units in owner-occupied premises containing no more than four dwelling units are excluded from the Act. Section 4(a)(1) permits consideration of conviction for drug-related manufacture or production of methamphetamine on federally assisted housing premises and lifetime registration under a State sex-offender registration program.
rules.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.
rules.interaction: Section 4(a)(1) expressly states exceptions; the adjacent oral-or-written-inquiry prohibition in section 4(a)(2) does not repeat them. Both formulations are preserved here. Act-wide enforcement is addressed in C.46:8-63.

conditions.description: The inquiry restrictions govern the period before a conditional offer.

rules.temporal_notes: Section 14 specifies the first day of the seventh month following enactment. Approval on June 18, 2021 makes July the first following month and January 2022 the seventh. Anticipatory administrative action was permitted earlier.
limitations: The supplied text does not further explain how the exceptions in section 4(a)(1) operate alongside section 4(a)(2).

“Conditional offer” means an offer to rent or lease a

to receive rents or benefits for the use or occupancy of any rental dwelling
unit.

“Rental dwelling unit” means a dwelling unit offered
for rent by a housing provider for residential purposes,
other than a dwelling unit in an
owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.

A

complete any housing application that includes any inquiries regarding an
applicant’s criminal record prior to the provision of a conditional offer,
except that a housing provider may consider whether an applicant has ever been
convicted of drug-related criminal activity for the manufacture or production
of methamphetamine on the premises of federally assisted housing, and whether
the applicant is subject to a lifetime registration requirement under a State
sex offender registration program.

A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

A housing provider
shall apply the standards established by this section to each applicant in a

information about an individual collected by criminal justice agencies

rules.title: Just cause required for fully and partially covered units
rules.requirement: Tenants in fully or partially covered units may be evicted only for just cause.
rules.key_value: Just cause required
rules.coverage_conditions: Units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, including government-owned or subsidized units classified into either coverage tier by Measure BB. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.
rules.exemptions: Units exempt from the Rent Ordinance are outside this stated requirement. For shared-kitchen or shared-bath housing, the exemption applies only when the landlord lived in a unit on the same property at the start of the tenancy. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.

rules.interaction: Partial coverage can preserve just-cause protection even when a unit is exempt from local rent control.
