rules.title: Rights disclosure for mobilehome tenancies commenced or renewed from July 1, 2022
rules.requirement: For a covered mobilehome tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, provide the prescribed rent-limit and just-cause disclosure as a lease/rental-agreement addendum or a written notice signed by the tenant, with a copy provided to the tenant. The disclosure must be at least 12-point type and is subject to section 1632.
rules.key_value: Commencement or renewal on or after July 1, 2022; at least 12-point type
rules.coverage_conditions: Rented mobilehome tenancies subject to section 1946.2; the section expressly excludes a mobilehome homeowner under section 798.9.
rules.exemptions: Section-wide exclusions remain applicable where their facts are met, including owner-occupied mobilehomes; resident-owner shared kitchen/bathroom housing; specified institutional, transient, and affordable housing; and separately alienable mobilehomes with the prescribed exemption notice and an owner who is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome-park management. The certificate-of-occupancy-within-15-years exclusion expressly does not cover mobilehomes. Qualifying local just-cause ordinances displace the section.
rules.quoted_span: For a tenancy in a mobilehome commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, as an addendum to the lease or rental agreement, or as a written notice signed by the tenant, with a copy provided to the tenant.
rules.interaction: Procedural disclosure referencing section 1947.12 and subject to section 1632. Unlike the non-mobilehome clause, this clause lists an addendum or signed notice rather than a provision within the original agreement.
rules.temporal_notes: Current section operative April 1, 2024, with a July 1, 2022 commencement/renewal applicability trigger. Supplied version amended effective January 1, 2026; repealed January 1, 2030. Original enactment of this disclosure is not separately established.
rules.penalty: Subdivision (g) makes a written termination notice void for noncompliance with the section.
limitations: The incorporated section 1632 and mobilehome-homeowner definitions are not supplied.

evidence.quote: An owner of residential real property subject to this section shall provide notice to the tenant as follows:

For a tenancy in a mobilehome commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, as an addendum to the lease or rental agreement, or as a written notice signed by the tenant, with a copy provided to the tenant.

The notification or lease provision shall be in no less than 12-point type, and shall include the following:
“California law limits the amount your rent can be increased. See Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code for more information. California law also provides that after all of the tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 12 months or more or at least one of the tenants has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 24 months or more, a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy. See Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code for more information.”
The notification or lease provision shall be subject to Section 1632.
(l) This section shall not apply to a homeowner of a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.9.

(k) For the purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply:
(1) “Owner” includes any person, acting as principal or through an agent, having the right to offer residential real property for rent, and includes a predecessor in interest to the owner.
(2) “Residential real property” means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.
(3) “Tenancy” means the lawful occupation of residential real
property and includes a lease or sublease.

(e) This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties or residential circumstances:
(1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940.

(2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in Section 1569.2 of the Health and Safety Code, or an adult residential facility, as defined in Chapter 6 of Division 6 of Title 22 of the Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the State Department of Social Services.
(3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school.
(4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property.

(A) A residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms, including, but not limited to, an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.

(6) A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner’s principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.

(7) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15
years, unless the housing is a mobilehome.

(8) Residential real property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following apply:
(A) The owner is not any of the following:
(i) A real estate investment trust, as defined in Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code.
(ii) A corporation.
(iii) A limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.
(iv) Management of a mobilehome park, as defined in Section 798.2.
(B) (i) The tenants have been
provided written notice that the residential property is exempt from this section using the following statement:
“This property is not subject to the rent limits imposed by Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code and is not subject to the just cause requirements of Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code. This property meets the requirements of Sections 1947.12 (d)(5) and 1946.2 (e)(8) of the Civil Code and the owner is not any of the following: (1) a real estate investment trust, as defined by Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code; (2) a corporation; or (3) a limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.”
(ii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for a tenancy existing before July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the
rental agreement.
(II) For a tenancy in a mobilehome existing before July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the rental agreement.
(iii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for any tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) must be provided in the rental agreement.
(II) For any tenancy in a mobilehome commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) shall be provided in the rental agreement.
(iv) Addition of a provision containing the notice required under clause (i) to any new or renewed rental agreement or fixed-term lease constitutes a similar provision for the purposes of subparagraph
(E) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (b).

(9) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement with a government agency, or other recorded document as affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code, or subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code or comparable federal statutes.

(i) (1) This section does not apply to the following residential real property:
(A) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted on or before September 1, 2019, in which case the local ordinance shall apply.
(B) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted or amended after September 1, 2019, that is more protective than this section, in which case the local ordinance shall apply. For purposes of this subparagraph, an ordinance is “more protective” if it meets all of the following criteria:
(i) The just cause for termination of a residential tenancy under the local ordinance is consistent with this section.
(ii) The ordinance further limits the reasons for termination of a residential tenancy, provides for higher relocation assistance amounts, or provides additional tenant protections that are not prohibited by any other provision of law.
(iii) The local government has made a binding finding within their local ordinance that the ordinance is more protective than the provisions of this section.
(2) A residential real property shall not be subject to both a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy and this section.

(B) For a tenancy in a mobilehome commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, as an addendum to the lease or rental agreement, or as a written notice signed by the tenant, with a copy provided to the tenant.

Hoboken, NJ
Hoboken City Code, ch. 158-2 (effective July 2025)
Prohibits landlords from using software, algorithms or data-sharing platforms to coordinate or recommend rents, lease terms, or occupancy.

WHAT THE NEW MUNICIPAL LAWS MEAN FOR EXISTING COMPLIANCE MEASURES
The new municipal cases and new regulations arise against an important backdrop: the multifamily housing industry and revenue-management vendors have already made significant changes in response to the various investigations and related legislation. Government settlements with several major property managers restrict the use of revenue-management software that relies on competitors' nonpublic information to generate rent recommendations, and various software providers have modified products to eliminate or restrict the use of competitors' nonpublic data in generating pricing recommendations. The federal government's resolution with RealPage likewise requires significant restrictions on the use of competitors' nonpublic, competitively sensitive information.
Those changes may materially reduce prospective risk under many of the new municipal ordinances, but they do not necessarily eliminate litigation over past conduct. Several local laws became effective, many prohibiting use of coordination services or software even if secured prior to the effective date of the law, while landlords and software providers were still modifying their practices, and some ordinances treat each affected unit and each month of prohibited use as a separate violation. The date on which a particular product or property ceased using prohibited data therefore becomes a critical issue in determining both liability and the scope of any putative class.
The municipal laws also place a premium on property-level documentation of software functionality. Owners and managers should be able to identify, for each covered jurisdiction, which revenue-management products were used, when relevant functionality was enabled or disabled, what data sources generated recommendations, and whether recommendations continued to rely on competitors' nonpublic information after a local prohibition became effective. Vendor representations that a product has been modified should be documented and tested against the definitions in the applicable ordinance rather than assumed to resolve compliance across jurisdictions.
These issues may also provide important defenses. A plaintiff's allegation that a landlord subscribed to RealPage, Yardi, or another revenue-management platform does not necessarily establish that every property used prohibited functionality throughout the proposed class period. Product versions, configuration changes, data sources, and effective dates may determine whether—and for how long—a particular local prohibition was implicated.
WHAT OWNERS AND PROPERTY MANAGERS SHOULD BE DOING
Owners and property managers should consider several immediate steps to understand and mitigate municipal regulation risk:
Create an ordinance-effective-date matrix: For every affected property, match the ordinance's effective date against the dates the pricing product and particular data functionality were used.
Test the ordinance's exclusions rather than relying on an “antitrust compliant” label: A product may satisfy a federal consent decree but still need to be assessed separately against a city's definition of “algorithmic device,” “coordinating service,” prohibited data, or permitted historical/public-data reporting.

rules.requirement: Provide equal treatment in rental availability, terms, conditions, and privileges regardless of race, creed or religion, color, national origin, sex, gender identity or expression, marital status, civil union status, ancestry, actual or perceived physical or mental disability, nationality, affectional or sexual orientation, familial status, or domestic partner status. rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental property within the LAD's stated coverage. Familial status includes families with children under 18 and/or pregnant women. Disability includes actual or perceived AIDS or HIV.

It permits a religious organization's preference for persons of the same religion. The familial-status prohibition does not apply to housing for older persons as defined in N.J.S.A. 10:5-5mm; that exception is specific to familial status.

residential purposes, with the following exceptions:

• The rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family
dwelling, the other occupancy unit of which is occupied
by the owner as his/her residence at the time of such
rentals;
• The rental of a room or rooms to another person or
persons by the owner or occupant of a one-family
dwelling occupied by him/her as his/her residence at
the time of such rental;

• In the sale, lease or rental of real property, preference
given to persons of the same religion by a religious
organization; and
• The prohibition against discrimination on the basis of
familial status does not apply to housing for older
persons (as defined in the LAD at N.J.S.A. 10:5-5mm).

The NJ Law Against Discrimination (LAD) prohibits
discrimination on the bases of race, creed (religion),
color, national origin, sex, gender identity or expression,
marital status, civil union status, ancestry, actual or
perceived physical or mental disability, nationality,
affectional or sexual orientation, familial status, and
domestic partner status. “ Familial status ” means
families with a child or children under 18 years old and/
or pregnant women, and “ disability” is used to include
persons afflicted with AIDS or HIV or thought to be
afflicted with AIDS.
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses. This
means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the
lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher the right to
rent an apartment based solely on that source of lawful
income.
3. What does this mean to me?
• All persons, regardless of their membership in one
of the protected classes stated above or source of
lawful income used for rent or mortgage payments,
are entitled to equal treatment in the terms,
conditions or privileges of the sale or rental of
any real property  (e.g., it is illegal to deny that
housing is available for inspection, sale or rent when
it really is available.);

rules.title: Written notice of the right to electronic security return
rules.requirement: A landlord that received security or rent electronically, or a successor that received rent electronically, must notify the tenant in writing of the right to receive remaining security electronically within a reasonable time after termination-intent notification or before lease end.
rules.key_value: Reasonable time after termination-intent notification, or before lease end
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenants whose payments trigger subdivision (h)(1)(A)(ii)(I); electronic return is to a tenant-designated financial account or another available electronic or virtual method agreed to in writing.
rules.exemptions: The notice subclause does not apply where the landlord or successor and tenant already made a written agreement designating another return method under subclause (I), or where tenancy terminates under Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(2), (3), or (4).
rules.interaction: The stated exceptions qualify this notice duty, not all security-return obligations.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset is unspecified; supplied version amended effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: The referenced termination grounds are not defined within D025.

rules.title: Relocation payment deadline and optional escrow
rules.requirement: Make relocation payment available within 15 days after service of the written eviction notice. At the landlord's sole discretion and cost, the landlord may instead deposit the money in escrow within that period. Escrow must pay actual pre-vacancy expenses for first and last month's rent, security deposit, utility connections, and moving within three working days after a payment request; release the balance upon certification that the unit is vacant. The bulletin permits escrow at a federally insured bank, savings and loan, or credit union, with a California Corporate Commission-licensed broker, or in a qualifying California attorney's client trust account reasonably accessible to tenants during business hours.

rules.title: Predecessor liability continues until statutory discharge conditions
rules.requirement: After transfer of the dwelling interest, the landlord or agent remains liable under section 15B until the specified deposit-transfer and written-notice condition, successor-compliance condition, or return-to-tenant condition is met.
rules.coverage_conditions: A prior residential landlord or agent after transfer of an interest for which security was held. Clause (a) requires deposit transfer and written notice of transfer plus the successor's name, business address, and business telephone number; clause (b) addresses successor compliance; clause (c) is return of the deposit.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: Read the listed discharge conditions with the transfer and successor notice obligations; a bare sale is not described as sufficient.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).

(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.
(b) Any lessor or his agent who receives a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give said tenant or prospective tenant at the time of receiving such security deposit a receipt indicating the amount of such security deposit, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom such security deposit is received, the date on which it is received, and a description of the premises leased or rented.  Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit.

(5) Whenever a lessor who receives a security deposit transfers his interest in the dwelling unit for which the security deposit is held, whether by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or trustee in bankruptcy, or otherwise, the lessor shall transfer such security deposit together with any interest which has accrued thereon for the benefit of the tenant who made such security deposit to his successor in interest, and said successor in interest shall be liable for the retention and return of said security deposit in accordance with the provisions of this section from the date upon which said transfer is made;  provided however, that the granting of a mortgage on such premises shall not be a transfer of interest.  The successor in interest shall, within forty-five days from the date of said transfer, notify the tenant who made such security deposit that such security deposit was transferred to him and that he is holding said security deposit.  Such notice shall also contain the lessor's name, business address, and business telephone number, and the name, business address, and business telephone number of his agent, if any.  Said notice shall be in writing.

Upon such transfer, the lessor or his agent shall continue to be liable with respect to the provisions of this section until:
(a) there has been a transfer of the amount of the security deposit so held to the lessor's successor in interest and the tenant has been notified in writing of the transfer and of the successor in interest's name, business address, and business telephone number;
(b) there has been compliance with this clause by the successor in interest;  or
(c) the security deposit has been returned to the tenant.

rules.title: Household income aggregation must use the same basis as for married residents
rules.requirement: A financial or income standard for rental housing must account for the aggregate income of people residing or proposing to reside together on the same basis as it accounts for the aggregate income of married people residing or proposing to reside together.
rules.key_value: Same income-aggregation basis as for married co-residents
rules.coverage_conditions: Use of financial or income eligibility standards in housing rental for people residing together or proposing to do so; the standard of comparison is how aggregate income is treated for married co-residents or proposed co-residents.
rules.interaction: Requires equal aggregation treatment; it does not itself specify a rent-to-income multiplier or prohibit every financial eligibility standard.

(3) If a repair to be done by the landlord or the landlord’s employee cannot reasonably be completed within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, or if the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord’s possession within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord may deduct the amount of a good faith estimate of the charges that will be incurred and provide that estimate with the itemized statement. If the reason for the estimate is because the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord’s possession, the itemized statement shall include the name, address, and telephone number of the person or entity. Within 14 calendar days of completing the repair or receiving the documentation,
the landlord shall complete the requirements in paragraphs (1) and (2) in the manner specified.
(4) The landlord need not comply with paragraph (2) or (3) if either of the following applies:
(A) The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).
(B) The tenant waived the rights specified in paragraphs (2) and (3). The waiver shall only be effective if it is signed by the tenant at the same time or after a notice to terminate a tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1 has been given, a notice under Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been given, or no earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease. The waiver shall
substantially include the text of paragraph (2).
(5) Notwithstanding paragraph (4), the landlord shall comply with paragraphs (2) and (3) when a tenant makes a request for documentation within 14 calendar days after receiving the itemized statement specified in paragraph (1). The landlord shall comply within 14 calendar days after receiving the request from the tenant.

rules.title: Successor liability for uncredited last-month rent and accrued interest
rules.requirement: If the prior landlord does not credit the last-month rent advance as required, the successor assumes responsibility for crediting the advance and paying all accrued interest to the tenant regardless of the transfer's nature. While the tenant still occupies the unit, the successor may satisfy the obligation by providing free use and occupancy for the period covered by the advance.
rules.coverage_conditions: A successor to residential property where the required credit of prepaid last-month rent was not made.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required. This subsection's liability excludes a city or town acquiring title under chapter 60 and a foreclosing mortgagee or mortgagee in possession that is a financial institution chartered by Massachusetts or the United States.
rules.interaction: Preserve the advance-rent period measure and accrued-interest component rather than substituting subsection (5)'s deposit-as-rent formula.

The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
limitations: The organizer category includes allowed upfront charges and their receipts/refunds. This rule concerns prepaid last-month rent, not a security deposit; its amounts, interest and remedies must remain distinct from deposit provisions.

rules.requirement: The no-fault eviction checklist requires filing a Landlord Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. This is a procedural obligation.
rules.coverage_conditions: No-fault evictions addressed by the RSO overview. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Los Angeles RSO generally covers listed property types first built on or before 1978-10-01 OR replacement units under LAMC §151.28: apartments, condominiums, townhomes, duplexes, at least two single-family dwelling units on the same parcel, residential units attached to commercial buildings, accessory dwelling units, and junior accessory dwelling units. Hotel, motel, rooming-house and boarding-house rooms require occupancy by the same tenant for more than 30 consecutive days. Mobilehomes and recreational vehicles in mobilehome parks are also covered. Resolve residual exceptions from verified RSO status.

All tenant not- at-fault evictions require payment of relocation assistance and the filing of a 
Declaration of Intent to Evict form with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) before 
evicting tenants from units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause 
Ordinance (JCO). Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices.

rules.title: Limits on rent demanded in advance after tenancy commencement
rules.requirement: After tenancy commencement, a landlord or successor may not demand rent in advance exceeding the current month's rent. Lawful advance payments for occupancy under section 15B bind all successors in interest.

rules.title: Nonpayment termination notice and conditional ten-day cure for tenants at will
rules.requirement: For neglect or refusal to pay rent due from a tenant at will, fourteen days' written notice to quit from the landlord is sufficient to determine the tenancy. If the tenant received no similar landlord notice in the preceding twelve months, payment or tender of all rent due to the landlord, the landlord's attorney, or the customary rent recipient within ten days after receipt prevents termination.
rules.key_value: 14 days notice; 10 days to cure if no similar notice in prior 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenant at will who neglects or refuses to pay rent due; cure protection requires no similar notice from the landlord during the twelve months preceding receipt of the notice.
rules.exemptions: The ordinary ten-day cure period is extended to the answer due date in a possession action if the notice omits the required cure-right notification.
rules.interaction: Read with the section's mandatory cure-right notification and its consequence for omission; fourteen days is not an unconditional right to possession.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot contains this provision with no pending or future-version label; its original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The organizer eviction category is used for termination and possession procedures; this provision does not itself establish a general just-cause requirement.
rules.quoted_span: Section 12. Estates at will may be determined by either party by three months' notice in writing for that purpose given to the other party; and, if the rent reserved is payable at periods of less than three months, the time of such notice shall be sufficient if it is equal to the interval between the days of payment or thirty days, whichever is longer. Such written notice may include an offer to establish a new tenancy for the same premises on terms different from that of the tenancy being terminated and the validity of such written notice shall not be affected by the inclusion of such offer. In case of neglect or refusal to pay the rent due from a tenant at will, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the tenancy; provided, that the tenancy of a tenant who has not received a similar notice from the landlord within the twelve months next preceding the receipt of such notice shall not be determined if the tenant, within ten days after the receipt thereof, pays or tenders to the landlord, the landlord's attorney, or the person to whom the tenant customarily pays rent, the full amount of any rent due. Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent shall contain the following notification to the tenant: ''If you have not received a notice to quit for nonpayment of rent within the last twelve months, you have a right to prevent termination of your tenancy by paying or tendering to your landlord, your landlord's attorney or the person to whom you customarily pay your rent the full amount of rent due within ten days after your receipt of this notice.'' If any notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent shall fail to contain such notification, the time within which the tenant receiving the notice would be entitled to pay or tender rent pursuant to this section shall be extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises. Failure to include such notice shall not otherwise affect the validity of the said notice. If the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due was caused by a failure or delay of the federal government, the commonwealth or any municipality, or any departments, agencies or authorities thereof, in the mailing or delivery of any subsistence or rental payment, check or voucher other than a salary payment to either the tenant or the landlord, the court in any action for possession shall continue the hearing not less than seven days in order to furnish notice of such action to the appropriate agency and shall, if all rent due with interest and costs of suit has been tendered to the landlord within such time, treat the tenancy as not having been terminated.

rules.title: Requested initial-inspection timing, scheduling, and notice
rules.requirement: On the tenant's request, the landlord or agent must make the initial inspection at a reasonable time no earlier than two weeks before termination or lease end, attempt a mutually acceptable appointment, and give at least 48 hours' written notice whether or not a mutual time can be agreed. The inspection must proceed with or without the tenant present unless the tenant withdrew the request, and both parties may sign a written waiver of the 48-hour notice.
rules.key_value: No earlier than 2 weeks before termination or lease end; at least 48 hours' written notice
rules.coverage_conditions: An initial inspection requested by a residential tenant under subdivision (f), occurring before any final inspection after the tenant vacates. If no mutual appointment can be agreed, the tenant must still wish to have the inspection for the notice requirement to operate.
rules.exemptions: No-request cases discharge the landlord's subdivision (f) duties; a withdrawn request removes the duty to proceed. Both parties may sign a waiver of the 48-hour notice, and subdivision (f) does not apply to termination under Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(2), (3), or (4).
rules.interaction: Initial inspection is intended to let the tenant remedy deficiencies and avoid security deductions.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Specified 2003 amendments to (f)(1) are declaratory of existing law under (r); no original onset is inferred from the footer amendment date 2026-01-01.
limitations: External termination grounds are retained by citation without importing their definitions.

(f) (1) Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before
the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. rules.title: Restoration escrow for disability modifications
rules.requirement: A landlord may require monthly escrow deposits for removing disability modifications only on proof that restoration will be expensive. Payments must be affordable, stop once the required restoration amount is reached, and earn interest for the tenant.

rules.coverage_conditions: Restoration of tenant-funded disability modifications to rental premises.
rules.exemptions: No restoration escrow absent proof that restoration costs will be expensive.

Modification of the Rental Premises for People with Disabilities 
 It is illegal for a landlord to refuse to rent to a tenant because of the tenant’s handicap or 
disability. The landlord is not required to modify existing rental premises occupied, or to be 
occupied, by a person with a disability. However, the landlord also cannot ref use to make 
reasonable changes (at the expense of the disabled person) as may be necessary to afford the 
disabled person full enjoyment of the premises. The tenant may be required to restore the premises 
to the condition that existed before the modificatio n, except for reasonable wear and tear. The 
landlord may also require a description of the modifications and proof of required permits 
(N.J.A.C. 13:13-3.4(f)). 
 The landlord may require the tenant deposit money into an escrow account each month to 
cover the costs of removal of the modifications when the tenant moves out. The landlord can only 
require the tenant to deposit the money into the escrow account if they can prove that the costs of 
restoring the premises to its original condition will be expensive. Payments into an escrow account 
must be affordable and must cease when the amount needed to restore the unit to its original 
condition is reached.  Interest on the account goes to the tenant.

rules.title: RSO termination-notice filing deadline
rules.requirement: All notices terminating tenancies in RSO units must be filed with LAHD within three business days after service on the tenant. This is a procedural filing duty.
rules.key_value: Three business days after service
rules.coverage_conditions: All rental units subject to the RSO. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Los Angeles RSO generally covers listed property types first built on or before 1978-10-01 OR replacement units under LAMC §151.28: apartments, condominiums, townhomes, duplexes, at least two single-family dwelling units on the same parcel, residential units attached to commercial buildings, accessory dwelling units, and junior accessory dwelling units. Hotel, motel, rooming-house and boarding-house rooms require occupancy by the same tenant for more than 30 consecutive days. Mobilehomes and recreational vehicles in mobilehome parks are also covered. Resolve residual exceptions from verified RSO status.

What Falls Under RSO
If you own rental property in the City of Los Angeles, it may be subject to the
city’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO)
.
Find out
if your property falls under this ordinance and what you need to know to be in compliance.
Generally, the RSO applies to rental properties that were first built on or before October 1, 1978, as well as replacement units under
LAMC Section 151.28
and if any of the following:
Apartment
Condominium (Rent amount is not regulated for tenancies that commenced after December 31, 1995)
Townhome (Rent amount is not regulated for tenancies that commenced after December 31, 1995)
Duplex
Two or more single-family dwelling units on the same parcel
Rooms in a hotel, motel, rooming house, or boarding house occupied by the same tenant for more than 30 consecutive days
Residential unit(s) attached to a commercial building
Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU)
Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit (JADU)
Mobile homes
and recreational vehicles in mobile home parks are also covered under the RSO.

Eviction Notices
All notices to terminate a tenancy for all rental units subject to
City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO
) must be filed with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) within
three (3) business days of service on the tenant
per Los Angeles Municipal Code 151.09.C.9 & 165.05.B.5. Click
here
for more information.

rules.title: Nondiscrimination in publicly assisted, multiple-dwelling, and contiguously located housing
rules.requirement: Covered housing actors may not deny or withhold rental housing because of race, religious creed, color, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation as qualified in the statute, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veteran or armed-forces status, blindness, hearing impairment, or other handicap. They also may not discriminate in housing terms, conditions, privileges, facilities, or services on the grounds listed in subsection 6(b), including possession of a trained guide dog because of blindness or hearing impairment. Subsection 6(b), unlike 6(a), does not expressly list genetic information.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners, lessees, sublessees, licensed real estate brokers, assignees, managing agents, persons with ownership, possession, rental, leasing, or sale rights, their agents or employees, and condominium or housing-cooperative unit-owner organizations, for publicly assisted, multiple-dwelling, or contiguously located housing.
rules.exemptions: The statutory sexual-orientation language excludes persons whose sexual orientation involves minor children as the sex object. Age protection does not apply to minors or the specified elderly and older-person housing: state- or federally aided elderly developments; low-income-housing-tax-credit developments intended for persons 55 or older or 62 or older; and communities expressly constructed for those age groups whose owner or manager registers biennially with the executive office of housing and livable communities. Housing intended for persons 55 or older or 62 or older must comply with 42 USC 3601 et seq. The section also preserves same-religion admission limitations or preferences by qualifying religious or religiously affiliated charitable or educational organizations.
rules.quoted_span: (a) to refuse to rent or lease or sell or negotiate for sale or otherwise to deny to or withhold from any person or group of persons such accommodations because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, which shall not include persons whose sexual orientation involves minor children as the sex object, age, genetic information, ancestry, or marital status of such person or persons or because such person is a veteran or member of the armed forces, or because such person is blind, or hearing impaired or has any other handicap;
rules.interaction:

rules.title: Residential rental application-fee cap
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent must not require an application or similar fee exceeding $50 to apply to lease or sublease residential property for dwelling purposes, subject to the stated exemptions and later annual adjustments.

rules.coverage_conditions: Fees required by landlords or their agents to apply to lease or sublease residential rental property for dwelling purposes. The source does not specify a per-person, per-household, or aggregate multi-fee unit.
rules.exemptions: A unit located in a one-family or two-family dwelling offered for rent is exempt, without an owner-occupancy condition. A New Jersey Real Estate Commission licensee is exempt unless the licensee is the property's landlord.

rules.title: Owner or family occupancy requires qualifying ownership, actual occupancy, and specified notice
rules.requirement: Owner/family occupancy is a no-fault ground only for an eligible owner or the owner's spouse, domestic partner, child, grandchild, parent, or grandparent intending to use the unit as a primary residence for at least 12 continuous months. The intended occupant must move in within 90 days after the tenant vacates and remain for at least 12 consecutive months, subject to the following exception: if the intended occupant moves in within 90 days but dies before completing 12 months of primary-residence occupancy, this is not considered a failure to comply with this section or a material violation by the owner under subdivision (h). This ground is unavailable if the intended occupant already occupies a rental unit on the property or a similar unit is already vacant there. For leases entered on or after July 1, 2020, or July 1, 2022 for mobilehomes, the tenant must agree in writing to termination OR the lease must authorize termination for the specified owner/family occupancy. The termination notice must name the intended occupants, state their relationship to the owner, and disclose the tenant's right to request proof of qualifying ownership or relationship; proof must be supplied on request and may include nonpublic documents. Adding the occupancy provision to a new or renewed lease counts as a similar provision for the renewal-refusal ground.
rules.key_value: Move in within 90 days; primary residence for at least 12 consecutive months, subject to the exception for an intended occupant who moves in timely but dies before completing 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Only tenancies protected by section 1946.2(a), using its 12-month/added-adult duration tests. For this ground, owner means a natural person with at least 25% recorded ownership; a natural person with any recorded interest when all recorded owners are specified relatives; or a natural person whose recorded interest is held through an LLC or partnership. Natural person includes a settlor or beneficiary of a qualifying family trust and, for entity-owned property, a beneficial owner with at least 25% ownership in the property. A family trust is a revocable living or irrevocable trust whose settlors and beneficiaries are related as siblings, spouses, domestic partners, children, parents, grandparents, or grandchildren. Beneficial owner means a natural person or family trust satisfying any specified substantial-control, at-least-25%-equity, or substantial-partnership-economic-benefit criterion.
rules.exemptions: An intended occupant's death before completing 12 months of primary-residence occupancy is not noncompliance or a material violation by the owner if the occupant moved in within 90 days after the tenant vacated. Section-wide exclusions apply: transient/tourist occupancy; specified hospital, religious, care, and adult residential facilities; institution-owned-and-operated dormitories; shared kitchen/bathroom housing with a resident principal-residence owner; single-family owner-occupied housing including the stated no-more-than-two rented units/bedrooms and mobilehome cases; qualifying continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures with neither unit an ADU/JADU; certificates of occupancy within 15 years except mobilehomes; recorded/subsidized affordable housing; and mobilehome homeowners. Separately alienable property requires both an eligible non-REIT/noncorporate/noncorporate-member-LLC/non-park-management owner and the prescribed written exemption notice, in the agreement for commencement/renewal on or after July 1, 2020 or July 1, 2022 for mobilehomes. Qualifying local ordinances displace the section.
rules.quoted_span: If the intended occupant moves into the rental unit within 90 days after the tenant vacates, but dies before having occupied the rental unit as a primary residence for 12 months, as required by clause (vi), this will not be considered a failure to comply with this section or a material violation of this section by the owner as provided in subdivision (h).
rules.interaction:
This is a conditional no-fault ground within the general just-cause rule, with relocation duties under subdivision (d). Subdivision (i) makes qualifying local just-cause ordinances applicable instead.

Intent to occupy the residential real property by the owner or the owner’s spouse, domestic partner, children, grandchildren, parents, or grandparents for a minimum of 12 continuous months as that person’s primary residence.

Addition of a provision allowing the owner to terminate the lease as described in this clause to a new or renewed rental agreement or fixed-term lease constitutes a similar provision for the purposes of subparagraph (E) of paragraph (1).
This subparagraph does not apply if the intended occupant occupies a rental unit on the property or if a vacancy of a similar unit already exists at the property.

The written notice terminating a tenancy for a just cause pursuant to this
subparagraph shall contain the name or names and relationship to the owner of the intended occupant. The written notice shall additionally include notification that the tenant may request proof that the intended occupant is an owner or related to the owner as defined in subclause (II) of clause (viii). The proof shall be provided upon request and may include an operating agreement and other nonpublic documents.

Clause (i) applies only if the intended occupant moves into the rental unit within 90 days after the tenant vacates and occupies the rental unit as a primary residence for at least 12 consecutive months.

If the intended occupant moves into the rental unit within 90 days after the tenant vacates, but dies before having occupied the rental unit as a primary residence for 12 months, as required by clause (vi), this will not be considered a failure to comply with this section or a material violation of this section by the owner as provided in subdivision (h).

If the intended occupant moves into the rental unit within 90 days after the tenant vacates, but dies before having occupied the rental unit as a primary residence for 12 months, as required by clause (vi), this will not be considered a failure to comply with this section or a material violation of this section by the owner as provided in subdivision (h).

“Owner” means any of the following:
(ia) An owner who is a natural person that has at least a 25-percent recorded ownership interest in the property.
(ib) An owner who is a natural person who has any recorded ownership interest in the property if 100 percent of the recorded ownership is divided among owners who are related to each other as sibling, spouse, domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, or grandchild.
(ic) An owner who is a natural person whose recorded interest in the property is owned through a limited liability company or partnership.

For purposes of subclause (II), “natural person” includes any of the following:
(ia) A natural person who is a settlor or beneficiary of a family trust.
(ib) If the property is owned by a limited liability company or partnership, a natural person who is a beneficial owner with at least a 25-percent ownership interest in the property.

“Family trust” means a revocable living trust or irrevocable trust in which the settlors and beneficiaries of the trust are persons who are related to each other as sibling, spouse, domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, or grandchild.

“Beneficial owner” means a natural person or family trust for whom, directly or indirectly and through any contract arrangement, understanding, relationship, or otherwise, and any of the following applies:
(ia) The natural person exercises substantial control over a partnership or limited liability company.
(ib) The natural person owns 25 percent or more of the equity interest of a partnership or limited liability company.
(ic) The natural person receives substantial economic benefits from the assets of a partnership.

(k) For the purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply:
(1) “Owner” includes any person, acting as principal or through an agent, having the right to offer residential real property for rent, and includes a predecessor in interest to the owner.
(2) “Residential real property” means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.
(3) “Tenancy” means the lawful occupation of residential real
property and includes a lease or sublease.

rules.title: Criminal records excluded from housing-eligibility decisions
rules.requirement: The developer or agent agrees not to consider arrests without conviction, including dismissed charges and diversion; convictions subject to judicial relief, including expungement, sealing and certificates for relief from disabilities; juvenile records; or convictions more than five years old when determining housing eligibility, subject to the stated criminal-history exceptions.
rules.key_value: Convictions more than 5 years old and other specified records excluded
rules.coverage_conditions: Providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; the policy also applies to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.
rules.exemptions: The arrest-and-conviction policy does not apply where a conviction has a direct relationship to the housing sought and/or there is an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety. Current criminal behavior is outside the guidance. Conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements prevail.
rules.citation: BOSTON FAIR CHANCE TENANT SELECTION POLICY, item 1(a)-(d)

The Developer/Agent (Agent) agrees to not consider any of the following categories when 
determining housing eligibility and or considering eviction: 
 
a) Arrests that did not result in conviction. This includes dismissed charges, diversion 
programs, and similar non-convictions. 
b) Convictions that are subject to a form of judicial relief, such as expungement, sealing, 
and certificates for relief from disabilities. 
c) Juvenile records 
d) A conviction more than 5 years old.

rules.title: Invalid termination notices, nonwaivable rights, and remedies for unlawful recovery of possession
rules.requirement: Any failure to comply with section 1946.2 renders the written termination notice void, and any waiver of rights under the section is void as against public policy. An owner attempting to recover possession in material violation is liable to the tenant for actual damages, discretionary reasonable attorney fees and costs, and, on a showing of willfulness or oppression, fraud, or malice, up to three times actual damages; punitive damages may also be awarded. The Attorney General and the city attorney or county counsel where the unit is located may seek injunctive relief.
rules.key_value: Actual damages; discretionary fees and costs; up to three times actual damages on specified culpability; possible punitive damages
rules.coverage_conditions: Rights and duties under section 1946.2. Notice invalidity applies to any noncompliance; the private damages provision specifically requires an attempt to recover possession in material violation. Enhanced damages require the additional culpability showing.
rules.exemptions: The section's excluded properties and circumstances remain outside its substantive duties: transient/tourist occupancy; specified hospital/religious/care facilities; institutional dormitories; resident-owner shared kitchen/bathroom housing; qualifying single-family owner-occupied residences/mobilehomes; qualifying owner-occupied two-unit structures without ADU/JADU units; recent certificates of occupancy within 15 years except mobilehomes; qualifying recorded/subsidized affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners; and separately alienable property meeting both owner-type restrictions and prescribed notice conditions. Qualifying local just-cause ordinances displace the section. Timely owner-occupant move-in followed by death before 12 months is expressly not noncompliance or a material violation.

An owner’s failure to comply with any provision of this section shall render the
written termination notice void.
rules.interaction:
Enforces the section's just-cause, procedural, relocation, and disclosure protections; does not independently create an additional termination ground.

limitations: No fixed per-violation penalty or limitations period is stated in this chunk.
The text does not specify how any punitive award is calculated.

An owner who attempts to recover possession of a rental unit in material violation of this section shall be liable to the tenant in a civil action for all of the following:
(A) Actual damages.
(B) In the court’s discretion, reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.
(C) Upon a showing that the owner has acted willfully or with oppression, fraud, or malice, up to three times the actual damages. An award may also be entered for punitive damages for the benefit of the tenant against the owner.

The Attorney General, in the name of the people of the State of California, and the city attorney or county counsel in the jurisdiction in
which the rental unit is located, in the name of the city or county, may seek injunctive relief based on violations of this section.
Any waiver of the rights under this section shall be void as contrary to public policy.

(k) For the purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply:
(1) “Owner” includes any person, acting as principal or through an agent, having the right to offer residential real property for rent, and includes a predecessor in interest to the owner.
(2) “Residential real property” means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.
(3) “Tenancy” means the lawful occupation of residential real
property and includes a lease or sublease.

(e) This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties or residential circumstances:
(1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940.

(2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in Section 1569.2 of the Health and Safety Code, or an adult residential facility, as defined in Chapter 6 of Division 6 of Title 22 of the Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the State Department of Social Services.
(3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school.
(4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property.

(5) Single-family owner-occupied residences, including both of the following:
(A) A residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms, including, but not limited to, an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.
(B) A mobilehome.

(6) A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner’s principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.

(7) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15
years, unless the housing is a mobilehome.

(8) Residential real property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following apply:
(A) The owner is not any of the following:
(i) A real estate investment trust, as defined in Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code.
(ii) A corporation.
(iii) A limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.
(iv) Management of a mobilehome park, as defined in Section 798.2.
(B) (i) The tenants have been
provided written notice that the residential property is exempt from this section using the following statement:
“This property is not subject to the rent limits imposed by Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code and is not subject to the just cause requirements of Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code. This property meets the requirements of Sections 1947.12 (d)(5) and 1946.2 (e)(8) of the Civil Code and the owner is not any of the following: (1) a real estate investment trust, as defined by Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code; (2) a corporation; or (3) a limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.”
(ii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for a tenancy existing before July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the
rental agreement.
(II) For a tenancy in a mobilehome existing before July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the rental agreement.
(iii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for any tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) must be provided in the rental agreement.
(II) For any tenancy in a mobilehome commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) shall be provided in the rental agreement.
(iv) Addition of a provision containing the notice required under clause (i) to any new or renewed rental agreement or fixed-term lease constitutes a similar provision for the purposes of subparagraph
(E) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (b).

(9) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement with a government agency, or other recorded document as affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code, or subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code or comparable federal statutes.

(i) (1) This section does not apply to the following residential real property:
(A) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted on or before September 1, 2019, in which case the local ordinance shall apply.
(B) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted or amended after September 1, 2019, that is more protective than this section, in which case the local ordinance shall apply. For purposes of this subparagraph, an ordinance is “more protective” if it meets all of the following criteria:
(i) The just cause for termination of a residential tenancy under the local ordinance is consistent with this section.
(ii) The ordinance further limits the reasons for termination of a residential tenancy, provides for higher relocation assistance amounts, or provides additional tenant protections that are not prohibited by any other provision of law.
(iii) The local government has made a binding finding within their local ordinance that the ordinance is more protective than the provisions of this section.
(2) A residential real property shall not be subject to both a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy and this section.
(3) A local ordinance adopted
after September 1, 2019, that is less protective than this section shall not be enforced unless this section is repealed.
(l) This section shall not apply to a homeowner of a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.9.

(m) This section shall become operative on April 1, 2024.

shared_scope_logic.logic: Residential scope is required, then independently test each OR exclusion with all internal AND requirements. The occupancy-duration condition belongs to substantive just-cause protection and is not a waiting period for the subdivision (f) disclosure duty.

rule_specific_logic.coverage: Section coverage AND an underlying applicable obligation/waiver; test the violated provision independently.
rule_specific_logic.exemptions: Any established complete section exclusion applies; a failed asserted termination ground is not an exclusion from tenant protection.
rule_specific_logic.triggers: Notice defect, material possession violation, and waiver are distinct branches.
rule_specific_logic.modifiers: Do not require materiality for every notice defect; reserve materiality for the damages trigger and aggravating mental state for enhanced damages.

required_facts.description: Whether property is subject to local just-cause ordinance; adoption/amendment date, consistent causes, additional protections and binding finding.
Identify REIT/corporation/LLC and every relevant member type, and mobilehome-park management status.
Evidence of owner principal residence in one unit both at tenancy inception and continuously thereafter.
Tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with owner who maintains principal residence at this property.
Applicable section violation, possession attempt, materiality, actual damages, willfulness/oppression/fraud/malice and claimant/enforcing authority.
Recorded deed/regulatory restrictions or qualifying subsidy agreement, covered income classes and legal terms; a tenant voucher alone does not establish this exclusion.
Number of separate dwelling units in this single structure, not portfolio holdings.
Actual certificate-of-occupancy issuance date, not construction-year proxy.
Whether a higher-education or K-12 institution both owns and operates this dormitory.
Nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elderly residential care, or defined adult residential facility status.
Whether the rental is a mobilehome; do not confuse renting a mobilehome with renting a park space as its homeowner.
Whether title is alienable separately from every other dwelling unit.
Single-family owner-occupied residence, number of rented units/bedrooms, ADU/JADU and mobilehome configuration.
Whether occupancy meets Civil Code 1940(b), not merely a short lease.
Whether either unit in the claimed two-unit structure is an ADU or JADU.
Whether the dwelling/unit is intended for human habitation; identify institutional and other uses.
Disclosure wording, type size, placement, signatures, delivery copy and date.
Whether the prescribed statement was provided and, when required, is included in the rental agreement.
Relevant renewal date for the exemption-notice placement rule.
Start date of the tenancy, distinct from tenant occupancy duration and property age.
Whether the occupant is a mobilehome homeowner within the cross-referenced section 798.9 definition.
Date of the particular agreement, notice, increase, demand or alleged conduct being evaluated; distinct from the query date.

rules.title: Rights disclosure for mobilehome tenancies existing before July 1, 2022
rules.requirement: For a covered mobilehome tenancy existing before July 1, 2022, provide the prescribed rent-limit and just-cause disclosure by written notice no later than August 1, 2022, or as a lease/rental-agreement addendum. The disclosure must be at least 12-point type and is subject to section 1632.
rules.key_value: Written-notice deadline August 1, 2022; at least 12-point type
rules.coverage_conditions: Mobilehome rental tenancies existing before July 1, 2022 that are subject to section 1946.2.
rules.exemptions: Mobilehome homeowners under section 798.9 are excluded. Other section-wide exclusions remain applicable when their facts are met, including owner-occupied mobilehomes, resident-owner shared kitchen/bathroom housing, specified transient/institutional/affordable housing, and separately alienable mobilehomes satisfying both the owner-type restrictions and prescribed exemption-notice requirements. rules.quoted_span: For a tenancy in a mobilehome existing prior to July 1, 2022, by written notice to the tenant no later than August 1, 2022, or as an addendum to the lease or rental agreement.
rules.interaction: A historical procedural-disclosure obligation within the current statute, referencing section 1947.12 and subject to section 1632.
rules.temporal_notes: The current section is operative April 1, 2024, amended effective January 1, 2026, and repealed January 1, 2030. August 1, 2022 is a historical deadline retained in the statute, not a new deadline as of 2026.
rules.penalty: Subdivision (g) makes a written termination notice void for noncompliance with the section.
limitations: The passage does not separately restate a deadline for the alternative addendum option.
No new cure deadline or original enactment date is established.

rules.title: Successor notice for credited last-month rent advance
rules.requirement: Within forty-five days after transfer of the landlord's interest in the dwelling unit, the successor must tell the tenant in writing that the last-month rent advance was credited and that the successor assumed responsibility. The successor in interest shall, within forty-five days from the date of said transfer, notify the tenant who made such rental advance that such rental advance was so credited, and that such successor has assumed responsibility therefor pursuant to the foregoing provision. (2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.

Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.

rules.requirement: A tenant's conviction, guilty plea or juvenile delinquency adjudication for a drug offense on the property may support eviction unless the stated sentence-related rehabilitation exception applies. rules.title: Required content of security-deposit records
rules.requirement: Every landlord accepting security must keep records detailing damage associated with the covered units, the end of occupancy for tenants charged with damage, and whether repairs occurred with their dates, costs, and receipts. The record must also contain copies of any receipts or condition statements given to a tenant or prospective tenant as required by section 15B.
rules.coverage_conditions: Records of all accepted residential security deposits, including units for which deposits were accepted or returned or for which the landlord sued a tenant.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: These records are subject to the inspection and retention requirements in the following paragraphs.

The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).

If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.
(b) Any lessor or his agent who receives a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give said tenant or prospective tenant at the time of receiving such security deposit a receipt indicating the amount of such security deposit, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom such security deposit is received, the date on which it is received, and a description of the premises leased or rented.  Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit.

(d) Every lessor who accepts a security deposit shall maintain a record of all such security deposits received which contains the following information:--
(i) a detailed description of any damage done to each of the dwelling units or premises for which a security deposit has been accepted, returned to any tenant thereof or for which the lessor has brought suit against any tenant;
(ii) the date upon which the occupancy of the tenant or tenants charged with such damage was terminated;  and
(iii) whether repairs were performed to remedy such damage, the dates of said repairs, the cost thereof, and receipts therefor.
Said record shall also include copies of any receipt or statement of condition given to a tenant or prospective tenant as required by this section.
