rules.title: Six-month rebuttable presumption for specified adverse tenancy notices
rules.requirement: Receipt of a qualifying termination, rent-increase, or substantial-tenancy-change notice within six months of the specified tenant activity, or qualifying activity by another person, creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal. Termination for nonpayment of rent is excepted from this presumption.
rules.key_value: 6-month rebuttable presumption
rules.coverage_conditions: Receipt of a tenancy-termination notice other than for nonpayment, a rent-increase notice, or notice of a substantial alteration of tenancy terms within six months after the tenant commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in the described action, exercised the described rights, made the described report or complaint, or organized or joined a tenants' union. The paragraph also covers the six months after another person takes such action for the tenant or in or relating to the tenant's building.
rules.exemptions: The termination-notice branch excludes nonpayment of rent; this exception does not authorize actual retaliatory conduct or eliminate liability otherwise proved.
rules.interaction: The presumption also expressly covers increases in rent; it is an evidentiary protection across the section rather than a general ban on every notice within six months.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot presents the provision without a pending or future-version label; the original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The presumption paragraph does not expressly repeat the first paragraph's unit-owner rent-payment activity; no unconditional extension of the presumption to that activity is asserted.
This rule does not establish a general just-cause requirement.
rules.quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities. Such presumption shall be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that such person's action was not a reprisal against the tenant and that such person had sufficient independent justification for taking such action, and would have in fact taken such action, in the same manner and at the same time the action was taken, regardless of tenants engaging in, or the belief that tenants had engaged in, activities protected under this section.

rules.title: Demolition or substantial-remodel termination conditions, notice, and return rights
rules.requirement: Intent to demolish or substantially remodel is a no-fault ground. Substantial remodeling must be either permit-requiring replacement or substantial modification of a structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system, OR lawful hazardous-material abatement, and must both be unsafe to accomplish while the tenant remains and require at least 30 consecutive days of vacancy. Cosmetic work alone and work safely performed while occupied do not qualify; tenants need not vacate on days they can lawfully and safely remain. The termination notice must state the intent, describe the remodel and expected duration or the expected demolition date, attach required permits or, only for hazardous-material abatement needing no permit, a signed contractor agreement reasonably detailing the work, and provide the prescribed return-right statement. If the described work is not commenced or completed, the owner must offer rerental at the prior agreement's terms and the rent in effect when the tenant vacated. The tenant must accept or reject within 30 days after receiving that offer and, if accepting, reoccupy within 30 days after acceptance. The notice must also tell a tenant interested in occupancy following remodeling to communicate that interest and provide an address, telephone number, and email address.
rules.key_value: At least 30 consecutive days of required vacancy; 30 days to respond to a reoffer; 30 days after acceptance to reoccupy
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenancies protected by section 1946.2(a), including its occupancy-duration tests, where the owner invokes demolition or substantial remodeling.
rules.exemptions: Cosmetic-only work and safely occupied work do not qualify. Section-wide exclusions remain: transient/tourist occupancy; specified hospital/religious/care facilities; institution-owned-and-operated dormitories; resident-owner shared kitchen/bathroom housing; qualifying single-family owner-occupied housing and mobilehomes; qualifying continuously owner-occupied two-unit structures without ADU/JADU units; non-mobilehome housing with a certificate of occupancy within 15 years; qualifying recorded/subsidized affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners; and separately alienable property satisfying both restricted owner types and prescribed exemption-notice requirements. Qualifying local just-cause ordinances displace this section.
rules.quoted_span: “substantially remodel” means either of the following that cannot be reasonably accomplished in a safe manner that allows the tenant to remain living in the place and that requires the tenant to vacate the residential real property for at least 30 consecutive days:
rules.interaction: A conditional no-fault ground that also triggers subdivision (d)'s relocation protections. The return-right notice is a procedural and remedial protection, not an additional termination ground.

conditions.value: permit-requiring replacement or substantial modification of specified building systems; lawful hazardous-material abatement
conditions.description: Either work type must also satisfy both vacancy predicates.
Required in addition to qualifying work and at least 30 consecutive days of necessary vacancy.
Days on which lawful, safe occupancy remains possible do not independently require vacancy.

rules.temporal_notes: Section-wide operative date; supplied amended version effective January 1, 2026. Individual amendment changes are not identified. Repealed January 1, 2030.
rules.penalty: Failure to comply renders the termination notice void; material violations may support subdivision (h) remedies.
limitations: The notice provision requests interest in returning after remodeling but does not separately state an unconditional right to return after successfully completed work.
No independent deadline for commencing or completing construction is supplied.

evidence.quote:
(D) (i) Intent to demolish or to
substantially remodel the residential real property.

“substantially remodel” means either of the following that cannot be reasonably accomplished in a safe manner that allows the tenant to remain living in the place and that requires the tenant to vacate the residential real property for at least 30 consecutive days:

(I) The replacement or substantial modification of any structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system that requires a permit from a governmental agency.
(II) The abatement of hazardous materials, including lead-based paint, mold, or asbestos, in accordance with applicable federal, state, and local laws.

For purposes of this subparagraph, a tenant is not required to vacate the residential
real property on any days where a tenant could continue living in the residential real property without violating health, safety, and habitability codes and laws. Cosmetic improvements alone, including painting, decorating, and minor repairs, or other work that can be performed safely without having the residential real property vacated, do not qualify as substantial remodel.

A written notice terminating a tenancy for a just cause pursuant to this subparagraph shall include all of the following information:
(I) A statement informing the tenant of the owner’s intent to demolish the property or substantially remodel the rental unit property.

“If the substantial remodel of your unit or demolition of the property as described in this notice of
termination is not commenced or completed, the owner must offer you the opportunity to re-rent your unit with a rental agreement containing the same terms as your most recent rental agreement with the owner at the rental rate that was in effect at the time you vacated. You must notify the owner within thirty (30) days of receipt of the offer to re-rent of your acceptance or rejection of the offer, and, if accepted, you must reoccupy the unit within thirty (30) days of notifying the owner of your acceptance of the offer.”

(III) A description of the substantial remodel to be completed, the approximate expected duration of the substantial remodel, or if the property is to be demolished, the expected date by which the property will be demolished, together with one of the following:
(ia) A copy of the permit or permits required to undertake the substantial remodel or demolition.
(ib) Only if a notice is issued pursuant to subclause (II) of clause (ii) and the remodel does not require any permit, a copy of the signed contract with the contractor hired by the owner to complete the substantial remodel, that reasonably details the work that will be undertaken to abate the hazardous materials as described in subclause (II) of clause (ii).

(IV) A notification that if the tenant is interested in reoccupying the rental unit following the substantial remodel, the tenant shall inform the owner of the tenant’s interest in reoccupying the rental unit following the substantial remodel and provide to the owner the tenant’s address, telephone number, and email address.
(m) This section shall become operative on April 1, 2024.
(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 203, Sec. 1.   (AB 1529)   Effective January 1, 2026.   Repealed as of January 1, 2030, by its own provisions.)

(k) For the purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply:
(1) “Owner” includes any person, acting as principal or through an agent, having the right to offer residential real property for rent, and includes a predecessor in interest to the owner.
(2) “Residential real property” means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.
(3) “Tenancy” means the lawful occupation of residential real
property and includes a lease or sublease.

(e) This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties or residential circumstances:
(1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940.

(2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in Section 1569.2 of the Health and Safety Code, or an adult residential facility, as defined in Chapter 6 of Division 6 of Title 22 of the Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the State Department of Social Services.
(3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school.
(4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property.

(5) Single-family owner-occupied residences, including both of the following:

(I) The replacement or substantial modification of any structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system that requires a permit from a governmental agency.
(II) The abatement of hazardous materials, including lead-based paint, mold, or asbestos, in accordance with applicable federal, state, and local laws.
(iii) For purposes of this subparagraph, a tenant is not required to vacate the residential

required_facts.description: Whether property is subject to local just-cause ordinance; adoption/amendment date, consistent causes, additional protections and binding finding.
Identify REIT/corporation/LLC and every relevant member type, and mobilehome-park management status.
Evidence of owner principal residence in one unit both at tenancy inception and continuously thereafter.
Tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with owner who maintains principal residence at this property.
Recorded deed/regulatory restrictions or qualifying subsidy agreement, covered income classes and legal terms; a tenant voucher alone does not establish this exclusion.
Number of separate dwelling units in this single structure, not portfolio holdings.
Actual certificate-of-occupancy issuance date, not construction-year proxy.
Whether a higher-education or K-12 institution both owns and operates this dormitory.
Nonprofit hospital, religious, extended care, licensed elderly residential care, or defined adult residential facility status.
Whether the rental is a mobilehome; do not confuse renting a mobilehome with renting a park space as its homeowner.
Whether title is alienable separately from every other dwelling unit.
Single-family owner-occupied residence, number of rented units/bedrooms, ADU/JADU and mobilehome configuration.
Whether occupancy meets Civil Code 1940(b), not merely a short lease.
Whether either unit in the claimed two-unit structure is an ADU or JADU.
Whether the dwelling/unit is intended for human habitation; identify institutional and other uses.
Disclosure wording, type size, placement, signatures, delivery copy and date.
Whether the prescribed statement was provided and, when required, is included in the rental agreement.
Continuous lawful occupancy start for each tenant and when additional adults joined; preserve each tenant separately.
Relevant renewal date for the exemption-notice placement rule.
Start date of the tenancy, distinct from tenant occupancy duration and property age.
Whether the occupant is a mobilehome homeowner within the cross-referenced section 798.9 definition.
Date of the particular agreement, notice, increase, demand or alleged conduct being evaluated; distinct from the query date.
Work scope, permit requirements and copies, hazardous-material abatement contract if no permit, safety during occupancy, required consecutive vacancy and completion/start status.
Offer terms/date received, tenant acceptance date, reoccupancy date and interest/contact details.

Asserted ground plus its substantiating facts, including actual default, material breach, nuisance, waste, criminal threat/activity, prohibited assignment, authorized entry refusal, unlawful use, ended employment/license, or tenant written notice/accepted surrender as applicable. A category label alone does not establish a ground.
Gross rates and effective dates over the preceding 12 months, identifying accepted discounts/concessions separately.

rules.title: Continuing liability after transfer of a last-month rent advance
rules.requirement: After transfer of the landlord's interest in the dwelling unit, the landlord or agent continues to be liable until the specified advance-credit and written-notice condition, successor-compliance condition, or tenant-credit-and-interest-payment condition is met.
rules.coverage_conditions: A prior residential landlord or agent after transfer involving prepaid last-month rent. Clause (a) requires crediting the advance to the successor and written tenant notice of transfer plus the successor's name, business address and business telephone number; clause (b) requires successor compliance; clause (c) requires credit to the tenant and payment of all accrued interest.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required. Liability imposed by subsection (7A) does not apply to a city or town acquiring title under chapter 60, or to a foreclosing mortgagee or mortgagee in possession that is a financial institution chartered by Massachusetts or the United States.
rules.interaction: A completed sale by itself is not described as sufficient to discharge advance-rent obligations.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
limitations: The organizer category includes allowed upfront charges and their receipts/refunds. This rule concerns prepaid last-month rent, not a security deposit; its amounts, interest and remedies must remain distinct from deposit provisions.
rules.quoted_span: Upon such transfer, the lessor or his agent shall continue to be liable with respect to the provisions of this section until:--(a) there has been a credit of the amount of the rental advance so held to the lessor's successor in interest and the tenant has been notified in writing of the transfer and of the successor in interest's name, business address, and business telephone number;  (b) there has been compliance with this clause by the successor in interest;  or (c) the rental advance has been credited to the tenant and all accrued interest has been paid thereon.

evidence.quote: (7A) Whenever a lessor who receives rent in advance for the last month of tenancy transfers his interest in the dwelling unit for which the rental advance was received, whether by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or trustee in bankruptcy, or otherwise, the lessor shall credit an amount equal to such rental advance together with any interest which has accrued thereon for the benefit of the tenant who made such rental advance, to the successor in interest of such lessor, and said successor in interest shall be liable for crediting the tenant with such rental advance, and for paying all interest accrued thereon in accordance with the provisions of this section from the date upon which said transfer is made;  provided, however, that the granting of a mortgage on such premises shall not be deemed a transfer of interest.  The successor in interest shall, within forty-five days from the date of said transfer, notify the tenant who made such rental advance that such rental advance was so credited, and that such successor has assumed responsibility therefor pursuant to the foregoing provision.  Such notice shall also contain the lessor's name, business address, and business telephone number, and the name, business address, and business telephone number of his agent, if any.  Said notice shall be in writing.
(9) The provisions of this section shall not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of one hundred days or less in duration which lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose.

In the event that the lessor fails to credit said rental advance to his successor in interest as required by this subsection, the successor in interest shall, without regard to the nature of the transfer, assume liability for crediting of the rental advance, and payment of all interest thereon to the tenant in accordance with the provisions of this section;  provided, however, that if the tenant still occupies the dwelling unit for which the rental advance was given, said successor in interest may satisfy such obligation by granting the tenant free use and occupancy of the dwelling unit for a period of time equivalent to the period of time covered by the rental advance.  The liability imposed by this subsection shall not apply to a city or town which acquires title to property pursuant to chapter sixty or to a foreclosing mortgagee or a mortgagee in possession which is a financial institution chartered by the commonwealth or by the United States.

Section 15B. (1) (a) No lease relating to residential real property shall contain a provision that a lessor may, except to inspect the premises, to make repairs thereto or to show the same to a prospective tenant, purchaser, mortgagee or its agents, enter the premises before the termination date of such lease.  A lessor may, however, enter such premises:
(9) The provisions of this section shall not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of one hundred days or less in duration which lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose.

(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.

(7A) Whenever a lessor who receives rent in advance for the last month of tenancy transfers his interest in the dwelling unit for which the rental advance was received, whether by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or trustee in bankruptcy, or otherwise, the lessor shall credit an amount equal to such rental advance together with any interest which has accrued thereon for the benefit of the tenant who made such rental advance, to the successor in interest of such lessor, and said successor in interest shall be liable for crediting the tenant with such rental advance, and for paying all interest accrued thereon in accordance with the provisions of this section from the date upon which said transfer is made;  provided, however, that the granting of a mortgage on such premises shall not be deemed a transfer of interest.  The successor in interest shall, within forty-five days from the date of said transfer, notify the tenant who made such rental advance that such rental advance was so credited, and that such successor has assumed responsibility therefor pursuant to the foregoing provision.  Such notice shall also contain the lessor's name, business address, and business telephone number, and the name, business address, and business telephone number of his agent, if any.  Said notice shall be in writing.

In the event that the lessor fails to credit said rental advance to his successor in interest as required by this subsection, the successor in interest shall, without regard to the nature of the transfer, assume liability for crediting of the rental advance, and payment of all interest thereon to the tenant in accordance with the provisions of this section;  provided, however, that if the tenant still occupies the dwelling unit for which the rental advance was given, said successor in interest may satisfy such obligation by granting the tenant free use and occupancy of the dwelling unit for a period of time equivalent to the period of time covered by the rental advance.  The liability imposed by this subsection shall not apply to a city or town which acquires title to property pursuant to chapter sixty or to a foreclosing mortgagee or a mortgagee in possession which is a financial institution chartered by the commonwealth or by the United States.

Upon such transfer, the lessor or his agent shall continue to be liable with respect to the provisions of this section until:--(a) there has been a credit of the amount of the rental advance so held to the lessor's successor in interest and the tenant has been notified in writing of the transfer and of the successor in interest's name, business address, and business telephone number;  (b) there has been compliance with this clause by the successor in interest;  or (c) the rental advance has been credited to the tenant and all accrued interest has been paid thereon.

rules.title: Tenant response and return period for the deposit condition statement
rules.requirement: The prescribed condition-statement notice directs the tenant to sign if accurate or attach a signed list of additional damage if inaccurate, and to return it within fifteen days after receipt or move-in, whichever is later. rules.coverage_conditions: A tenant receiving the condition statement required when the landlord accepts a residential security deposit.

rules.quoted_span: "This is a statement of the condition of the premises you have leased or rented.  You should read it carefully in order to see if it is correct.  If it is correct you must sign it.  This will show that you agree that the list is correct and complete.  If it is not correct, you must attach a separate signed list of any damage which you believe exists in the premises.  This statement must be returned to the lessor or his agent within fifteen days after you receive this list or within fifteen days after you move in, whichever is later.  If you do not return this list, within the specified time period, a court may later view your failure to return the list as your agreement that the list is complete and correct in any suit which you may bring to recover the security deposit.''

rules.title: Demolition or substantial-remodel ground and required supporting notice
rules.requirement: A landlord may recover possession in good faith to demolish or substantially remodel. Substantial remodel means either permit-requiring replacement or substantial modification of a structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system, or lawful hazardous-material abatement; in either case, the work must be unsafe to reasonably accomplish with the tenant present and require at least 30 continuous days of vacancy. Tenants need not vacate on days they can lawfully remain under health, safety, and habitability laws. Cosmetic work alone and work safely performable without vacancy do not qualify. If permits are required, the landlord must post the permit application at the property within three business days after submission and obtain permits before issuing the termination notice. The notice must be certified under penalty of perjury and contain the intent to demolish/remodel, the prescribed return-offer statement, work description and expected remodel duration or demolition date, permit copies or the specified no-permit abatement contract, an explanation of the safety and 30-continuous-day vacancy necessity, and the §98.0706(b)(1)(C) return-offer notification.
rules.key_value: At least 30 continuous days of necessary vacancy; permit application posted within 3 business days
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: Good-faith demolition or substantial remodel; remodel requires qualifying permit-requiring structural/electrical/plumbing/mechanical system work OR lawful hazardous-material abatement AND unsafe to perform with tenant present AND vacancy>=30 CONTINUOUS days. Cosmetic-only or safely occupied work fails remodel definition; tenant need not vacate on legally safe days. Required permits:post application within 3 business days and obtain before termination notice. No-permit signed contract substitute only for hazardous-material abatement. Additional event and branch tests: Good-faith demolition or substantial remodel; remodel requires qualifying permit-requiring structural/electrical/plumbing/mechanical system work OR lawful hazardous-material abatement AND unsafe to perform with tenant present AND vacancy>=30 CONTINUOUS days. No-fault recovery requires honest intent without ulterior motives.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Division exemptions apply. Cosmetic-only or safely performable occupied work is excluded from substantial-remodel ground, not from all tenant rights.

No-fault just cause is any of the following actions 
taken by the landlord in good faith, meaning the landlord acts without ulterior 
motives and with honest intent:

The landlord seeks to recover possession to demolish or to 
substantially remodel the residential rental property.

For purposes of section 98.0704(b)(4), substantially remodel 
means either of the following that cannot be reasonably 
accomplished in a safe manner with the tenant in place and that 
requires the tenant to vacate the residential rental property for 
at least 30 continuous days:

(i) the replacement or substantial modification of any 
structural, electrical, plumbing, or mechanical system 
that requires a permit from a governmental agency; or  
(ii) the abatement of hazardous materials, including lead-
based paint, mold, or asbestos, in accordance with 
applicable federal, state, and local laws.

For purposes of section 98.0704(b)(4), a tenant is not required 
to vacate the residential rental property on any days where a 
tenant could continue living in the residential rental property 
without violating federal, state, or local laws regarding health, 
safety, and habitability. Cosmetic improvements alone, 
including painting, decorating, and minor repairs, or other 
work that can be performed safely without having the 
residential rental property vacated, do not qualify as 
substantial remodel.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

evidence.quote:
§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

rules.title: Process A charges only considered applications, with limited inadvertent-charge relief
rules.requirement: Under subdivision (c)(2)(A), applicants must not be charged until their applications are actually considered. An inadvertent charge caused by concurrent submissions avoids violating that restriction only if the unconsidered applicant is refunded within seven days, with application of the fee to another landlord-offered unit available as an alternative at the applicant's discretion.
rules.key_value: No charge before consideration; specified inadvertent-charge refund within 7 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential screening fees under process (A), which additionally requires receipt-order consideration, written criteria, and approval of the first qualifying applicant. Landlord means residential property owner, acting personally or by an agent; applicant includes guarantors and cosignors.

The section preserves housing-assistance-program deposit and fee provisions.
rules.interaction: A tenant-discretionary fee transfer is an alternative the landlord may offer; it is not unilateral authority to retain the fee or move the applicant to another unit.

rules.title: Increases must not be unconscionable and must comply with local limits
rules.requirement: A rent increase cannot be so unreasonable as to shock a fair and honest person's conscience and must comply with applicable municipal ordinances. The fact-sensitive assessment considers increase size, expenses and profitability, comparable local rents, relative bargaining power and judicial knowledge. A tenant can challenge the increase; if upheld, payment is necessary to avoid eviction.
rules.key_value: Unconscionability standard; no numeric formula
rules.coverage_conditions: Anti-Eviction Act covered tenancy and a rent increase, with separate verification of any applicable municipal ordinance; unconscionability depends on amount, expenses/profitability, comparable rents, bargaining positions and judicial assessment.
rules.exemptions: The guide says the Act may not apply to owner-occupied two- or three-unit premises with no more than two rental units. Transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house occupants are excluded. However, hotel or motel occupants who reside continually and have no alternate residence remain covered under the guide. A unit held in trust for an immediate family member who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies it is excluded. No fixed percentage safe harbor is supplied.
rules.citation: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; Fromet Properties v. Buel, 294 N.J. Super. 601 (App. Div. 1996); Hale v. Farrakhan, 390 N.J. Super. 335 (App. Div. 2007)

evidence.quote:
The increase in rent must not be 
unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest 
person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.

Factors used in defining unconscionable 
are the amount of the increase; the landlord’s expenses and profitability; how the existing and 
proposed rent compared to rents charged at similar rental properties in the same ge ographic area; 
the relative bargaining position of the parties; and the Judge’s general knowle dge

If the court finds that 
the rent increase is not unconscionable or in violation of a rent control ordinance, the tenant will 
have to pay the increase in order to avoid being evicted.

Applicability 
 The Anti-Eviction Act applies to most residential rental properties including single-family 
homes, mobile homes and land in a mobile home park, apartment buildings, and complexes. This 
law also applies to rooming and boarding homes (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 to -84).

Exceptions 
 This law may not apply to two - or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two (2) or 
fewer rental units. It does not apply to hotel guests, motel guests, or guest houses rented to a

fewer rental units. It does not apply to hotel guests, motel guests, or guest houses rented to a 
transient guest or seasonal tenant. However, hotel and motel guests are c overed under this law if, 
the occupant has no alternate residence and resides at the hotel or motel on a continual basis.

Additionally, this law does not apply to a unit held in trust on behalf of a member of the immediate 
family, if that family member is developmentally disabled, and permanently occupies the dwelling 
unit.

The Department does not have jurisdiction over the administratio n of the courts, nor can 
the Department render legal advice. This publication is based on existing New Jersey statutes, 
regulations, and court cases that concern landlord-tenant relations; however, this publication is not 
a complete summary of all laws, regulations, and court cases that concern landlord-tenant relations 
in New Jersey. Any person who plans to initiate a legal action resulting from a landlord -tenant 
dispute may wish to consult the appropriate enforcing agency, a county legal services agency, 
private counsel, or an owner’s, tenant’s, or mobile home organization. A list of additional agencies 
and organizations that may be available to provide assistance is located in the appendix section of 
this publication.  Please be advised that this guide may be amended by the Department as required, 
and will be posted on the Department’s website accordingly.

Notice requirements for rent increases are contained in the Anti -Eviction Act ( N.J.S.A. 
2A:18-61.1 et seq.). This law provides that before an owner can evict a tenant for nonpayment of 
an increased rent, they must first serve the tenant with a valid notice to quit and notice of rent 
increase. This notice does not mean that the tenant must actually leave; the tenant has the right to 
remain as long as they pay any legal increase in rent. The increase in rent must not be 
unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest 
person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.  
 The definition of unconscionable is fact sensitive. Factors used in defining unconscionable 
are the amount of the increase; the landlord’s expenses and profitability; how the existing and 
proposed rent compared to rents charged at similar rental properties in the same ge ographic area; 
the relative bargaining position of the parties; and the Judge’s general knowle dge (Fromet 
Properties v. Buel, 294 N.J. Super. 601 (App. Div. 1996); Hale v. Farrakhan, 390 N.J. Super. 
335 (App. Div. 2007)). 
If an increase is determined to be unconscionable or a tenant has not received proper notice, 
the tenant may file a complaint with a municipal rent control board where one exists. Where there 
is no municipal rent control and a rent increase is charged that a tenant does not pay on the ground 
that it is unconscionable, the landlord may file an eviction action for non -payment of the rent 
increase. A judge would decide if the increase was unconscionable or not. If the court finds that 
the rent increase is not unconscionable or in violation of a rent control ordinance, the tenant will 
have to pay the increase in order to avoid being evicted.

If a tenant fails to pay rent after being given notice of a rent increase and a Notice to Quit, 
the landlord may file a suit for eviction. The rent increase must not be unconscionable and 
must comply with all other laws or municipal ordinances, including rent control.

 The definition of unconscionable is fact sensitive. Factors used in defining unconscionable 
are the amount of the increase; the landlord’s expenses and profitability; how the existing and 
proposed rent compared to rents charged at similar rental properties in the same ge ographic area; 
the relative bargaining position of the parties; and the Judge’s general knowle dge (Fromet 
Properties v. Buel, 294 N.J. Super. 601 (App. Div. 1996); Hale v. Farrakhan, 390 N.J. Super. 
335 (App. Div. 2007)). 
If an increase is determined to be unconscionable or a tenant has not received proper notice, 
the tenant may file a complaint with a municipal rent control board where one exists. Where there 
is no municipal rent control and a rent increase is charged that a tenant does not pay on the ground 
that it is unconscionable, the landlord may file an eviction action for non -payment of the rent 
increase. A judge would decide if the increase was unconscionable or not. If the court finds that 
the rent increase is not unconscionable or in violation of a rent control ordinance, the tenant will 
have to pay the increase in order to avoid being evicted.

rules.title: Liability for threatened or actual reprisals against protected residential-tenant activity
rules.requirement: A person or agent who threatens or takes reprisals against a residential tenant for the protected enforcement, reporting, organizing, statutory-rights, or unit-owner rent-payment activity is liable for damages. Recovery is the greater of actual damages or a rent-based award of at least one and no more than three months' rent, plus suit costs including a reasonable attorney's fee.
rules.key_value: Greater of actual damages or a rent-based damages award from 1 to 3 months' rent, plus suit costs and reasonable attorney's fee
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenants protected for: commencing, proceeding with, or obtaining relief in a judicial or administrative action to obtain damages under or enforce federal, state, or local residential-premises laws, regulations, by-laws, or ordinances; exercising rights under chapter 164 section 124D; reporting actual or suspected covered health, building, municipal, state, or federal violations to a board of health, Boston commissioner of housing inspection, or another board regulating residential premises; making such reports or complaints in writing to the landlord or agent; organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization; or making or expressing an intention to make rent payments to an organization of unit owners under chapter 183A section 6(c). Liability applies to any person or agent threatening or taking reprisals.
rules.interaction: Protects the full listed set of activities; the following paragraph separately creates a conditional evidentiary presumption for specified tenancy actions.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot presents the provision without a pending or future-version label; the original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The source cross-references chapter 164 section 124D and chapter 183A section 6(c) without reproducing their full substantive requirements.
The eviction category identifies protection against retaliatory adverse tenancy action, not a general just-cause requirement.

rules.title: 2026 annual general adjustment
rules.requirement: Eligible landlords may increase 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than January 1, 2026. The 2026 AGA may not adjust rents for tenants whose tenancies began on or after January 1, 2025 and whose rents were set under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.
rules.key_value: 2026 AGA: 1.0% of 2025 permanent rent ceilings
rules.coverage_conditions: Eligible landlords and covered rent ceilings under Rent Board Regulation 1148; its additional qualification and tenant-notice conditions must be satisfied. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. This rent-amount regulation requires FULL coverage; partially covered units retain other protections but not this rent cap.
rules.exemptions: The exclusion requires BOTH a tenancy beginning on or after January 1, 2025 AND rent set pursuant to Costa-Hawkins. Exclude 2026 rent adjustment if start>=2025-01-01 AND initial rent set under Costa-Hawkins. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.

rules.title: Lawful-income and lawful-rent-payment nondiscrimination
rules.requirement: Do not discriminate in rental access or terms based on the source of lawful income or lawful rent payment. In particular, do not deny a lawful Section 8 HUD voucher recipient an apartment solely because of that income source.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental property covered by the LAD and to a tenant's lawful income or lawful rent-payment source.
rules.exemptions: The brochure's general property exceptions cover a single apartment or flat in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling and rooms rented by an owner or occupant in that person's occupied one-family residence, with residence determined at the time of rental. It also permits religious organizations to prefer persons of the same religion. The older-person housing exception concerns only familial-status discrimination and does not state a lawful-income exception.
rules.quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses. This
means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the
lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher the right to
rent an apartment based solely on that source of lawful
income.

conditions.description: The protection concerns lawful income or lawful rent-payment sources, including lawful receipt of a Section 8 HUD voucher.

rules.temporal_notes: The guidance describes an operative prohibition but provides no effective date. The brochure bears revision notation 06.18.15.
limitations: No statutory section for this prohibition or operative date is supplied.

The source does not establish whether the guidance was updated after its 2015 revision.

rules.title: Discriminatory neighborhood representations and solicitations affecting rentals prohibited
rules.requirement: No person may directly or indirectly induce, attempt to induce, prevent, or attempt to prevent a dwelling rental through representations about the entry or prospective entry of persons with the characteristics listed in subsection 13(a), or the effects of that entry. The prohibition also covers unsolicited communications intended to induce a rental when the solicitor knew or should have known the solicitation would reasonably be associated with such neighborhood entry.
rules.coverage_conditions: Any person affecting rental of any dwelling through the specified conduct. Listed characteristics are age, race, color, religion, sex, gender identity, national or ethnic origin, economic level, handicap, or having a child.
rules.exemptions: No conduct-specific exception is stated.

rules.title: HSNA rights cannot be waived or contractually limited
rules.requirement: HSNA requirements cannot be waived. A lease, contract or other agreement purporting to waive or limit a tenant's or former homeowner's substantive or procedural HSNA rights is contrary to public policy, unenforceable and void. This protects the ordinance's rights without independently creating a just-cause eviction requirement.
rules.key_value: Waivers and contractual limitations are unenforceable and void
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants and former homeowners covered by Boston's HSNA when landlords or foreclosing owners intend to end tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy.
rules.exemptions: The ordinance's listed exempt residences are those in hospitals, skilled nursing facilities or health facilities, and those in nonprofit facilities primarily providing short-term substance-abuse treatment, assistance or therapy.
rules.quoted_span:
The requirements of this Ordinance may not be waived, and any term of any
lease, contract, or other agreement that purports to waive or limit a tenant’s or
former homeowner’s substantive or procedural rights under this Ordinance are
contrary to public policy, unenforceable, and void.
rules.interaction:
Private agreements cannot waive or limit HSNA rights; an HSNA violation nevertheless does not halt the eviction process.

rules.title: Ordinary deposit return, deductions and remedies
rules.requirement: Within 30 days after tenancy termination, return the deposit and earned interest less permissible deductions by personal delivery, registered mail or certified mail. Send an itemized deduction list by registered or certified mail within the same period. Deductions may cover damage beyond ordinary wear and other amounts due under the lease, but none may be made while the tenant remains in possession. A landlord may sue for a deficiency; wrongful withholding may support double damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees.
rules.key_value: 30 days after tenancy termination; potential recovery of double the amount wrongfully withheld
rules.coverage_conditions: Deposits governed by the Security Deposit Law. If a tenant leaves early without legal cause, the guide treats termination as rerental or lease expiry, whichever occurs first, provided lease-required notice was given.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings unless the tenant opts in as described. Qualifying displacement and Safe Housing Act termination have separate return deadlines.
rules.quoted_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant
rules.interaction:
Special return deadlines are separately described for displacement and domestic-violence termination.

evidence.quote:
If a tenant terminates the lease agreement prior to the expiration of the lease pursuant to 
the Safe Housing Act , (N.J.S.A. 46:8-9.6), the tenant is entitled to the return of their security 
deposit. Within 15 business days after the lease  is terminated, the landlord shall make available 
the return of the tenant’s security deposit, plus any interest earned, to the tenant or the tenant’s 
agent.

The Security Deposit Law applies to most  residential rental properties, including mobile 
homes. The exception is an owner-occupied two-, or three-family dwelling. A tenant in an owner-
occupied two-, or three-family dwelling may, however, make this provision applicable to their 
tenancy 30 days  after sending a  written  request  to the landlord  that  the landlord  fulfill  the 
requirements of the Security Deposit Law.

Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant

Deductions may 
include the cost of any damages over and above normal wear and tear, and any other money due 
the landlord under the terms of the lease. The landlord must return the money either by personal 
delivery, registered, or certified mail.

If there are a ny deductions made from the security deposit 
by the landlord, an itemized list of these deductions must also be sent to the tenant by registered 
or certified mail within 30 days from the termination of the tenancy.

If the amount of money owed 
to the landlord for damages or unpaid rent is greater than the amount of the security deposit, the 
landlord may sue for the difference. No deductions shall be made from a security deposit of a 
tenant who remains in possession of the rental premises.

If a landlord fails to return the security deposit within 30 days, or the tenant disagrees with 
the amount deducted, the tenant may sue for double the amount of the security deposit that the 
tenant contends was wrongfully withheld. If the tenant is successful, the court ma y award the 
tenant double the amount wrongly withheld, together with court costs and reasonable attorney’s 
fees

However, if the tenant breaks the lease and moves out of the dwelling 
unit prior to the expiration of the lease, without l egal cause, the lease is not considered to be

rules.title: Just cause and a written statement of cause for covered tenancy terminations
rules.requirement: An owner may not terminate a covered tenancy without just cause stated in the written termination notice after the tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 12 months. If additional adult tenants are added before an existing tenant reaches 24 months, protection applies only when all tenants have at least 12 months of continuous lawful occupancy OR at least one tenant has 24 months. Permitted at-fault grounds are rent default; material lease breach, including violation after written corrective notice; statutory nuisance; statutory waste; refusal, after the owner's written request, to renew an expired written lease for a similar duration and similar lawful provisions; specified criminal activity or threats; prohibited assignment or subletting; refusal of legally authorized entry; unlawful use; failure of a terminated employee, agent, or licensee to vacate; or failure to surrender possession after the tenant's written termination notice or a written surrender offer accepted in writing. The renewal-refusal ground applies to written leases ending on or after January 1, 2020, or January 1, 2022 for mobilehome tenancies. No-fault grounds are qualifying owner or family occupancy, withdrawal from the rental market, compliance with specified governmental or court orders or a local ordinance necessitating vacancy, and qualifying demolition or substantial remodeling. Owner occupancy and remodeling have additional conditions described in separate rules.
rules.key_value: 12 months; alternatively all tenants 12 months or at least one tenant 24 months when additional adults are added before an existing tenant reaches 24 months
rules.coverage_conditions: Lawful residential occupancy, including leases, subleases, and rented dwellings or units in mobilehome parks. Owner includes a person acting directly or through an agent with the right to offer the property for rent and a predecessor in interest. The duration test concerns tenant occupancy, not building age.
rules.exemptions: Excluded are transient/tourist hotel occupancy under section 1940(b); accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, or specified adult residential facility; school or higher-education dormitories owned and operated by the institution; housing sharing a kitchen or bathroom with an owner whose principal residence is there; single-family owner-occupied residences, including an owner-occupant renting no more than two units or bedrooms, including ADUs/JADUs, and an owner-occupied mobilehome; a two-unit single structure with neither unit an ADU/JADU where the owner occupied one unit as a principal residence at tenancy inception and continues occupying it; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, except mobilehomes; specified recorded or subsidized affordable housing; and mobilehome homeowners under section 798.9. Separately alienable property, including a mobilehome, is exempt only if the owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome-park management, AND tenants receive the prescribed exemption statement. That statement must be in the rental agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, or July 1, 2022 for mobilehomes; for tenancies existing before the applicable date, it need not be in the agreement. Qualifying local just-cause ordinances displace this section as described in interaction.
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.interaction:
Local just-cause ordinances adopted on or before September 1, 2019 displace this section. Later adopted or amended ordinances displace it only if their causes are consistent with this section, they further restrict termination or increase relocation assistance or provide other lawful tenant protections, AND they contain a binding finding of greater protection. A property is not subject to both regimes. A less-protective ordinance adopted after September 1, 2019 is unenforceable unless this section is repealed. Adding the prescribed exemption notice to a new or renewed lease counts as a similar provision for the renewal-refusal ground.

evidence.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

(1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940.
(2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in Section 1569.2 of the Health and Safety Code, or an adult residential facility, as defined in Chapter 6 of Division 6 of Title 22 of the Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the State Department of Social Services.
(3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school.
(4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property.

(5) Single-family owner-occupied residences, including both of the following:
(A) A residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms, including, but not limited to, an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.
(B) A mobilehome.
(6) A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner’s principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an accessory dwelling unit or a junior accessory dwelling unit.
(7) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15
years, unless the housing is a mobilehome.

(8) Residential real property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following apply:
(A) The owner is not any of the following:
(i) A real estate investment trust, as defined in Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code.
(ii) A corporation.
(iii) A limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.
(iv) Management of a mobilehome park, as defined in Section 798.2.

The tenants have been
provided written notice that the residential property is exempt from this section using the following statement:
“This property is not subject to the rent limits imposed by Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code and is not subject to the just cause requirements of Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code. This property meets the requirements of Sections 1947.12 (d)(5) and 1946.2 (e)(8) of the Civil Code and the owner is not any of the following: (1) a real estate investment trust, as defined by Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code; (2) a corporation; or (3) a limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.”

(ii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for a tenancy existing before July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the
rental agreement.
(II) For a tenancy in a mobilehome existing before July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) may, but is not required to, be provided in the rental agreement.
(iii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (II), for any tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, the notice required under clause (i) must be provided in the rental agreement.
(II) For any tenancy in a mobilehome commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2022, the notice required under clause (i) shall be provided in the rental agreement.

Addition of a provision containing the notice required under clause (i) to any new or renewed rental agreement or fixed-term lease constitutes a similar provision for the purposes of subparagraph
(E) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (b).

(9) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement with a government agency, or other recorded document as affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code, or subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in Section 50093 of the Health and Safety Code or comparable federal statutes.

If any additional adult tenants are added to the lease before an existing tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 24 months, then this subdivision shall only apply if either of the following are satisfied:
(1) All of the tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the residential real property for 12 months or more.
(2) One or more tenants have continuously and lawfully
occupied the residential real property for 24 months or more.

(A) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted on or before September 1, 2019, in which case the local ordinance shall apply.
(B) Residential real property subject to a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy adopted or amended after September 1, 2019, that is more protective than this section, in which case the local ordinance shall apply.

For purposes of this subparagraph, an ordinance is “more protective” if it meets all of the following criteria:
(i) The just cause for termination of a residential tenancy under the local ordinance is consistent with this section.
(ii) The ordinance further limits the reasons for termination of a residential tenancy, provides for higher relocation assistance amounts, or provides additional tenant protections that are not prohibited by any other provision of law.
(iii) The local government has made a binding finding within their local ordinance that the ordinance is more protective than the provisions of this section.

(2) A residential real property shall not be subject to both a local ordinance requiring just cause for termination of a residential tenancy and this section.
(3) A local ordinance adopted
after September 1, 2019, that is less protective than this section shall not be enforced unless this section is repealed.

(1) “Owner” includes any person, acting as principal or through an agent, having the right to offer residential real property for rent, and includes a predecessor in interest to the owner.
(2) “Residential real property” means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.
(3) “Tenancy” means the lawful occupation of residential real
property and includes a lease or sublease.
(l) This section shall not apply to a homeowner of a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.9.
(m) This section shall become operative on April 1, 2024.

(n) This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed.
