Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

All tenant not- at-fault evictions require payment of relocation assistance and the filing of a 
Declaration of Intent to Evict form with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) before 
evicting tenants from units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause 
Ordinance (JCO). Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices. 
 Not-At-Fault Reasons for Eviction
1. The landlord evicts for the occupancy of her/himself, spouse, grandchildren, children,  
parents or grandparents, or a resident manager (Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC)  
151.09.A.8, 165.03.H.). Evictions for the purpose of resident manager occupancy are 
allowed only if required by law or an affordable housing covenant, or a regulatory  
agreement. Landlords must comply with the restrictions and requirements of LAMC Section  
151.30.
2. The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.
3. The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.
4. The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both the owner and plaintiff and seeks 
to recover possession to vacate the property prior to sale (LAMC 151.09.A.12, 165.03.K.).
5. Residential Hotel Unit conversion or demolition (LAMC 151.09.A.13, 165.03.L.).
6. The landlord seeks to recover possession of the rental unit to convert the subject property 
to an affordable housing accommodation (LAMC 151.09.A.14, 165.03.M.).
7. The landlord demolishes the property or converts the use of the property to condominiums, 
stock cooperatives, community apartment projects, hotels, and commercial uses, regardless 
of whether the property is subject to the RSO OR JCO (LAMC 47.06 & 47.07).

violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices. 
 Not-At-Fault Reasons for Eviction
1. The landlord evicts for the occupancy of her/himself, spouse, grandchildren, children,  
parents or grandparents, or a resident manager (Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC)  
151.09.A.8, 165.03.H.). Evictions for the purpose of resident manager occupancy are 
allowed only if required by law or an affordable housing covenant, or a regulatory  
agreement. Landlords must comply with the restrictions and requirements of LAMC Section  
151.30.
2. The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.
3. The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.
4. The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both the owner and plaintiff and seeks 
to recover possession to vacate the property prior to sale (LAMC 151.09.A.12, 165.03.K.).
5. Residential Hotel Unit conversion or demolition (LAMC 151.09.A.13, 165.03.L.).
6. The landlord seeks to recover possession of the rental unit to convert the subject property 
to an affordable housing accommodation (LAMC 151.09.A.14, 165.03.M.).
7. The landlord demolishes the property or converts the use of the property to condominiums, 
stock cooperatives, community apartment projects, hotels, and commercial uses, regardless 
of whether the property is subject to the RSO OR JCO (LAMC 47.06 & 47.07).

rules.title: Receipt for prepaid last-month rent at the time of payment
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent receiving last-month rent in advance at or before tenancy commencement must immediately provide a receipt specifying amount, receipt date, intended last-month use, recipient identity and represented landlord identity, and the premises. It must also state the statutory interest entitlement and advise the tenant to provide a forwarding address at termination for the interest.
rules.key_value: Receipt at the time the last-month rent advance is paid
rules.coverage_conditions: A tenant or prospective tenant pays last-month rent in advance to a residential landlord or agent at or before tenancy commencement. The interest disclosure states five percent annually or lesser interest received from the bank, payable under subsection (2)(a).
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: This is the advance-rent receipt, not the separate signed security-deposit receipt under subsection (2)(b).
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
limitations: The organizer category includes allowed upfront charges and their receipts/refunds. This rule concerns prepaid last-month rent, not a security deposit; its amounts, interest and remedies must remain distinct from deposit provisions.
rules.quoted_span: (2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.

Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.

rules.requirement: On receiving security or within ten days after tenancy commencement, whichever is later, the landlord or agent must provide a separate signed statement of the premises' present condition and existing damage. It must include the prescribed notice in twelve-point bold type at the top of the first page.
rules.key_value: Later of deposit receipt or 10 days after commencement; 12-point bold notice
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential lessors or agents accepting a deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant. The damage list includes existing sanitary/building-code violations certified by the relevant local official or adjudicated by a court.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: The notice explains tenant signature/correction duties, return timing, and the possible evidentiary consequence of silence.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
limitations: The requirement summarizes the prescribed notice; use the exact source text, not this summary, when evaluating notice wording.
rules.quoted_span:
(c) Any lessor of residential real property, or his agent, who accepts a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall, upon receipt of such security deposit, or within ten days after commencement of the tenancy, whichever is later, furnish to such tenant or prospective tenant a separate written statement of the present condition of the premises to be leased or rented.  Such written statement shall also contain a comprehensive listing of any damage then existing in the premises, including, but not limited to, any violations of the state sanitary or state building codes certified by a local board of health or building official or adjudicated by a court and then existing in the premises.  Such statement shall be signed by the lessor or his agent and contain the following notice in twelve-point bold-face type at the top of the first page thereof:
"This is a statement of the condition of the premises you have leased or rented.  You should read it carefully in order to see if it is correct.  If it is correct you must sign it.  This will show that you agree that the list is correct and complete.  If it is not correct, you must attach a separate signed list of any damage which you believe exists in the premises.  This statement must be returned to the lessor or his agent within fifteen days after you receive this list or within fifteen days after you move in, whichever is later.  If you do not return this list, within the specified time period, a court may later view your failure to return the list as your agreement that the list is complete and correct in any suit which you may bring to recover the security deposit.''

Section 15B. (1) (a) No lease relating to residential real property shall contain a provision that a lessor may, except to inspect the premises, to make repairs thereto or to show the same to a prospective tenant, purchaser, mortgagee or its agents, enter the premises before the termination date of such lease.  A lessor may, however, enter such premises:
(9) The provisions of this section shall not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of one hundred days or less in duration which lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose.

(e) A security deposit shall continue to be the property of the tenant making such deposit, shall not be commingled with the assets of the lessor, and shall not be subject to the claims of any creditor of the lessor or of the lessor's successor in interest, including a foreclosing mortgagee or trustee in bankruptcy;  provided, however, that the tenant shall be entitled to only such interest as is provided for in subsection (3)(b).
(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.
(b) Any lessor or his agent who receives a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give said tenant or prospective tenant at the time of receiving such security deposit a receipt indicating the amount of such security deposit, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom such security deposit is received, the date on which it is received, and a description of the premises leased or rented.  Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit.

This statement must be returned to the lessor or his agent within fifteen days after you receive this list or within fifteen days after you move in, whichever is later. rules.title: Habitability and repair deductions as eviction defenses
rules.requirement: A tenant may defend nonpayment eviction using a landlord's failure to remedy vital habitability defects after reasonable notice and time to repair, including necessary repair deductions or rent setoff. The tenant must prove the defects, lack of tenant causation, notice and landlord failure. A landlord may still sue; the guide cautions that payment may be necessary if the defense fails.
rules.key_value: Fact-dependent nonpayment defense
rules.coverage_conditions: Vital-facility defects affecting habitability, not caused by the tenant, with landlord notice and adequate opportunity to repair.
rules.exemptions: Maintenance issues that do not threaten safety or habitability do not qualify; not every defect or inconvenience is a breach.

Remedies if the landlord fails to maintain the property in a habitable condition 
1.  Repair and Deduct 
If the landlord does not keep the premises in a  habitable condition, a tenant may repair any vital 
deficiencies and deduct the amount of the repair from the rent. The landlord’s failure to maintain 
the property could also lead to what is called a constructive eviction by the tenant (see below for 
explanation). The tenant may seek rent abatement (a reduction in rent) or withhold the rent or a 
portion of the rent if the property is not habitable (Marini v. Ireland, 56 N.J. 130 (1970); Dowler 
v. Boczkowski, 148 N.J. 512 (1997)) 
30 
Before applying the remedies  of repair and deduct, constructive eviction, rent abatement, or 
withholding the rent or a portion of the rent, the following must apply: 
1. The defect must be of a “vital facility.” Vital facilities are those items necessary to make
the rental unit habitable. Example of defects of vital facilities include broken toilets, no hot
or cold water, lack of heat or electricity, broken windows, or air conditioning.
2. The tenant must not have caused the condition.
3. The tenant must have notified the landlord that the deficient condition existed and allowed
the landlord adequate time to fix the defect. Notice to the landlord should be given by the
tenant in writing and by certified mail, return receipt requested.
A maintenance problem that does not threaten residents’ sa fety, or does not affect
habitability, does not provide a basis for rent withholding or repair and deduct. Rent withholding 
was authorized when the New Jersey Supreme Court held that the obligation of a tenant to pay 
rent and the obligation, (whether written or not) on the part of a landlord to maintain the property 
in a livable condition are mutually dependent (Berzito v. Gambino Rental Abatement, 114 N.J. 
Super. 124 (1971), 63 N.J. 460 (1973); Housing Authority of City of Newark v. Scott, 137 N.J. 
Super. 110 (App. Div. 1975)).  
The New Jersey Supreme Court has permitted the self-help remedy of “repair and deduct.” 
A landlord promises at the beginning of a lease that the vital facilities needed to make the dwelling 
unit livable are in good condition and th e property will be maintained. When there are defects in 
the vital facilities, a tenant must first notify the landlord of the situation and allow a reasonable 
amount of time for the landlord to make repairs or replacements. If a landlord fails to take action, 
a tenant may have the repairs made and deduct the cost from future rent. However, a landlord may 
still take a tenant to court for nonpayment of rent. As a defense, the tenant would have to prove 
the presence of defects, the failure of the owner to act despite having received reasonable notice, 
and the need to make repairs. In the event the matter goes to court, the tenant will very likely be 
required to deposit the full amount of the rent with the court. If there is a finding in favor of the 
landlord, in most cases, the unpaid rent must be paid by the end of the court day to avoid eviction. 
If there are defects in the vital facilities and the landlord has not repaired them after 
receiving proper and timely notice from the tenant, the tenant may either seek a decrease in rent 
by court action or simply withhold rent. A landlord may bring an eviction action for nonpayment 
of rent. As a defense, the tenant must prove the necessity to make repairs and the failure of the 
landlord to act despite having received reasonable notice. To avoid possible eviction in the event 
the court finds in favor of the landlord, the tenant should save the amount of money withheld so 
that he will be able to pay it if ordered by the judge. It is advisable to set up a separate bank account 
for this purpose. 
As to air conditioning, the Superior Court, Appellate Division has held that air conditioning 
that is part of the original tenancy may be considered a “vital facility,” and air conditioning failure 
affects the habitability of the premises.

2. Constructive eviction  – Constructive eviction occurs when a tenant breaks the lease without
penalties because the landlord is guilty of neglect or default, which makes the premises unsafe,
31 
unfit, or unsuitable for occupanc y. Reste Realty v. Cooper , 53 N.J. 444 (1969) , established the 
foundation for constructive eviction. If a tenant invokes the remedy of constructive eviction, and 
the landlord is found to be negligent in maintaining the rental unit, the tenant is entitled t o the 
return of the security deposit and is not responsible for the rent for the balance of the lease or the 
cost of re-renting the property.  
3. Rent abatement (reduction)  – Upon entering into a lease, the tenant’s promise to pay rent and
the landlord’s warranty of habitability are interdependent. In Berzito v. Gambino, 63 N.J. 460
(1973), the court held that a tenant claiming that the landlord did not maintain the property in a
habitable condition may initiate an action to recover all or part of the deposit paid when the lease
was finalized or all of the rent paid. If the court finds that the landlord did not maintain the property
in a habitable condition, the tenant will be charged only with the reasonable rental value of the
property in its imperfect condition during the tenancy.
4. Withholding the rent or a portion of the rent  – If the landlord breaches his obligation of
maintaining the property at an adequate standard of habitability, a tenant may withhold the rent or
a portion of the rent to be used as a set-off, because of the deficient condition. If the landlord
institutes an eviction proceeding for non-payment of rent, the tenant is entitled to use the landlord’s
breach of obligation to provide a habitable residence as a defense and justification for the set-off
(deduction of rental payment) (Marini v. Ireland, 56 N.J. 130 (1970))

required to deposit the full amount of the rent with the court. If there is a finding in favor of the 
landlord, in most cases, the unpaid rent must be paid by the end of the court day to avoid eviction. 
If there are defects in the vital facilities and the landlord has not repaired them after 
receiving proper and timely notice from the tenant, the tenant may either seek a decrease in rent 
by court action or simply withhold rent. A landlord may bring an eviction action for nonpayment 
of rent. As a defense, the tenant must prove the necessity to make repairs and the failure of the 
landlord to act despite having received reasonable notice. To avoid possible eviction in the event 
the court finds in favor of the landlord, the tenant should save the amount of money withheld so 
that he will be able to pay it if ordered by the judge. It is advisable to set up a separate bank account 
for this purpose. 
As to air conditioning, the Superior Court, Appellate Division has held that air conditioning 
that is part of the original tenancy may be considered a “vital facility,” and air conditioning failure 
affects the habitability of the premises.

31 
unfit, or unsuitable for occupanc y. Reste Realty v. Cooper , 53 N.J. 444 (1969) , established the

the landlord is found to be negligent in maintaining the rental unit, the tenant is entitled t o the 
return of the security deposit and is not responsible for the rent for the balance of the lease or the 
cost of re-renting the property.  
3. Rent abatement (reduction)  – Upon entering into a lease, the tenant’s promise to pay rent and
the landlord’s warranty of habitability are interdependent. In Berzito v. Gambino, 63 N.J. 460
(1973), the court held that a tenant claiming that the landlord did not maintain the property in a
habitable condition may initiate an action to recover all or part of the deposit paid when the lease
was finalized or all of the rent paid. If the court finds that the landlord did not maintain the property
in a habitable condition, the tenant will be charged only with the reasonable rental value of the
property in its imperfect condition during the tenancy.

maintaining the property at an adequate standard of habitability, a tenant may withhold the rent or
a portion of the rent to be used as a set-off, because of the deficient condition. If the landlord
institutes an eviction proceeding for non-payment of rent, the tenant is entitled to use the landlord’s
breach of obligation to provide a habitable residence as a defense and justification for the set-off
(deduction of rental payment) (Marini v. Ireland, 56 N.J. 130 (1970))

Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

All tenant not- at-fault evictions require payment of relocation assistance and the filing of a 
Declaration of Intent to Evict form with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) before 
evicting tenants from units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause 
Ordinance (JCO). Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices. 
 Not-At-Fault Reasons for Eviction
1. The landlord evicts for the occupancy of her/himself, spouse, grandchildren, children,  
parents or grandparents, or a resident manager (Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC)  
151.09.A.8, 165.03.H.). Evictions for the purpose of resident manager occupancy are 
allowed only if required by law or an affordable housing covenant, or a regulatory  
agreement. Landlords must comply with the restrictions and requirements of LAMC Section  
151.30.
2. The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.
3. The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.
4. The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both the owner and plaintiff and seeks 
to recover possession to vacate the property prior to sale (LAMC 151.09.A.12, 165.03.K.).
5. Residential Hotel Unit conversion or demolition (LAMC 151.09.A.13, 165.03.L.).
6. The landlord seeks to recover possession of the rental unit to convert the subject property 
to an affordable housing accommodation (LAMC 151.09.A.14, 165.03.M.).
7. The landlord demolishes the property or converts the use of the property to condominiums, 
stock cooperatives, community apartment projects, hotels, and commercial uses, regardless 
of whether the property is subject to the RSO OR JCO (LAMC 47.06 & 47.07).

6. The landlord seeks to recover possession of the rental unit to convert the subject property 
to an affordable housing accommodation (LAMC 151.09.A.14, 165.03.M.).

rules.title: No discriminatory denial or unavailability of a dwelling
rules.requirement: A dwelling must not otherwise be made unavailable or denied in rental housing because of the protected characteristics listed in subdivision (k), including perceived characteristics and protected associations.
rules.coverage_conditions: The rental application of subdivision (k)'s otherwise-make-unavailable-or-deny prohibition. Its list is race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, familial status, source of income, disability, genetic information, veteran or military status, and national origin. Source of income includes lawful, verifiable tenant or representative payments, payments to the owner on the tenant's behalf, public assistance, housing subsidies, Section 8, and HUD-VASH; an owner is not a tenant representative unless the source is HUD-VASH. Subdivision (m) includes perceived traits and association.
rules.exemptions: An income-level or income-source inquiry alone is not source-of-income discrimination under (p)(2); this does not authorize discriminatory denial because of an income source.
rules.interaction: This paragraph's list does not expressly include marital status or ancestry; those terms must not be silently copied from other subdivisions, which may independently apply.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset unspecified; source version amended effective 2024-01-01.
limitations: This record is restricted to rental-housing denial, without asserting that other subdivisions protect fewer characteristics.

When an owner is occupying a home and is renting to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics. However, the owner still cannot make, print, or publish discriminatory statements, notices, or advertisements.
When sharing a living area in a single dwelling, the owner or occupant may state or imply that the housing is available only to person of one sex.

Housing specifically for seniors may be limited based on age.
Under some circumstances, housing for homeless youth may be limited based on age.
Can a housing provider refuse to rent to families with children?
Generally, housing providers cannot discriminate against families with children. This is called “familial status” discrimination and protections include:
Prohibiting landlords and other types of housing providers from refusing to rent to someone because their household includes children.
Requiring that admission and occupancy requirements  be enforced the same for everyone, including families with children. For example, if a housing provider allows up to four people to live in a one-bedroom unit, they must allow a family of two parents and two children, or a mother or father with three children, to reside in the unit.
Prohibiting housing providers from having conditions or rules that discriminate against households with children, such as charging a higher security deposit to households with children or excluding children from playing in common areas open to other tenants.
However, housing that has been specifically designed for senior citizens (persons 55 and older in some cases or 62 and older in others) can exclude people based on age, including families with children. To qualify as “senior housing,” a housing accommodation must meet specific legally defined requirements, which may include a minimum number of units, age-based residency limits, and design features.
Is it legal to develop and market housing for seniors?
Yes, but only when the facility or community is:
Provided under any state or federal program that the Federal Department of Housing and Urban Development has determined to be specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons
Designed to meet the physical and social needs of senior citizens; or
A mobile home park that:
Is intended for, and solely occupied by, people aged 62 years or older; or
Is intended and operated for occupancy by people aged 55 years or older and that meets a set of requirements including: at least 80% of the occupied units are intended to be occupied by at least one person who is 55 or older, the park publishes and adheres to policies and procedures demonstrating the intent for occupancy by people 55 or older, and the park complies with HUD’s rules for verification of occupancy.

(k) To otherwise make unavailable or deny a dwelling based on discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, familial status, source of income, disability, genetic information, veteran or military status, or national origin.

For the purposes of this section, a housing owner or landlord is not considered a representative of
a tenant unless the source of income is a federal Department of Housing and Urban Development Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing voucher.
(2) For the purposes of this section, it shall not constitute discrimination based on source of income to make a written or oral inquiry concerning the level or source of income.

criteria.condition: For applicant exclusion only, an owner occupying a home AND renting to one additional person may exclude based on protected traits; this does NOT authorize discriminatory statements/notices/advertisements and is not stated as an exemption from all ongoing-tenant protections.

evidence.quote: When an owner is occupying a home and is renting to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics. However, the owner still cannot make, print, or publish discriminatory statements, notices, or advertisements.

criteria.condition: When sharing a living area in a single dwelling, owner OR occupant may state/imply availability only to a person of one sex. Keep this limited shared-living statement qualification distinct from a blanket advertising exemption.

evidence.quote: When sharing a living area in a single dwelling, the owner or occupant may state or imply that the housing is available only to person of one sex.

criteria.condition: Qualified senior housing can restrict admission by age, including families with children; homelessness-youth age limits exist only under unspecified circumstances. A senior label alone is insufficient: apply the legally defined program/design/occupancy requirements. For mobilehome parks: intended and solely occupied by people 62+ OR intended/operated for 55+ AND at least 80% of occupied units intended for one 55+ occupant AND published/adhered intent policies AND HUD occupancy verification. These are admission qualifications, not blanket deposit or termination exemptions.

evidence.quote:
Housing specifically for seniors may be limited based on age.
Under some circumstances, housing for homeless youth may be limited based on age.
Can a housing provider refuse to rent to families with children?
Generally, housing providers cannot discriminate against families with children. This is called “familial status” discrimination and protections include:
Prohibiting landlords and other types of housing providers from refusing to rent to someone because their household includes children.
Requiring that admission and occupancy requirements  be enforced the same for everyone, including families with children. For example, if a housing provider allows up to four people to live in a one-bedroom unit, they must allow a family of two parents and two children, or a mother or father with three children, to reside in the unit.
Prohibiting housing providers from having conditions or rules that discriminate against households with children, such as charging a higher security deposit to households with children or excluding children from playing in common areas open to other tenants.
However, housing that has been specifically designed for senior citizens (persons 55 and older in some cases or 62 and older in others) can exclude people based on age, including families with children. To qualify as “senior housing,” a housing accommodation must meet specific legally defined requirements, which may include a minimum number of units, age-based residency limits, and design features.
Is it legal to develop and market housing for seniors?
Yes, but only when the facility or community is:
Provided under any state or federal program that the Federal Department of Housing and Urban Development has determined to be specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons
Designed to meet the physical and social needs of senior citizens; or
A mobile home park that:
Is intended for, and solely occupied by, people aged 62 years or older; or
Is intended and operated for occupancy by people aged 55 years or older and that meets a set of requirements including: at least 80% of the occupied units are intended to be occupied by at least one person who is 55 or older, the park publishes and adheres to policies and procedures demonstrating the intent for occupancy by people 55 or older, and the park complies with HUD’s rules for verification of occupancy.

criteria.condition: A dwelling is otherwise made unavailable OR denied because of a subdivision (k) characteristic: race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity/expression, sexual orientation, familial status, income source, disability, genetic information, veteran/military status OR national origin. Use this list, not another clause list.

evidence.quote: (k) To otherwise make unavailable or deny a dwelling based on discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, familial status, source of income, disability, genetic information, veteran or military status, or national origin.

rules.title: Unit-type and subsidy coverage for security-deposit interest
rules.requirement: The table marks fully and partially covered units as subject to security-deposit interest and the listed exempt units as not subject to that local requirement.
rules.key_value: Deposit interest: fully and partially covered Yes; exempt No
rules.coverage_conditions: Fully covered types: most pre-1980 multifamily units, single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies, and single-family homes with five or more individually leased rooms. Partially covered types: units built and receiving a certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning on or after January 1, 1996, and most condominiums. Starred types include Housing Choice Voucher/Section 8, Shelter Plus Care, VASH Voucher, LIHTC, California Community Housing Agency, HOME, City of Berkeley Housing Trust Fund, and Mental Health Safety Act subsidies; Rental Supplement Program, Section 8 Loan Management Set Aside, and Project-based Section 8 follow these unit types if the project has no HUD-insured or HUD-held mortgage. Section 202 elderly and Section 811 disability units, and the latter three subsidy types with HUD-insured or HUD-held project mortgages, are partially covered regardless of type and receive deposit-interest coverage. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.
rules.exemptions: A duplex must have been owner-occupied December 31, 1979 and have an owner currently living in one unit to qualify as an exempt Golden Duplex. Shared-kitchen or shared-bath units are exempt if the owner lived on the property when the tenancy began. Tenancies starting after November 7, 2018 are exempt on properties where one unit is an ADU and either unit is owner-occupied. University rental units such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives are also exempt. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.

sources.quote: This table is intended as a guide. Individual circumstances may differ.

rules.title: Termination of employment-conditioned tenancy
rules.requirement: When residence is conditioned on employment by the landlord and that employment ends, the landlord may seek eviction with a Notice to Quit three days before filing.
rules.key_value: 3-day Notice to Quit
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenancy expressly conditioned on working for the landlord, including as superintendent or janitor.
rules.exemptions: The guide says the Act may not apply to owner-occupied two- or three-unit premises with no more than two rental units. Transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house occupants are excluded. However, hotel or motel occupants who reside continually and have no alternate residence remain covered under the guide. A unit held in trust for an immediate family member who is developmentally disabled and permanently occupies it is excluded.
rules.quoted_span:
If a tenant resides in the property on the condition that, he is employed by the landlord as 
a superintendent, janitor, or in some other job and that employment is terminated the 
landlord may file a suit for eviction. A Notice to Quit must be served on the tenant three 
days prior to filing a suit for eviction
rules.interaction: A residential eviction ground; no employment-law rule is extracted.

evidence.quote:
If a tenant resides in the property on the condition that, he is employed by the landlord as 
a superintendent, janitor, or in some other job and that employment is terminated the 
landlord may file a suit for eviction. A Notice to Quit must be served on the tenant three 
days prior to filing a suit for eviction

Applicability 
 The Anti-Eviction Act applies to most residential rental properties including single-family 
homes, mobile homes and land in a mobile home park, apartment buildings, and complexes. This 
law also applies to rooming and boarding homes (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 to -84).

Exceptions 
 This law may not apply to two - or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two (2) or 
fewer rental units. It does not apply to hotel guests, motel guests, or guest houses rented to a

fewer rental units. It does not apply to hotel guests, motel guests, or guest houses rented to a 
transient guest or seasonal tenant. However, hotel and motel guests are c overed under this law if, 
the occupant has no alternate residence and resides at the hotel or motel on a continual basis.

Additionally, this law does not apply to a unit held in trust on behalf of a member of the immediate 
family, if that family member is developmentally disabled, and permanently occupies the dwelling 
unit.

rules.title: Written-lease nonpayment notice and opportunity to cure
rules.requirement: When rent due under a written lease is neglected or refused, the landlord may determine the lease with fourteen days' written notice to quit. The lease is not determined on that basis if, on or before the answer is due in the landlord's action to recover possession, the tenant pays or tenders to the landlord or the landlord's attorney all rent then due, interest, and suit costs.
rules.key_value: 14 days written notice; cure by the answer due date
rules.coverage_conditions: Rent due under a written lease; written notice from landlord to tenant; cure in the landlord's action to recover possession.
rules.exemptions: Timely payment or tender of all rent then due with interest and costs of suit prevents determination under this provision.
rules.interaction: The notice and cure provisions operate together; a notice alone does not eliminate the statutory cure opportunity.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot contains this provision with no pending or future-version label; its original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The organizer eviction category is used for termination and possession procedures; this provision does not itself establish a general just-cause requirement.
rules.quoted_span: Section 11. Upon the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due under a written lease, fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease, unless the tenant, on or before the day the answer is due, in an action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises, pays or tenders to the landlord or to his attorney all rent then due, with interest and costs of suit. If the neglect or refusal to pay the rent due was caused by a failure or delay of the federal government, the commonwealth or any municipality, or any departments, agencies or authorities thereof, in the mailing or delivery of any subsistence or rental payment, check or voucher other than a salary payment to either the tenant or the landlord, the court in any such action shall continue the hearing not less than seven days in order to furnish notice of such action to the appropriate agency and shall, if all rent due with interest and costs of suit has been tendered to the landlord within such time, treat the tenancy as not having been terminated.

rules.title: Deposit return after Safe Housing Act termination
rules.requirement: After a qualifying domestic-violence lease termination, make the deposit and interest available within 15 business days and give written collection-location and hours notice within three business days, by personal delivery or mail to the last known address. Give a duplicate to the relocation officer or, if none, municipal clerk. Make funds available during normal business hours for 30 days in the rental property's municipality, with itemized earnings and deductions; redeposit or reinvest unclaimed funds after that period. Permissible deductions include rent due and damage beyond ordinary wear.
rules.key_value: 15 business days availability; 3 business days notice; 30-day collection period
rules.coverage_conditions: A tenant terminates under the Safe Housing Act before lease expiry. Written notice must state that the tenant or the tenant's child faces an imminent threat of serious physical harm from a specified person, identified in the notice, if the tenant remains on the premises. One qualifying document is required: a certified copy of a permanent restraining order issued under New Jersey's Prevention of Domestic Violence Act of 1991 protecting the tenant or child from the person named in the notice; a certified copy of a permanent restraining order from another jurisdiction issued under that jurisdiction's domestic-violence laws and protecting the tenant or child from the person named in the notice; a law-enforcement agency record documenting domestic violence or certifying that the tenant or child is a victim; medical documentation of domestic violence from a health care provider; certification of victim status from a certified Domestic Violence Specialist or director of a designated domestic-violence agency; or documentation or certification of victim status from a licensed social worker. Termination occurs on the thirtieth day after the landlord receives a qualifying document and the tenant's written notice of intent to vacate and terminate the lease.
rules.exemptions: Transient and seasonal rentals are excluded. Public housing or redevelopment-agency premises require notice consistent with relevant public-housing regulations.

rules.requirement: Do not publish discriminatory advertising of any kind relating to a proposed rental.

The NJ Law Against Discrimination (LAD) prohibits
discrimination on the bases of race, creed (religion),
color, national origin, sex, gender identity or expression,
marital status, civil union status, ancestry, actual or
perceived physical or mental disability, nationality,
affectional or sexual orientation, familial status, and
domestic partner status. “ Familial status ” means
families with a child or children under 18 years old and/
or pregnant women, and “ disability” is used to include
persons afflicted with AIDS or HIV or thought to be
afflicted with AIDS.
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses. This
means, for example, that a landlord cannot deny the
lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher the right to
rent an apartment based solely on that source of lawful
income.
3. What does this mean to me?
• All persons, regardless of their membership in one
of the protected classes stated above or source of
lawful income used for rent or mortgage payments,
are entitled to equal treatment in the terms,
conditions or privileges of the sale or rental of
any real property  (e.g., it is illegal to deny that
housing is available for inspection, sale or rent when
it really is available.);
• No discriminatory advertising  of any kind relating
to the proposed sale or rental is permitted;

4. What types of property does this apply to?
The provisions of the LAD apply to the sale or rental of all
property including open land, whether for business or
residential purposes, with the following exceptions:
• The rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family
dwelling, the other occupancy unit of which is occupied
by the owner as his/her residence at the time of such
rentals;
• The rental of a room or rooms to another person or
persons by the owner or occupant of a one-family
dwelling occupied by him/her as his/her residence at
the time of such rental;
• In the sale, lease or rental of real property, preference
given to persons of the same religion by a religious
organization; and
• The prohibition against discrimination on the basis of
familial status does not apply to housing for older
persons (as defined in the LAD at N.J.S.A. 10:5-5mm).

rules.title: Authorized deposit-waiver fee must cover tenant-specific rent or damage
rules.requirement: Any regulations authorizing a deposit-waiver fee must require the landlord to use the fee to cover unpaid rent or unit damage applicable to that tenant's lease.
rules.coverage_conditions: Statutory requirements for regulations, if promulgated by the executive office of housing and livable communities, authorizing a landlord and tenant or prospective tenant to agree to a fee instead of a security deposit; the source alone does not establish that such regulations exist.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: Read together with all conditions in subsection (1)(b)(iii); these are conditional regulatory standards, not unconditional authorization for a landlord to charge a substitute fee.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
limitations: The requirement concerns the content of any authorizing regulations. No adopted regulation, program commencement date, or currently available fee option is established by this document.

rules.title: Substantive and notice conditions for material lease-breach eviction
rules.requirement: A material lease term must be mutually agreed upon; its alleged breach must cause substantial, actual landlord damage; and the landlord must demonstrate unreasonable tenant behavior. Before an eviction notice, the landlord must give a notice to stop the violation specifying the term and describing the violation and resulting harm in enough detail for a reasonable person to understand. A termination notice for a lease breach must clearly describe the alleged breach.
rules.key_value: Mutually agreed term AND substantial actual damage AND unreasonable behavior; prior notice to stop
rules.coverage_conditions: Eviction for violation of a material lease term under Berkeley's Rent Ordinance. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.
rules.exemptions: Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.
rules.quoted_span:
Material lease terms only include mutually agreed upon lease terms.
The alleged violation must cause substantial, actual damage to the landlord.
The landlord must demonstrate that the tenant’s behavior was unreasonable.
The landlord’s notice to the tenant to stop the violation (which is required before the landlord can serve an eviction notice) must specify the lease term, and describe the violation and resulting harm in enough detail for a reasonable person to understand.

evidence.quote:
New requirements to evict tenants for violations of a material term of the lease
NEW:
Material lease terms only include mutually agreed upon lease terms.
The alleged violation must cause substantial, actual damage to the landlord.
The landlord must demonstrate that the tenant’s behavior was unreasonable.
The landlord’s notice to the tenant to stop the violation (which is required before the landlord can serve an eviction notice) must specify the lease term, and describe the violation and resulting harm in enough detail for a reasonable person to understand.

rules.title: Buyout compensation threshold
rules.requirement: A buyout agreement must provide an amount greater than the relocation assistance available under §98.0706(c). The next sentence expressly declares an agreement for less than the relocation assistance owed to be a violation and void. The required agreement warning also identifies below-entitlement agreements under federal, state, or local law as void. Preserve the stricter 'greater than' obligation and the narrower express 'less than' voidness language.
rules.key_value: Must exceed available local relocation assistance; below owed assistance expressly void
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. The separately defined Tenant and this rule's trigger govern the initial scope inquiry. Applicability of the narrower Tenancy duration/fixed-term definition to this independent Tenant right is unresolved in the supplied text; do not use it as an automatic exclusion. Rule-specific applicability: Covered buyout amount assessed against local relocation available/owed. Duty says amount GREATER than entitlement; express voidness says LESS THAN. Preserve equality uncertainty and federal/state/local warning. Additional event and branch tests: Landlord pays money or other consideration for tenant to vacate; offer includes oral/written discussion or bargaining and tenant counteroffer does not end it. An agreement settling a PENDING unlawful-detainer action is excluded from the buyout-agreement definition. Covered buyout amount assessed against local relocation available/owed.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles. The Section 98.0702 Tenancy duration/fixed-term definition is not established here as an additional blanket Division-wide exemption from this independent Tenant right.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0703 Exemptions 
This Division shall not apply to the following types of residential rental properties or 
residential circumstances: 
(a) transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in California Civil Code 
section 1940(b), as may be amended; 
(b) short-term residential occupancy, as defined in and subject to Chapter 5, 
Article 10, Division 1 of this Code, as may be amended;  
 
(c) housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement 
with a government agency, or other document as affordable housing for 
persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be amended;  
(d)  housing subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable 
housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as 
defined in California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be 
amended, or comparable federal statutes. This exemption shall not include

(f) housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended

adult residential facility, as defined in Title 22, Division 6, Chapter 6 of the

(g) dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or an

Non-profit transitional housing means temporary housing operated by a non-profit 
organization for up to 24 months with supportive services to individuals and families 
with the goal of interim stability and support to successfully move to and maintain

(i) single-family residence occupied by the landlord as the landlord’s principal

(1) a residence in which the landlord-occupant rents or leases no more

(j) a property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in

(l) residential rental property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate

evidence.quote:
§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

rules.coverage_conditions: Covered types include most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current tenancies beginning before 1996; single-family homes with at least five rooms individually rented under separate leases; units built and receiving a certificate of occupancy after June 1980; single-family tenancies beginning on or after January 1, 1996; and most condominiums. The starred types include Housing Choice Voucher/Section 8, Shelter Plus Care, VASH Voucher, LIHTC, California Community Housing Agency, HOME, City of Berkeley Housing Trust Fund, and Mental Health Safety Act subsidies, plus Rental Supplement Program, Section 8 Loan Management Set Aside, and Project-based Section 8 when the project has no HUD-insured or HUD-held mortgage. Section 202 elderly and Section 811 disability units, and the three latter subsidy types with HUD-insured or HUD-held project mortgages, are partially covered regardless of unit type and retain just-cause protection. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.
rules.exemptions: Golden Duplex: owner-occupied on December 31, 1979 AND currently owner-occupied in one unit. Shared kitchen/bath: owner lived on the property when the tenancy began. ADU property: tenancy began after November 7, 2018 AND one unit is an ADU AND either unit is owner-occupied. Also exempt are university rental units such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.
rules.citation: Guide to Coverage under Berkeley’s Rent Stabilization and Eviction for Just Cause Ordinance

shared_scope_logic.logic: Determine full/partial/exempt using source guide, keeping any unresolved most/overlap issue unknown. Both full AND partial classifications retain just-cause and deposit-interest coverage, whereas local rent-amount controls require full coverage. Any complete exemption excludes these particular ordinance protections, not all other laws.
Select with berkeley_rent_classification; either full OR partial is enough, but unresolved classification remains unknown.

rule_specific_logic.exemptions: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles.
rule_specific_logic.triggers: Determine just-cause protection for proposed eviction using unit/tenancy/subsidy classification.
rule_specific_logic.modifiers: Partial rent-control exemption does not remove just-cause.

required_facts.description: Resolved full/partial/exempt classification, accounting for guide qualifiers such as most and any overlapping classifications that the guide does not resolve.
Whether this duplex was owner-occupied on December 31, 1979.
Whether an owner currently resides in a dwelling on the subject property; principal-residence and historical conditions are separate facts.
Whether owner lived in a unit on this same property when the relevant tenancy began.
Actual asserted reason for possession recovery, with at-fault/no-fault and statutory branch identified.
Date the certificate of occupancy was issued; construction year is not a substitute.
Date the building was constructed, distinct from certificate-of-occupancy issuance.
Whether one unit on the property is an accessory dwelling unit.
Whether the project has a mortgage insured or held by HUD.
Rooms separately rented on individual leases in a single-family rooming house; not total bedrooms or building units.
Applicable city and state boundaries for the unit.
Whether tenant shares either kitchen or bathroom facilities with the owner.
Specific government subsidy/program labels, preserving project-based versus tenant-based assistance.
Property/unit use type, including apartment, condominium, townhome, single-family, rooming-house, hotel, dormitory, ADU, mobilehome park or institutional use.
Date this tenancy commenced; distinct from construction, notice, execution or move-out date.

rules.title: Recommended CORI verification and consistent review
rules.requirement: Agents are strongly encouraged to validate Criminal Offender Records Information through DCJIS and to assign the same staff to assess whether CORI warrants housing denial. These are recommended practices, not mandatory screening requirements.
rules.key_value: Voluntary DCJIS validation and consistent review staff
rules.coverage_conditions: Providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or having income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; the policy also applies to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.
rules.exemptions: The policy excludes current criminal behavior and states exceptions for a conviction directly related to the housing sought and/or unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others' safety. Conflicting federal or state criminal-history requirements prevail.
rules.citation: BOSTON FAIR CHANCE TENANT SELECTION POLICY, items 2-3

rules.title: Offer a pre-move-out inspection
rules.requirement: Offer a walk-through inspection during the last two weeks of the tenancy to identify repair or cleaning issues and give the tenant an opportunity to correct them before deposit deductions.
rules.key_value: During the last 2 weeks of the tenancy
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenancy approaching termination, read with supplied Civil Code 1950.5(f): landlord first gives written inspection/attendance-right notice; performance of the initial inspection then depends on tenant request and no withdrawal, at a reasonable time no earlier than two weeks before termination or lease end.
rules.exemptions: Subdivision (f) does not apply to termination under CCP 1161(2), (3), or (4). Tenant choice not to request discharges subsequent inspection duties; withdrawal removes duty to proceed. Both parties may sign a written waiver of the 48-hour appointment notice only. These conditions do not erase the preceding duty to inform an otherwise covered tenant of the inspection option.

rules.title: Disposition of security when the landlord's interest ends
rules.requirement: When the landlord's interest in the premises ends by sale, assignment, death, receivership, or otherwise, the landlord or agent must within a reasonable time either transfer the remaining security after lawful deductions to the successor and give the required notice, or return it to the tenant with the required accounting. Either compliant alternative relieves the landlord of further liability for the held security.
rules.key_value: Within a reasonable time after the landlord's interest ends
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security held when the landlord's interest terminates. Deductions must be lawful under subdivision (e), transfer requires the notice under (i)(1), and tenant return must include the subdivision (h) accounting.
rules.interaction: Noncompliance can trigger the successor and predecessor liability rules in subdivision (k).
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset is unknown; footer states the supplied version was amended effective 2026-01-01.

Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.

Protected Units: (1) Residential dwelling units that are or were subject to a recorded covenant, ordinance, or law that restricts 
rents to levels affordable to persons and families of lower or very low income within the past five years. (2) Residential 
dwelling units that are or were subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police 
power within the past five years.  This includes all RSO units. (3) Residential dwelling units that are or were rented by lower or 
very low income households within the past five years. (4) Residential dwelling units that were withdrawn from rent or lease in 
accordance the Ellis Act within the past 10 years.

The RPO only applies to Protected Units that will be demolished for the 
purpose of new construction.

Right of First Refusal to the new 
building for some tenants

Requirements for Landlords 
To terminate tenancy for the purpose of demolition of a Protected Unit1, a landlord must: 
1. File with LAHD a Declaration of Intent to Evict for units regulated by the JCO per the Los Angeles
Municipal Code (LAMC) Section 165.03.I(1) or file with LAHD a  Notice of Intent to Withdraw Units
From Rental Housing Use for units regulated by the RSO.  Only RSO units are subject to the Ellis
Act provisions (LAMC 151.22-151.28).  All RSO units are Protected Units.
2. Serve tenants with a written notice to move out and file a copy of it with LAHD within 3 business
days online at https://lahd.service-now.com/efs. For more information go to
housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices
3. Pay relocation assistance to tenants in compliance with the State law’s Housing Crisis Act
(California Government Code Section 66300 et seq.) or the City laws, whichever is higher.  City
laws require all tenants be paid relocation assistance in the amounts required by the RSO or JCO
within 15 days of serving a notice to terminate tenancy, which must be enhanced for lower income
tenants if the project is subject to the Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO), effective 2/11/2025
under Ordinances # 188481 and #188482.  The RSO and JCO amounts must also be enhanced for
lower income tenants under the HCA regardless of the RPO applicability.  Parties are encouraged
to seek legal advice to understand the HCA State law if the RPO does not apply to them.
*The regular RSO or JCO relocation rules apply as described in the A. Relocation Assistance
Bulletin: No-Fault Evictions Under the RSO & JCO if the units to be demolished are not Protected

rents to levels affordable to persons and families of lower or very low income within the past five years. (2) Residential 
dwelling units that are or were subject to any form of rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police 
power within the past five years.  This includes all RSO units. (3) Residential dwelling units that are or were rented by lower or 
very low income households within the past five years. (4) Residential dwelling units that were withdrawn from rent or lease in 
accordance the Ellis Act within the past 10 years.

Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) 
The Housing Crisis Act of 2019 (HCA) originally introduced replacement requirements and occupant 
protections through Senate Bill (SB) 330 and has since been updated by SB 8 and Assembly Bill (AB) 1218. 
On February 11, 2025, the Los Angeles City Council adopted the RPO which codified and expanded upon 
replacement requirements and occupant protections of the HCA, and enhanced requirements for 
Restricted Affordable Units.  The RPO only applies to Protected Units that will be demolished for the 
purpose of new construction.  
The RPO’s occupant protections include: 1) Right to Relocation, 2) Right to Remain in the unit up to 6 
months prior to start of construction activities, which includes a 6-month notice to move out, 3) Right 
to Return to the same unit if the demolition does not proceed, 4) Right of First Refusal to the new 
building for some tenants and 5) Tenant Notification Requirements.  For more details, please go the Los 
Angeles City Planning Department’s website https://planning.lacity.gov/ and review the Fact Sheet: 
Replacement Unit Requirements and Occupant Protections.
