rules.title: Reasonable accommodations in applicant-facing housing policies
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers must make reasonable exceptions, changes, or adjustments to rules, policies, practices, or services when necessary for an applicant with a disability to have an equal housing opportunity. Examples include allowing a third party to cosign a lease or pay rent, allowing a live-in aide, or modifying lease terms. Requests need not be written or use special words. Providers must consider requests promptly and, if unable to grant one immediately, must engage in an interactive process with the requestor in an effort to come up with a solution. If a provider determines that it cannot grant the request, it must work with the requestor to try to identify another accommodation that is equally effective in meeting their needs. The interactive process should occur in a timely manner and should be negotiated in good faith.
rules.coverage_conditions: An applicant must indicate a need for a policy or practice exception, change, or adjustment because of a disability. The guidance defines disability as a mental or physical impairment or condition limiting a major life activity.
rules.exemptions: The guidance identifies requests that cannot be reasonable accommodations: reducing rent, permitting illegal drug use, causing a direct threat to others' health and safety, causing substantial physical damage to others' property, or adding an elevator to a building without one. The general owner-occupied exception permits protected-characteristic applicant exclusion when the owner occupies the home and rents to one additional person; the guidance does not separately explain how that exception affects accommodation duties.
rules.quoted_span: A reasonable accommodation is an exception, change, or adjustment in rules, policies, practices, or services that is necessary to allow a tenant, resident, or applicant with a disability to have an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
rules.interaction: r-0310 coexists r-0358 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.

conditions.description: The adjustment must be necessary to provide an equal housing opportunity and must qualify as reasonable.

rules.temporal_notes: No operative date or fixed response deadline is stated; urgency and other factors affect the required response time.
limitations: This record addresses accommodations relevant to rental admission and screening; the guidance also addresses broader occupancy accommodations.
No statutory section is supplied.

evidence.quote: The refusal to grant reasonable accommodations and modifications constitutes unlawful discrimination under state and federal law.

A reasonable accommodation is an exception, change, or adjustment in rules, policies, practices, or services that is necessary to allow a tenant, resident, or applicant with a disability to have an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.

Allowing a third party to cosign the lease or pay the rent
Allowing a tenant to have a live-in aide
Modifying the terms of a lease

Examples of requests that cannot be reasonable accommodations include:
Reducing the rent
Permitting the use of illegal drugs
Something that would cause a direct threat to the health and safety of others, such as allowing an emotional support animal that bites at other tenants
Something that would cause substantial physical damage to the property of others
Adding an elevator to a building without one

A request for reasonable accommodation does not need to be in writing. The person making the request does not need to use any specific words – including “reasonable accommodation” – to make the request as long as they indicate needing an exception, change, or adjustment to a practice or policy because of a disability.

Requests for accommodations must be considered promptly by the housing provider. The time necessary to respond to a request depends on various factors, including whether the accommodation is needed on an urgent basis. Failure to respond to a request for a reasonable accommodation constitutes unlawful housing discrimination.
If a housing provider cannot immediately grant a requested accommodation, they must engage in an “interactive process” with the requestor in an effort to come up with a solution.

If the housing provider determines that they cannot grant the request, they must work with the requestor to try to identify if there is another accommodation that is equally effective in meeting their needs. The interactive process should occur in a timely manner and should be negotiated in good faith.
When an owner is occupying a home and is renting to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics.
The Fair Employment and Housing Act defines a disability as a mental or physical impairment, or condition that limits a major life activity.

What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

What is the definition of a disability?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act defines a disability as a mental or physical impairment, or condition that limits a major life activity. Examples of major life activities include cooking, cleaning, bathing, working, paying bills, and shopping. For example, if a person has a mental health condition that makes it difficult to shop for groceries and clean their apartment, they would be considered to be disabled under California fair housing law.
People that are perceived to have a disability (whether or not they are actually disabled) are also protected under the law. For example, if a landlord discriminates against a tenant because they think the tenant has a mental health condition, this would violate the law, even if the person didn’t have a mental health condition.
Additionally, people who are associated with a person who has a disability are also included in the laws protections. For example, refusing to rent to a tenant that has a family member with a mental health condition that will be visiting the tenant, would violate the law.
For more information, please see CRD’s
Disability Discrimination Factsheet
Are tenants or applicants with disabilities entitled to special treatment?
Yes. Tenants, residents, and applicants with disabilities are entitled to reasonable accommodations and/or modifications that are necessary to allow them an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing, including a housing unit and any common areas. The refusal to grant reasonable accommodations and modifications constitutes unlawful discrimination under state and federal law. See below for examples of reasonable accommodations.
For more information, please see CRD’s
Disability Discrimination Factsheet
What is a reasonable accommodation?
A reasonable accommodation is an exception, change, or adjustment in rules, policies, practices, or services that is necessary to allow a tenant, resident, or applicant with a disability to have an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.

Examples of requests that cannot be reasonable accommodations include:
Reducing the rent
Permitting the use of illegal drugs
Something that would cause a direct threat to the health and safety of others, such as allowing an emotional support animal that bites at other tenants
Something that would cause substantial physical damage to the property of others
Adding an elevator to a building without one

When an applicant or tenant requests a reasonable accommodation, does it have to be in writing?
No. A request for reasonable accommodation does not need to be in writing. The person making the request does not need to use any specific words – including “reasonable accommodation” – to make the request as long as they indicate needing an exception, change, or adjustment to a practice or policy because of a disability.
When and how should a housing provider respond to a request for reasonable accommodation?
Requests for accommodations must be considered promptly by the housing provider. The time necessary to respond to a request depends on various factors, including whether the accommodation is needed on an urgent basis. Failure to respond to a request for a reasonable accommodation constitutes unlawful housing discrimination.
If a housing provider cannot immediately grant a requested accommodation, they must engage in an “interactive process” with the requestor in an effort to come up with a solution. If the housing provider determines that they cannot grant the request, they must work with the requestor to try to identify if there is another accommodation that is equally effective in meeting their needs. rules.title: Good-faith demolition, commercial conversion, or withdrawal ground
rules.requirement: The landlord may seek possession in good faith to demolish, convert to commercial use, or remove the unit from rental housing use. For RSO units, the bulletin treats these as Ellis Act evictions requiring compliance with LAMC 151.22–151.28.
rules.coverage_conditions: RSO- or JCO-covered rental units; a good-faith recovery of possession for one of the specified purposes. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Eviction-related procedure is stated for ALL Los Angeles RSO OR JCO rental properties; verify relevant program property classification and keep disputed scope unknown. Substantive program scope: For these substantive no-fault grounds, require EITHER verified RSO property/tenancy coverage OR verified JCO property coverage AND (tenant has lived in the same unit for at least six months OR the original lease has expired, whichever occurs first). Apply the elapsed/original-lease test only to the JCO branch. Verify the particular ground and its other conditions separately. The all-properties filing rule in D040 lines 73-75 does not establish substantive JCO tenancy coverage.
rules.exemptions: The bulletin applies its Ellis Act procedures only to RSO units.
rules.quoted_span:
The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.
rules.interaction: Demolition for new construction can additionally trigger HCA and RPO protections.
limitations: The referenced Ellis Act and municipal withdrawal procedures are not fully reproduced.
Full withdrawal procedures absent.

evidence.quote:
The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.

Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

All tenant not- at-fault evictions require payment of relocation assistance and the filing of a 
Declaration of Intent to Evict form with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) before 
evicting tenants from units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause 
Ordinance (JCO). Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices. 
 Not-At-Fault Reasons for Eviction
1. The landlord evicts for the occupancy of her/himself, spouse, grandchildren, children,  
parents or grandparents, or a resident manager (Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC)  
151.09.A.8, 165.03.H.). Evictions for the purpose of resident manager occupancy are 
allowed only if required by law or an affordable housing covenant, or a regulatory  
agreement. Landlords must comply with the restrictions and requirements of LAMC Section  
151.30.
2. The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.
3. The landlord evicts to comply with a governmental agency’s Order to Vacate (LAMC  
151.09.A.11, 165.03.J.). Prior to giving notice to tenants, landlords must file a Landlord  
Declaration of Intent to Evict.
4. The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both the owner and plaintiff and seeks 
to recover possession to vacate the property prior to sale (LAMC 151.09.A.12, 165.03.K.).
5. Residential Hotel Unit conversion or demolition (LAMC 151.09.A.13, 165.03.L.).
6. The landlord seeks to recover possession of the rental unit to convert the subject property 
to an affordable housing accommodation (LAMC 151.09.A.14, 165.03.M.).
7. The landlord demolishes the property or converts the use of the property to condominiums, 
stock cooperatives, community apartment projects, hotels, and commercial uses, regardless 
of whether the property is subject to the RSO OR JCO (LAMC 47.06 & 47.07).

2. The landlord seeks in good faith to recover possession of the rental unit to demolish, convert 
to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For 
RSO units, these are considered Ellis Act (California Government Code 7060.4) evictions, and 
the landlord must comply with the requirements of LAMC 151.22-151.28.

to a commercial use, or remove it from rental housing use (LAMC 151.09.A.10, 165.03.I). For

stock cooperatives, community apartment projects, hotels, and commercial uses, regardless

rules.title: Possible statutory damages for bad-faith security claims or retention
rules.requirement: Bad-faith claims or retention of security contrary to the section, or bad-faith replacement demands contrary to subdivision (k), may expose the landlord or successor to statutory damages up to twice the security amount in addition to actual damages. The court may award bad-faith damages when warranted even if the injured party did not specifically request them.
rules.key_value: Up to 2 times the security amount, plus actual damages
rules.coverage_conditions: A residential landlord or successor making the specified bad-faith claim, retention, or replacement demand; the text authorizes a potential court award rather than automatic damages for every violation.
rules.exemptions: Under (k)(3), a successor who after inquiry and reasonable investigation has a good-faith belief that remaining lawful security was transferred to the successor or returned to the tenant under (i) is not liable for subdivision (m) damages or security not transferred under (i).
rules.interaction: The successor's good-faith exception must be considered alongside the possible damages remedy; subdivision (h)(7) separately bars security claims after bad-faith accounting noncompliance.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset is not specified; supplied version amended effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: No conclusion that a particular actor acted in bad faith or owes a particular damages amount is made.
rules.quoted_span:
(m) The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord or the landlord’s successors in interest of the security or any portion thereof in violation of this section, or the bad faith demand of replacement of security in violation of subdivision (k), may subject the landlord or the landlord’s successors in interest to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages. The court may award damages for bad faith whenever the facts warrant that award,
regardless of whether the injured party has specifically requested relief. In an action under this section, the landlord or the landlord’s successors in interest shall have the burden of proof as to the reasonableness of the amounts claimed or the authority pursuant to this section to demand additional security deposits.

rules.title: Rent increases may not be reprisals for protected tenant activity
rules.requirement: A rent increase imposed as a reprisal for a residential tenant's protected activity is subject to section 18's damages and cost liability. This is a motive-based limit on rent increases, not a numerical rent cap.
rules.key_value: Retaliatory increases prohibited; no percentage or dollar increase cap stated
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential tenants protected for: commencing, proceeding with, or obtaining relief in a judicial or administrative action to obtain damages under or enforce federal, state, or local residential-premises laws, regulations, by-laws, or ordinances; exercising rights under chapter 164 section 124D; reporting actual or suspected covered health, building, municipal, state, or federal violations to a board of health, Boston commissioner of housing inspection, or another board regulating residential premises; making such reports or complaints in writing to the landlord or agent; organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization; or making or expressing an intention to make rent payments to an organization of unit owners under chapter 183A section 6(c). Liability applies to any person or agent threatening or taking reprisals.
rules.interaction: The six-month presumption in the next paragraph expressly identifies rent-increase notices; its timing rule concerns proof of retaliation and does not limit the underlying liability to six months. Damages follow the section's greater-of-actual-damages-or-one-to-three-months-rent comparison, plus suit costs and a reasonable attorney's fee.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied official General Laws snapshot presents the provision without a pending or future-version label; the original effective date is not stated.
limitations: The source cross-references chapter 164 section 124D and chapter 183A section 6(c) without reproducing their full substantive requirements.

Section 18. Any person or agent thereof who threatens to or takes reprisals against any tenant of residential premises for the tenant's act of, commencing, proceeding with, or obtaining relief in any judicial or administrative action the purpose of which action is to obtain damages under, or otherwise enforce, any federal, state or local law, regulation, by-law or ordinance, which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or exercising the tenant's rights pursuant to section one hundred and twenty-four D of chapter one hundred and sixty-four; or reporting to the board of health or, in the city of Boston to the commissioner of housing inspection or to any other board having as its objective the regulation of residential premises a violation or a suspected violation of any health or building code or of any other municipal by-law or ordinance, or state or federal law or regulation which has as its objective the regulation of residential premises; or reporting or complaining of such violation or suspected violation in writing to the landlord or to the agent of the landlord; or for organizing or joining a tenants' union or similar organization, or for making or expressing an intention to make, a payment of rent to an organization of unit owners pursuant to paragraph (c) of section six of chapter one hundred and eighty-three A shall be liable for damages which shall not be less than one month's rent or more than three month's rent, or the actual damages sustained by the tenant, whichever is greater, and the costs of the suit, including a reasonable attorney's fee.
The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action, exercised such rights, made such report or complaint, or organized or joined such tenants' union or within six months after any other person has taken such action or actions on behalf of the tenant or in, or relating to, the building in which the tenant resides, shall create a rebuttable presumption that such notice or other action is a reprisal against the tenant for engaging in such activities. Such presumption shall be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that such person's action was not a reprisal against the tenant and that such person had sufficient independent justification for taking such action, and would have in fact taken such action, in the same manner and at the same time the action was taken, regardless of tenants engaging in, or the belief that tenants had engaged in, activities protected under this section.

shared_scope_logic.logic: Residential tenant AND at least one complete protected activity branch. Written requirement applies to direct landlord complaints, not automatically every report to a public authority. Cross-referenced rights must be established if decisive.

rule_specific_logic.coverage: Shared scope and retaliatory motive; not a numeric cap.
rule_specific_logic.exemptions: No source blanket exemption for market-rate units or small owners.
rule_specific_logic.triggers: Retaliatory increase; six-month notice presumption may help prove motive but is not sole liability path.
rule_specific_logic.modifiers: Property address or size does not establish motive; rent increase amount alone cannot decide compliance.

rules.title: Protected-characteristic inquiries and records prohibited for other covered housing
rules.requirement: Covered actors may not cause written or oral inquiries or records about rental applicants' characteristics listed in subsection 7(c), including possession of a trained guide dog because of blindness or hearing impairment.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to applicants for other covered housing and the housing actors specified in subsection 7.
rules.exemptions: Excludes leasing a single apartment or flat in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling where the owner resides in the other unit. The statutory sexual-orientation qualification excludes persons whose sexual orientation involves minor children as the sex object. Age protection excludes minors, specified state- or federally aided elderly housing, specified low-income-housing-tax-credit older-person housing, and expressly constructed older-person communities with biennial registration. The specified older-person housing must comply with 42 USC 3601 et seq. The section preserves qualifying religious organizations' same-religion admission limitations and preferences, without expressly explaining their effect on inquiries.
rules.quoted_span: (c) to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record concerning the race, color, religious creed, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, which shall not include persons whose sexual orientation involves minor children as the sex object, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veteran status or membership in the armed services, blindness, hearing impairment or other handicap or because such person possesses a trained dog guide as a consequence of blindness or hearing impairment, of the person seeking to rent or lease or buy any such accommodation or land;
rules.interaction: The owner-occupied two-family exception belongs to subsection 7. The older-person housing provision expressly incorporates the cited federal law.
rules.temporal_notes: No operative date is supplied.
limitations: Referenced housing definitions are absent.
The text does not expressly resolve the interaction between religious admission preferences and inquiry restrictions.

evidence.quote: The word ''age'' as used in this subsection shall not apply to persons who are minors nor to residency in state-aided or federally-aided housing developments for the elderly nor to residency in housing developments assisted under the federal low income housing tax credit and intended for use as housing for persons 55 years of age or over or 62 years of age or over, nor to residency in communities consisting of either a structure or structures constructed expressly for use as housing for persons 55 years of age or over or 62 years of age or over if the housing owner or manager register biennially with the executive office of housing and livable communities. For the purpose of this subsection, housing intended for occupancy by persons fifty-five or over and sixty-two or over shall comply with the provisions set forth in 42 USC 3601 et seq.

For the owner, lessee, sublessee, real estate broker, assignee or managing agent of other covered housing accommodations or of land intended for the erection of any housing accommodation included under subsection 10, 11, 12, or 13 of section one, or other person having the right of ownership or possession or right to rent or lease or sell, or negotiate for the sale or lease of such land or accommodations, or any agent or employee of such a person or any organization of unit owners in a condominium or housing cooperative:

(c) to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record concerning the race, color, religious creed, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, which shall not include persons whose sexual orientation involves minor children as the sex object, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veteran status or membership in the armed services, blindness, hearing impairment or other handicap or because such person possesses a trained dog guide as a consequence of blindness or hearing impairment, of the person seeking to rent or lease or buy any such accommodation or land;

provided, however, that this subsection shall not apply to the leasing of a single apartment or flat in a two family dwelling, the other occupancy unit of which is occupied by the owner as his residence.

Notwithstanding the provisions of any general or special law nothing herein shall be construed to bar any religious or denominational institution or organization, or any organization operated for charitable or educational purposes, which is operated, supervised or controlled by or in connection with a religious organization, from limiting admission to or giving preference to persons of the same religion or denomination

7. (b) to discriminate against any person because of his race, color, religious creed, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, which shall not include persons whose sexual orientation involves minor children as the sex object, age, genetic information, ancestry, or marital status, veteran status or membership in the armed services, blindness, or hearing impairment or other handicap, or because such person possesses a trained dog guide as a consequence of blindness or hearing impairment in the terms, conditions or privileges of such accommodations or land or the acquisition thereof, or in the furnishing of facilities and services in the connection therewith or (c) to cause to be made any written or oral inquiry or record concerning the race, color, religious creed, national origin, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, which shall not include persons whose sexual orientation involves minor children as the sex object, age, genetic information, ancestry, marital status, veteran status or membership in the armed services, blindness, hearing impairment or other handicap or because such person possesses a trained dog guide as a consequence of blindness or hearing impairment, of the person seeking to rent or lease or buy any such accommodation or land; provided, however, that this subsection shall not apply to the leasing of a single apartment or flat in a two family dwelling, the other occupancy unit of which is occupied by the owner as his residence. The word ''age'' as used in this subsection shall not apply to persons who are minors nor to residency in state-aided or federally-aided housing developments for the elderly nor to residency in housing developments assisted under the federal low income housing tax credit and intended for use as housing for persons 55 years of age or over or 62 years of age or over, nor to residency in communities consisting of either a structure or structures constructed expressly for use as housing for persons 55 years of age or over or 62 years of age or over if the housing owner or manager register biennially with the executive office of housing and livable communities. For the purpose of this subsection, housing intended for occupancy by persons fifty-five or over and sixty-two or over shall comply with the provisions set forth in 42 USC 3601 et seq.

Notwithstanding the provisions of any general or special law nothing herein shall be construed to bar any religious or denominational institution or organization, or any organization operated for charitable or educational purposes, which is operated, supervised or controlled by or in connection with a religious organization, from limiting admission to or giving preference to persons of the same religion or denomination or from taking any action with respect to matters of employment, discipline, faith, internal organization, or ecclesiastical rule, custom, or law which are calculated by such organization to promote the religious principles for which it is established or maintained.

rules.title: RSO no-fault relocation assistance
rules.requirement: No-fault evictions require payment of tenant relocation assistance.
rules.coverage_conditions: RSO no-fault evictions. Listed grounds are owner or immediate-family occupancy, resident-manager occupancy, demolition and permanent market withdrawal, government order, and affordable-housing conversion. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Los Angeles RSO generally covers listed property types first built on or before 1978-10-01 OR replacement units under LAMC §151.28: apartments, condominiums, townhomes, duplexes, at least two single-family dwelling units on the same parcel, residential units attached to commercial buildings, accessory dwelling units, and junior accessory dwelling units. Hotel, motel, rooming-house and boarding-house rooms require occupancy by the same tenant for more than 30 consecutive days. Mobilehomes and recreational vehicles in mobilehome parks are also covered. Resolve residual exceptions from verified RSO status.
rules.exemptions: Replacing a resident manager with another is exempt subject to manager-tenant caveat; required eviction for natural-disaster hazard is exempt only if not caused by landlord negligence.

What Falls Under RSO
If you own rental property in the City of Los Angeles, it may be subject to the
city’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO)
.
Find out
if your property falls under this ordinance and what you need to know to be in compliance.
Generally, the RSO applies to rental properties that were first built on or before October 1, 1978, as well as replacement units under
LAMC Section 151.28
and if any of the following:
Apartment
Condominium (Rent amount is not regulated for tenancies that commenced after December 31, 1995)
Townhome (Rent amount is not regulated for tenancies that commenced after December 31, 1995)
Duplex
Two or more single-family dwelling units on the same parcel
Rooms in a hotel, motel, rooming house, or boarding house occupied by the same tenant for more than 30 consecutive days
Residential unit(s) attached to a commercial building
Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU)
Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit (JADU)
Mobile homes
and recreational vehicles in mobile home parks are also covered under the RSO.

Types of Evictions Requiring Payment of Tenant Relocation Assistance
No-fault evictions require the payment of
relocation assistance
.
Checklist for No-Fault Evictions
File a
Landlord Declaration of Intent to Evict
filed with the LAHD.
Give the tenant a 30-day and 60-day written notice (some evictions require 120-day notice or up to a 1-year extension).
Payment of
tenant relocation assistance
.

Exemptions from Relocation Assistance Payments 
Landlords are exempt from paying relocation assistance when: 
1. Evicting a resident manager to replace him/her with another resident manager. If the
resident manager is a Manager -Tenant receiving free or reduced rent with no other
compensation, he/she may be entitled to relocation assistance. (See RAC Regulations
920.00, Managers as Tenants.)
2. They are required to evict due to hazardous conditions caused by a natural disaster ,
which is not caused by the landlord's negligence.

rules.title: Termination notice void for failure to strictly comply with §98.0706
rules.requirement: Failure to strictly comply with §98.0706 makes any termination notice required by that section void, in addition to other remedies. This is a procedural invalidity rule.
rules.key_value: Required termination notice void
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: Landlord fails strict compliance with applicable 98.0706 requirement; termination notice under that section is void. Do not deem unactivated Commission reporting duties violated. Additional event and branch tests: Landlord fails strict compliance with applicable 98.0706 requirement; termination notice under that section is void. At-fault reporting waits 30 days after portal creation and public notice; parallel no-fault condition also applies. No-fault reporting also waits 30 days after portal creation and public notice.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. Where a claimed coverage or exemption branch depends on an incorporated external definition, establish that definition and its facts; the Division does not reproduce all referenced statutes or local chapters. A category label alone is insufficient. Rule-specific qualifications: Apply only the complete exemption branches of the selected profiles.

§98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0703 Exemptions 
This Division shall not apply to the following types of residential rental properties or 
residential circumstances: 
(a) transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in California Civil Code 
section 1940(b), as may be amended;

Article 10, Division 1 of this Code, as may be amended;

California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be amended;

housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as 
defined in California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be 
amended, or comparable federal statutes. This exemption shall not include 
Section 8;

rules.title: Dominant-motive just cause required for eviction
rules.requirement: A covered eviction must have a just-cause reason that is the landlord's dominant motive. Expiration of the rental agreement or change of ownership alone is insufficient. The 17 summarized grounds are: nonpayment, habitual late payment, or frequent bounced checks; failure to cure a substantial lease breach; severe, continuing or recurring nuisance or substantial interference; illegal use subject to the stated exclusions; refusal after written request to renew an expired agreement for a like term on materially identical terms; refusal after written notice to cease to allow legally required access; the sole remaining occupant at term-end being an unapproved subtenant; owner occupancy or limited immediate-family occupancy; good-faith recovery to sell under an approved condominium conversion; demolition or permanent removal of an individual unit; capital improvements or rehabilitation work that will make the unit temporarily uninhabitable while the work is performed, with the tenant required to be allowed to reoccupy the unit immediately after the work is completed; substantial rehabilitation of an essentially uninhabitable building at least 50 years old with work costing at least 75% of new construction; Ellis Act withdrawal of all rental units in a building; required lead remediation or abatement; demolition or permanent removal under a City development agreement; expiration of a Good Samaritan agreement with an eviction notice served within 60 days; or demolition necessary for a development project under Planning Code Section 317.
rules.key_value: 17 summarized just-cause grounds; dominant-motive requirement
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units covered by the Rent Ordinance's eviction provisions, including some tenancies exempt from rent-increase limitations: newly constructed units first obtaining a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979; tenancies eligible for a Costa-Hawkins rent increase; and some tenancies with rents regulated by another government agency. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Verify San Francisco Rent Ordinance eviction coverage independently from rent control. Some tenancies exempt from rent-increase limits remain covered: newly constructed units first receiving a certificate of occupancy after 1979-06-13, tenancies eligible for a Costa-Hawkins rent increase, and some tenancies regulated by another government agency. The summary does not provide a complete exemption list.
rules.exemptions: Illegal use excludes mere occupancy of an unwarranted unit and a single Chapter 41A short-term-rental violation cured within 30 days of the landlord's written notice. Subtenant approval may be oral or implied by landlord conduct. Good Samaritan occupancy means temporary replacement housing at reduced rent following emergency or disaster displacement. Owner-relative occupancy is available only in limited circumstances not detailed here.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction. Note that the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute "just cause" for eviction.
rules.interaction:
Exemption from municipal rent-increase limits does not necessarily exempt a tenancy from eviction protections. Several grounds expressly reference other laws.
r-0014 coexists r-0368 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.

rules.title: Self-help eviction and lockouts prohibited
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent cannot force removal, padlock or change locks, disconnect utilities, block entry or use unlawful possession of belongings to evict an occupant. Physical eviction requires a court officer acting after a judge issues a removal warrant. A successful tenant may recover possession, damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees; when restoration of possession is inappropriate the guide states treble damages.

“Self-help” Evictions  
Self-help evictions occur when the landlord or someone acting on the landlord’s behalf 
enters into the dwelling unit without the permission of the tenant and without a judgment from the 
Court and forces the tenant to move. A lockout occurs when the landlord padlocks the door or 
changes the locks while the tenant are not home and then refuses to allow the tenant back into the 
premises. A lockout also occurs when the landlord shuts off the utilities in attempt to force the 
tenant to move. Self-help evictions, or lockouts, made by the landlord are illegal in New Jersey. 
If a landlord attempts a self -help eviction or lockout, the tenant should call the police. If 
the landlord refuses to allow the tenant back into the premises after  the police have warned the 
landlord about the illegal procedures, the landlord may be charged with disorderly conduct.

 A landlord or their agent may not padlock, disconnect utilities or otherwise block entry to

a premise by a landlord after the eviction may be done only in accordance with the Abandoned 
Property Law, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-72 to 84, Only an officer of the court can legally physically evict a 
tenant, after a judge has issued a Warrant for Removal.   
 A person who is illegally evicted may file a complaint with the Cler k of the Landlord -
Tenant Section, Special Civil Part of the Law Division, or the Chancery Division, of the Superior 
Court, in the county in which the act was committed.  In a successful action by a tenant evicted 
through forcible entry and detainer, the co urt may award possession of the dwelling unit and all 
damages, including court costs and reasonable attorney fees. If the dwelling unit cannot be returned 
to the tenant as a result of the self-help eviction, the court may award damages.

Filing a complaint for unlawful entry and detainer 
 Any legal action for a forcible unlawful entry and detainer, forcible detainer, and unlawful 
detainer shall be brought before the Superior Court, and the court may hear and make a 
determination in that action. If a landlord enters the rental premises unlaw fully, a trespass 
complaint may be filed by the tenant with the local police department, under the New Jersey 
Criminal Code for “defiant trespass” (N.J.S.A. 2A:39-6).  
 A tenant or landlord depending on the judge’s decision shall be entitled to possession of 
the real property and shall recover all damages that may have been caused by the unlawful entry

person to possession of the premises, treble (3x) damages shall be awarded (N.J.S.A. 2A:39-8).

rules.title: Rolling 12-month maximum rent increase with geographic CPI calculation
rules.requirement: Over any 12-month period, an owner may not increase a covered unit's gross rental rate by more than the lesser of 5% plus the applicable percentage change in cost of living or 10%, measured against the lowest gross rental rate charged for that unit during the 12 months before the increase takes effect. Accepted owner-offered discounts, incentives, concessions, and credits are excluded when determining that gross baseline. Use the applicable metropolitan CPI-U for all urban consumers/all items, or California CPI-U from the Department of Industrial Relations if no applicable metropolitan index is published. For increases effective before August 1, compare April of the preceding year to April of the year before it; for increases effective on or after August 1, compare April of that year to April of the preceding year. Substitute March when no April amount is published for the applicable area. Round the percentage change to the nearest one-tenth of 1%. If no prior tenant remains in lawful possession when a new tenancy begins, the owner may establish an initial rate outside subdivision (a); subsequent increases are limited.
rules.key_value: Maximum increase = min(5% + applicable CPI change, 10%) over any 12 months, using the lowest prior-12-month gross rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential dwellings or units intended for human habitation, including rented units in mobilehome parks; tenancy includes leases and subleases. Owner includes a person acting directly or through an agent with the right to offer the property for rent and a predecessor in interest. Listed metropolitan indexes cover Los Angeles and Orange counties; Riverside and San Bernardino counties; San Diego County; and Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Francisco, and San Mateo counties, respectively, including successor indexes. On or after January 1, 2021, a newly published BLS metropolitan CPI-U applies to increases effective on or after August 1 of the calendar year when its specified 12-month change is first published.
rules.exemptions: Excluded are housing restricted by deed, governmental regulatory agreement, or other recorded document as affordable to very-low-, low-, or moderate-income households, or subject to qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreements; dormitories owned and operated by higher-education or K–12 institutions; housing under valid public rent/price control consistent with Chapter 2.7 that permits a lower annual increase; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, except mobilehomes; qualifying two-unit single structures with neither unit an ADU/JADU where the owner occupied one unit as a principal residence at tenancy inception and continues occupancy; and mobilehome homeowners under section 798.9. Separately alienable property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if the owner is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with any corporate member, or mobilehome-park management AND tenants receive the prescribed written exemption notice. That notice must be in the agreement for tenancies commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, or July 1, 2022 for mobilehomes; for earlier existing tenancies, it need not be in the agreement. Initial rent for a wholly new tenancy is excepted as stated in the requirement.
rules.quoted_span: Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
rules.interaction:
Qualifying stricter public rent control removes housing from this section. The section neither expands nor limits local rent-regulation authority consistent with Chapter 2.7 and does not authorize otherwise impermissible local limits. Adding the prescribed exemption notice counts as a similar lease provision under section 1946.2(b)(1)(E).

calendar year.
(iii) The percentage change shall be rounded to the nearest one-tenth of 1 percent.

rules.title: Post the tenant-rights notice in an accessible interior common area
rules.requirement: Post the tenant-rights notice in an interior common area if the property has one accessible to all tenants.
rules.coverage_conditions: A property has an interior common area accessible to all tenants. The notice describes ordinance coverage, applicable rent-increase petition rights, and exemptions. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.

Exclude Golden Duplex only if owner-occupied on 1979-12-31 AND currently occupied by an owner; shared kitchen/bath only if owner lived on property when tenancy began; ADU-property tenancy only if begun AFTER 2018-11-07 AND property has an ADU AND either unit owner-occupied; also university rentals such as dormitories and nonprofit cooperatives. Do not substitute portfolio unit counts.

rules.title: Limits on disability-accommodation verification
rules.requirement: When an accommodation need is not obvious, a housing provider may request only information necessary to establish disability, describe the accommodation, and show the disability-related need for it. Providers cannot seek a particular diagnosis, disability severity, medical records or history, or unrelated disability or medical information. Documentation need not come from a doctor: it may come from a reliable, knowledgeable third party or reliable information supplied by the requester, including disability-benefit proof or the requester's own credible statement.
rules.key_value: Verification limited to disability, requested accommodation, and their necessary relationship
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to verification of disability-related accommodation requests, including requests connected with rental admission. Third-party reliability is assessed case by case, including familiarity with the disability or accommodation need.
rules.exemptions: When the need is obvious or known, the guidance says further inquiry is unnecessary.
rules.quoted_span:
However, if the need for a reasonable accommodation or modification is obvious or known, further inquiry is not necessary. If the need is not obvious, the housing provider may only request information that:
Is necessary to establish that the individual has a disability
Describes the needed accommodation or modification
Is needed to show the relationship between the individual’s disability and how the requested accommodation or modification is necessary to afford the individual with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing.
rules.interaction: r-0030 coexists r-0373 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.

conditions.description: Only the stated necessary information may be requested when the need is not obvious.

rules.temporal_notes: No operative date is stated.

evidence.quote:
However, if the need for a reasonable accommodation or modification is obvious or known, further inquiry is not necessary. If the need is not obvious, the housing provider may only request information that:
Is necessary to establish that the individual has a disability
Describes the needed accommodation or modification
Is needed to show the relationship between the individual’s disability and how the requested accommodation or modification is necessary to afford the individual with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing.

A housing provider cannot seek information about:
A particular diagnosis or medical condition
The severity of the disability
Medical records
Medical history
Other disability or medical issues unrelated to the request

Documentation can come from any reliable third party who is in a position to know about the individual’s disability or the disability-related need for accommodation, such as a health care provider, therapist, social worker, non-medical service provider, member of a peer support group, parent, child, or other relative.

Reliable documentation of an individual’s disability and/or their need for a reasonable accommodation or modification can also be provided by the person making the request. This may include proof of receipt of disability-related benefits, such as SSI or SSDI or the requestor’s own credible statement.

The determination of whether a third party is reliable is determined on a case-by-case basis and may take into account how the third party is familiar with the individual’s disability and/or the disability-related need for the accommodation.

What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

Can a housing provider ask for documentation to verify the need for a reasonable accommodation or modification?
Yes. However, if the need for a reasonable accommodation or modification is obvious or known, further inquiry is not necessary. If the need is not obvious, the housing provider may only request information that:
Is necessary to establish that the individual has a disability
Describes the needed accommodation or modification
Is needed to show the relationship between the individual’s disability and how the requested accommodation or modification is necessary to afford the individual with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing.

A housing provider cannot seek information about:
A particular diagnosis or medical condition
The severity of the disability
Medical records
Medical history
Other disability or medical issues unrelated to the request
Does documentation of the need for an accommodation or modification have to be from a doctor?
No. Documentation can come from any reliable third party who is in a position to know about the individual’s disability or the disability-related need for accommodation, such as a health care provider, therapist, social worker, non-medical service provider, member of a peer support group, parent, child, or other relative. Reliable documentation of an individual’s disability and/or their need for a reasonable accommodation or modification can also be provided by the person making the request. This may include proof of receipt of disability-related benefits, such as SSI or SSDI or the requestor’s own credible statement. The determination of whether a third party is reliable is determined on a case-by-case basis and may take into account how the third party is familiar with the individual’s disability and/or the disability-related need for the accommodation.

Therefore, housing providers must allow
reasonable accommodations for ESAs under the rules described in these FAQs. This includes existing rules regarding what type of documentation establishes someone’s disability-related need for a reasonable accommodation to have an ESA.

evidence.quote:
What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

criteria.condition: Provider considers information to verify a disability-related accommodation/modification request. If need is obvious OR known, further inquiry is unnecessary; otherwise request only disability existence, needed change and necessary disability/need relationship.

evidence.quote:
Can a housing provider ask for documentation to verify the need for a reasonable accommodation or modification?
Yes. However, if the need for a reasonable accommodation or modification is obvious or known, further inquiry is not necessary. If the need is not obvious, the housing provider may only request information that:
Is necessary to establish that the individual has a disability
Describes the needed accommodation or modification
Is needed to show the relationship between the individual’s disability and how the requested accommodation or modification is necessary to afford the individual with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy the housing.

criteria.condition: No diagnosis, severity, medical records/history or unrelated medical information. Documentation may be from reliable knowledgeable third party OR reliable requester information including benefit proof/credible statement; no doctor-only requirement.

evidence.quote:
A housing provider cannot seek information about:
A particular diagnosis or medical condition
The severity of the disability
Medical records
Medical history
Other disability or medical issues unrelated to the request
Does documentation of the need for an accommodation or modification have to be from a doctor?
No. Documentation can come from any reliable third party who is in a position to know about the individual’s disability or the disability-related need for accommodation, such as a health care provider, therapist, social worker, non-medical service provider, member of a peer support group, parent, child, or other relative. Reliable documentation of an individual’s disability and/or their need for a reasonable accommodation or modification can also be provided by the person making the request. This may include proof of receipt of disability-related benefits, such as SSI or SSDI or the requestor’s own credible statement. The determination of whether a third party is reliable is determined on a case-by-case basis and may take into account how the third party is familiar with the individual’s disability and/or the disability-related need for the accommodation.

at rent payment dates, beginning within 30 days after receipt of Notice of Tax Reduction. The first

Property Tax Rebate for Tenants 
 The Tenants’ Property Tax Rebate Act (N.J.S.A. 54:4-6.2 to – 6.13; N.J.A.C. 5:33-3.1 et 
seq.), as amended in 1998, may require owners of properties with five (5) or more rental units to 
pass on to their tenants as a rent credit or cash rebate, the full amount of any current property tax 
reduction. Reductions are calculated by comparing the current year’s taxes with a previous year 
(beginning with 1998) that shows a larger tax amount. The difference is the amount to be rebated 
to tenants. Municip alities with rent control ordinances that do not permit landlords to pass tax 
increases along to tenants are not subject to the law. The law also contains exceptions for certain 
types of rental properties. See N.J.S.A. 54:4-6.3 for the list of the types of  properties that are 
exempt. 
 In each municipality, where a rebate is due, a notice of property tax reduction ( N.J.S.A. 
54:4-6.7) is sent from the local tax collector to the building owners within 30 days after tax bills 
are issued to the building owner. Generally, rebates are to be distributed in monthly installments 
at rent payment dates, beginning within 30 days after receipt of Notice of Tax Reduction. The first 
rebate is to be cumulative from January and all are to be completed by December 31. However, if 
the notice is received after November 1, the rebate is to be completed by June 30 of the following 
year.  
 Under the law, in  eligible municipalities, a property rebate is due to tenants only when 
property taxes are reduced because of: 1) a municipal wide revaluation of all real estate and only 
in the first year the revaluation takes effect, 2) generally, when the property tax rate in the current 
year is lower than the base year (usually 1998), 3) taxpayers in the municipality receive tax rate 
credit through the Regional Efficiency Aid Program (REAP)  (N.J.S.A. 54:4-8.76 et seq .). The 
entire amount of the REAP credit must be passed through to tenants.

rules.title: Protection notice and guide at commencement or renewal
rules.requirement: For a covered tenancy commencing or renewed on or after June 24, 2023, the landlord must include the prescribed protection notice and Tenant Protection Guide in the lease, or provide them as written notice signed by the tenant when the lease is signed, with a copy to the tenant. The prescribed notice must be at least 12-point font and comply with Civil Code §1632. It explains the state rent-limit reference, the local statement-of-cause requirement, and possible additional protections for seniors and disabled tenants. This is a procedural disclosure requirement.
rules.key_value: At lease signing; at least 12-point font
rules.coverage_conditions: Unit is San Diego residential rental property intended for human habitation; units in mobilehome parks are included subject to the separate mobilehome exclusions. Lawful continuous occupancy entitlement must exceed 30 days; exclude a fixed-term lease of three months or less, including renewals/extensions of that lease for a fixed term of three months or less. This tests lawful entitlement, not an already-completed 30-day occupancy waiting period. Rule-specific applicability: Tenancy commences OR renews on/after 2023-06-24; provide protection notice and Guide in lease OR tenant signed written notice at lease signing, with copy. Lawful entitlement>30 days is a definition, not a wait-before-first-notice period. Additional event and branch tests: Tenancy commences OR renews on/after 2023-06-24; provide protection notice and Guide in lease OR tenant signed written notice at lease signing, with copy.
rules.exemptions: Any fully established §98.0703(a)–(g) class excludes the Division: transient/tourist hotel occupancy under Civil Code §1940(b); short-term occupancy defined in and subject to Municipal Code Chapter 5 Article 10 Division 1; housing restricted by deed, government agreement or other document as affordable for very-low-, low- or moderate-income persons/families; housing subject to a qualifying affordable-housing subsidy agreement, EXCEPT tenant-based Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher housing is not excluded by this subsidy branch; mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended-care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, adult residential facility, or nonprofit transitional housing; dormitories owned AND operated by a higher-education or K–12 institution. Nonprofit transitional housing has the separate up-to-24-month supportive-service definition. For the nonprofit transitional class, verify temporary operation by a nonprofit up to 24 months with supportive services toward permanent housing. Exclude if tenant shares a bathroom OR kitchen with landlord AND landlord maintains their principal residence there. Exclude the landlord-occupied principal-residence single-family home, including the stated rental of no more than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior accessory dwelling units, and a mobilehome. Preserve the source categories and do not replace them with owner-portfolio size. Exclude only when there are two separate dwelling units in one structure AND landlord occupied one as principal residence at tenancy beginning AND continues occupancy. Exclude housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, UNLESS the housing is a mobilehome. Evaluate the rolling interval at the relevant event date. Separately alienable residential property, including a mobilehome, is excluded only if landlord is NOT a REIT, NOT a corporation, NOT an LLC with at least one corporate member, and NOT mobilehome-park management, AND the prescribed written exemption notice has been provided. Notice may be in the lease for a tenancy existing before 2024-01-01; it MUST be in the lease for a tenancy commenced or renewed on/after 2024-01-01. §98.0701 Purpose and Intent 
The purpose and intent of this Division is to promote stability in the San Diego rental 
housing market and limit adverse impacts on displaced tenants forced to find 
replacement housing in the expensive and limited San Diego housing market. This 
Division protects the rights of tenants by requiring just cause for termination of a 
tenancy consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, limiting the grounds for 
termination of a tenancy, requiring greater tenant relocation assistance in specified 
circumstances, and providing additional tenant protections. The rights conferred by 
this Division are in addition to any existing rights provided to tenants by state or 
federal law.

Residential rental property means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human 
habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

§98.0703 Exemptions 
This Division shall not apply to the following types of residential rental properties or 
residential circumstances: 
(a) transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in California Civil Code 
section 1940(b), as may be amended; 
(b) short-term residential occupancy, as defined in and subject to Chapter 5, 
Article 10, Division 1 of this Code, as may be amended;  
 
(c) housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement 
with a government agency, or other document as affordable housing for 
persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be amended;  
(d)  housing subject to an agreement that provides housing subsidies for affordable 
housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income, as 
defined in California Health and Safety Code section 50093, as may be 
amended, or comparable federal statutes. This exemption shall not include 
Section 8;  
Ch. Art. Div.

(3-2024) 
 
 
 
(e) mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law (California Civil 
Code sections 798-799.11), as may be amended;  
 
(f) housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended 
care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly, as defined in 
California Health and Safety Code section 1569.2, as may be amended, an 
adult residential facility, as defined in Title 22, Division 6, Chapter 6 of the 
Manual of Policies and Procedures published by the California Department of 
Social Services, as may be amended, or non- profit transitional housing; 
(g) dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or an 
institution offering instruction to any grade from kindergarten through 12;

Non-profit transitional housing means temporary housing operated by a non-profit 
organization for up to 24 months with supportive services to individuals and families 
with the goal of interim stability and support to successfully move to and maintain 
permanent housing, which may cover housing costs and accompanying supportive 
services for program participants.

(i) single-family residence occupied by the landlord as the landlord’s principal 
place of residence, including both of the following:  
 
(1) a residence in which the landlord-occupant rents or leases no more 
than two bedrooms, two accessory dwelling units, or two junior 
accessory dwelling units, as defined in section 113.0103; and  
 
(2) a mobilehome.

(j) a property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in 
which the landlord occupies one of the dwelling units as the landlord’s 
principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the 
landlord continues in occupancy;

(k) housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 
15 years, unless the housing is a mobilehome; and

(l) residential rental property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate 
from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following 
apply: 
(1) The landlord is not any of the following:

Tenancy means the lawful right or entitlement of a tenant to continuously use or 
occupy a residential rental property for more than 30 days. A tenancy does not
