rules.title: JCO relocation assistance for no-fault evictions
rules.requirement: The JCO requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions; tenants evicted for an at-fault reason are not entitled to relocation assistance under this guidance. The no-fault discussion qualifies payment as something the owner may have to provide.
rules.coverage_conditions: JCO-covered tenancies in most non-RSO Los Angeles residential properties, after six months in the same unit or expiration of the original lease, whichever occurs first. Listed no-fault grounds include owner or immediate-family occupancy; legally or covenant-required resident-manager occupancy; demolition, permanent withdrawal, or nonresidential conversion; government vacate orders; HUD ownership and sale; residential-hotel conversion or demolition; and affordable-housing conversion. Additional source-reviewed applicability: City of Los Angeles residential property generally outside RSO; newer than 1978-10-01 buildings and single-family-only properties can be covered. Check nonexhaustive JCO exceptions: transient hotels, licensed care, fraternity/sorority, owner roommate, certain cooperatives, qualifying nonprofit homeless/short-treatment facilities, and certain HACLA/government properties. Labels require missing detailed conditions. Tenant has lived in SAME unit at least 6 months OR original lease expired, whichever first; either branch suffices.
rules.exemptions: At-fault evictions carry no relocation entitlement under this guidance. JCO coverage exceptions include transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, certain cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless or short-term substance-abuse treatment facilities, and some HACLA- or government-owned properties; the list is not exhaustive. Payment exception: replace resident manager with another, subject to manager-tenant free/reduced-rent-with-no-other-pay qualification; OR natural-disaster hazard eviction not caused by landlord negligence.
rules.quoted_span: It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
rules.interaction:
Relocation assistance is a consequence of qualifying no-fault eviction, separate from the just-cause requirement itself.
r-0418 coexists r-0164 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.
limitations: No payment amounts, deadlines, or detailed eligibility qualifications are supplied.

In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

evidence.quote:
Just Cause For Eviction Ordinance (JCO)
If you own rental property in the City of Los Angeles, it may be subject to the
Just Cause Ordinance
(JCO).  It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.
Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

rules.title: Forfeiture of deposit retention and damage-counterclaim rights
rules.requirement: A landlord forfeits the right to retain any security for any reason, or to counterclaim for premises damage in a tenant's deposit-recovery action, upon any of the listed subsection (6) failures.
rules.key_value: Any listed subsection (6) failure forfeits retention/counterclaim rights
rules.coverage_conditions: The triggers are failure to use the subsection (3) account; failure to furnish a compliant damage itemization within thirty days after occupancy ends; attempted enforcement of a conflicting provision in a tenant-signed lease or attempted waiver; failure to transfer security or successor noncompliance with subsection (5); or failure to return the lawful deposit balance and interest within thirty days after termination.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: The separate treble-damages provision selects only clauses (a), (d), and (e); it is not triggered by every subsection (6) failure solely by being listed here.

rules.title: Exclusive authorized categories of deposit deductions
rules.requirement: Deposit deductions are limited to unpaid rent or water charges not validly withheld or deducted, unpaid real-estate-tax increases due under a section 15C-compliant escalation clause, and reasonable repairs of qualifying tenant-related damage excluding wear and tear. No deduction may be made for another purpose.
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security deductions made on return under subsection (4); damage may be caused by the tenant, a person under the tenant's control, or a person present with the tenant's consent.

rules.title: Reasonable disability accommodations in housing policies and services
rules.requirement: For housing covered by subsections 6 and 7, refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services is handicap discrimination when the accommodations may be necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies under subsections 6 and 7 to accommodations that may be necessary for a handicapped person's equal housing opportunity.
rules.exemptions: An accommodation paid for by the owner or other ownership-right holder is not reasonable and is not required if it imposes undue hardship. Factors include nature and cost, material effects on marketability, overall housing-business size, number and type of units, budget and assets, and ability to recover costs through a federal tax deduction. Housing covered through subsection 7 retains that subsection's owner-occupied two-family leasing exemption.

rules.title: Authority and consultation prerequisite for deposit-waiver fee regulations
rules.requirement: The executive office of housing and livable communities may promulgate regulations authorizing agreed fees instead of security deposits, subject to the statutory conditions. It must consult the attorney general's office before promulgating those regulations.

rules.title: Good-faith estimated deductions and later completed accounting
rules.requirement: When landlord or employee repairs cannot reasonably be completed within 21 calendar days after vacancy, or outside service, material, or supply documents are not possessed within that period, the landlord may deduct a good-faith estimate and include it with the statement, identifying the outside provider and contact details when missing documents are the reason. The landlord must complete the requirements of subdivision (h)(1)-(2) within 14 calendar days after the repair is completed or the documentation is received.
rules.key_value: 21-day initial condition; completed accounting within 14 calendar days of completion or document receipt
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security accounting in the specifically stated unfinished-landlord-work or unavailable-third-party-document circumstances; required provider details are name, address, and telephone number. The initial statement and remainder return remain governed by paragraph (h)(1).
rules.exemptions: Paragraph (h)(4) excuses paragraphs (2)-(3) for repair and cleaning deductions totaling no more than $125 or a tenant-signed waiver substantially containing paragraph (2)'s text, signed at or after notice under section 1946 or 1946.1 or Code of Civil Procedure section 1161, or no earlier than 60 days before fixed-term expiration. Paragraph (h)(5) overrides those exceptions upon a tenant documentation request within 14 calendar days after statement receipt and requires compliance within 14 calendar days after the landlord receives the tenant's request.
rules.interaction: This procedure permits an estimate in the initial accounting, not an unlimited postponement of the initial statement or remaining-security return.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The source identifies a 2026-01-01 version amendment but no separate original onset for this procedure.

(a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:

(h) (1) No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, but not earlier than the time that either the landlord or the tenant provides a notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1, Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or not earlier than 60 calendar days prior to
the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant as follows:

(2) The landlord shall also include, along with and at the same time the itemized statement is sent, copies of documents showing charges incurred and deducted by
the landlord to repair or clean the premises, as follows:
(A) If the landlord or landlord’s employee did the work, the itemized statement shall reasonably describe the work performed. The itemized statement shall include the time spent and the reasonable hourly rate charged.
(B) If the landlord or landlord’s employee did not do the work, the landlord shall provide the tenant a copy of the bill, invoice, or receipt supplied by the person or entity performing the work. The itemized statement shall provide the tenant with the name, address, and telephone number of the person or entity, if the bill, invoice, or receipt does not include that information.
(C) If a deduction is made for materials or supplies, the landlord shall
provide a copy of the bill, invoice, or receipt. If a particular material or supply item is purchased by the landlord on an ongoing basis, the landlord may document the cost of the item by providing a copy of a bill, invoice, receipt, vendor price list, or other vendor document that reasonably documents the cost of the item used in the repair or cleaning of the unit.
(D) If a deduction is made for repairs or cleanings allowed by this section, the landlord shall provide photographs taken pursuant to subdivision (g), along with a written explanation of the cost of the allowable repairs or cleanings, as described in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive. The landlord may provide such photographs to the tenant by mail, email, computer flash drive, or by providing a link where the tenant may view the photographs online.

(4) The landlord need not comply with paragraph (2) or (3) if either of the following applies:
(A) The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).
(B) The tenant waived the rights specified in paragraphs (2) and (3). The waiver shall only be effective if it is signed by the tenant at the same time or after a notice to terminate a tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1 has been given, a notice under Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been given, or no earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease. (a) This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.
(b) As used in this section, “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following:
(1) The compensation of a landlord for a
tenant’s default in the payment of rent.
(2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.
(3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. The amendments to this paragraph enacted by the act adding this sentence shall apply only to tenancies for which the tenant’s right to occupy begins after January 1, 2003.
(4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the
security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

(h) As used in this section, “landlord” means an owner of residential rental property.
(i) As used in

rules.title: Application screening fee limited by actual costs and the adjustable statutory ceiling
rules.requirement: An application screening fee must not exceed the actual out-of-pocket information-gathering costs plus the reasonable value of the landlord's or agent's time, and must also remain within the statutory per-applicant ceiling. The statute states a $30 base ceiling that may be adjusted annually commensurate with Consumer Price Index increases beginning January 1, 1998.
rules.key_value: Lesser of actual information costs plus reasonable time value and the CPI-adjustable $30 statutory base ceiling
rules.coverage_conditions: A residential rental property owner or agent charging an applicant for information gathering, including personal references or consumer credit reports, subject to the availability and alternative-process conditions in subdivision (c). Applicant includes an entity or individual requesting the residential rental or agreeing to be a guarantor or cosignor. The section defines application screening fee as the specified nonrefundable payment for purchasing a consumer credit report and validating, reviewing, or otherwise processing the rental application; its express refund provisions still apply.
rules.exemptions: The fee is not security under section 1950.5 or an advance fee under Business and Professions Code section 10026. The section does not preempt federal or state housing-assistance-program provisions governing deposits and fees.
rules.interaction: Fee limits and permission to charge operate together with subdivision (c)'s availability and alternative-process prerequisites; the statutory term nonrefundable does not erase refunds expressly required elsewhere in the section.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. January 1, 1998 is the stated start for annual CPI adjustments, not a computed 2026 fee amount or the original onset of every duty. Footer identifies the supplied version as amended effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: D026 supplies neither the relevant CPI series values nor a calculated 2026 maximum, so no current numerical maximum is invented.
Other housing-assistance-program rules and external definitions are not reproduced here.

evidence.quote: (a) Notwithstanding Section 1950.5, when a landlord or their agent receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant, the landlord or their agent may charge, pursuant to subdivision (c), that applicant an application screening fee to cover the costs of obtaining information about the applicant. The information requested and obtained by the landlord or their agent may include, but is not limited to, personal reference checks and consumer credit reports produced by consumer credit reporting agencies as defined in Section 1785.3. A landlord or their agent may, but is not required to, accept and rely upon a consumer credit report presented by an applicant.

(c) (1) A landlord or their agent shall not charge an applicant an application screening fee when they know or should have known that no rental unit is available at that time or will be available within a reasonable period of time.
(2) A landlord or their agent may charge an applicant an application screening fee only if the landlord or their agent, at the time the application screening fee is collected, offers any of the following:
(A) An application screening process that complies with all of the following:
(i) Completed applications are considered, as provided for in the landlord’s established screening criteria, in the order in which the completed applications were received. The landlord’s screening criteria shall be provided to the applicant in writing together with the application form.
(ii) The first applicant who meets the landlord’s established screening criteria is approved for tenancy.
(iii) Applicants are not
charged an application screening fee unless or until their application is actually considered.
(iv) Clause (iii) shall not be considered violated if a landlord or their agent inadvertently collects an application screening fee from an applicant as the result of multiple concurrent application submissions, provided that the landlord or their agent issues a refund of the application screening fee within seven days to any applicant whose application is not considered. The landlord may offer, as an alternative to refunding the screening fee, the option, at the applicant’s discretion, for the screening fee paid by the applicant to be applied to an application for another rental unit offered by the landlord. A landlord or their agent shall not be required to refund an application screening fee to an applicant whose application is denied, after consideration, because the applicant does not meet the landlord’s established screening criteria.
(B) An application screening process in which the landlord or their agent returns the entire screening fee to any applicant who is not selected for tenancy, regardless of the reason, within 7 days of selecting an applicant for tenancy or 30 days of when the application was submitted, whichever occurs first.

The Department does not have jurisdiction over the administratio n of the courts, nor can

regulations, and court cases that concern landlord-tenant relations; however, this publication is not 
a complete summary of all laws, regulations, and court cases that concern landlord-tenant relations 
in New Jersey. Any person who plans to initiate a legal action resulting from a landlord -tenant 
dispute may wish to consult the appropriate enforcing agency, a county legal services agency, 
private counsel, or an owner’s, tenant’s, or mobile home organization. A list of additional agencies 
and organizations that may be available to provide assistance is located in the appendix section of 
this publication.  Please be advised that this guide may be amended by the Department as required, 
and will be posted on the Department’s website accordingly.

Foreclosure 
 Recent changes to federal law have strengthened a tenant’s rights in foreclosure 
proceedings.  However, the federal law does not preempt any State or local law that provides 
longer time periods or other additional protections for tenants  in foreclosure proceedings .  
Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction in New Jersey. In Chase Manhattan Bank v. 
Josephson, 135 N.J. 209 (1994) the court held that when a lender or other buyer takes possession 
of the property, the residential tenant comes with the property. Before a tenant can be evicted due 
to foreclosure, the landlord must provide the tenant with a 90 -day notice to qui t when the 
foreclosed property has been purchased by a buyer who wants to personally occupy it as his or her 
primary residence. However, if a tenant has a lease agreement that goes beyond the 90 days the 
landlord may not take action to evict the tenant unt il after the lease expires and the 90 -day notice 
to quit has been given.  The 90-day notice may be given 90 days before the lease expires.  Month-
to-month tenants and two- and three-family owner-occupied units are not exempt from the 90-day 
notice requirements.

Any person acquiring a foreclosed property containing one or more residential rental units 
must provide notices to the tenants in English and Spanish, within 10 business days after the sale, 
letting tenants know that ownership has changed hands and that the tenants are not required to 
move because of the foreclosure.

rules.title: Transfer of security and accrued interest to a successor
rules.requirement: When the landlord transfers its interest in the dwelling by sale, assignment, death, receivership, bankruptcy trusteeship, or otherwise, it must transfer the tenant's deposit and accrued interest to the successor. From the transfer date, the successor is responsible for retention and return under section 15B.
rules.coverage_conditions: A landlord that received residential security transfers its interest in the corresponding dwelling.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required. Granting a mortgage alone is not a transfer of interest for this subsection.
rules.interaction: Transfer is accompanied by successor notice duties and does not automatically erase the predecessor's continuing liability under the following paragraphs.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).

rules.title: Housing discrimination prohibition for persons covered by Civil Code section 51
rules.requirement: A person subject to Civil Code section 51 as applied to housing must not discriminate in rental housing on the listed protected grounds or another basis prohibited by that section. Selection preferences based on age in a federally approved housing program do not constitute age discrimination in housing under the stated provision.
rules.coverage_conditions: Persons subject to Civil Code section 51 in its application to housing accommodations, here limited to rental housing. Listed grounds are sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, color, race, religion, ancestry, national origin, familial status, marital status, disability, genetic information, source of income, and veteran or military status, with perception and association included under (m). Source of income includes lawful, verifiable tenant or representative payments and payments to an owner on a tenant's behalf, public assistance, housing subsidies, Section 8, and HUD-VASH; the owner is not a tenant representative unless the source is HUD-VASH.
rules.exemptions: Age-based selection preferences imposed in connection with a federally approved housing program are not age discrimination as stated in (d). Written or oral income-level or income-source inquiries are not themselves source-of-income discrimination under (p)(2).
rules.interaction: The Civil Code section 51 coverage limitation and additional prohibited bases remain cross-references; this record does not invent their content or extend the age statement to every age preference.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset unspecified; source version amended effective 2024-01-01.
limitations: Civil Code section 51's covered-person definition and any additional prohibited bases are not reproduced in D027.

rules.title: Reoffer and moving-expense reimbursement after failed owner occupancy
rules.requirement: If the intended occupant does not move in within 90 days after the tenant vacates, or does not maintain the unit as a primary residence for at least 12 consecutive months, the owner must offer the unit back to the displaced tenant at the rent and lease terms in effect when the tenant vacated and reimburse reasonable moving expenses exceeding relocation assistance already paid. If the intended occupant timely moves in but dies before completing 12 months, that circumstance is not noncompliance or a material violation by the owner.
rules.key_value: 90-day move-in deadline; 12 consecutive months; reasonable moving expenses above prior relocation assistance
rules.coverage_conditions: A tenant displaced under the owner/family occupancy ground of section 1946.2(b)(2)(A), subject to that ground's ownership, tenancy-duration, and lease requirements.
rules.exemptions: Death after timely move-in is the express exception. Section-wide exclusions also remain applicable: transient/tourist occupancy; specified hospital/religious/care facilities; institutional dormitories; resident-owner shared kitchen/bathroom housing; qualifying single-family owner-occupied housing and mobilehomes; qualifying owner-occupied two-unit structures without ADU/JADU units; non-mobilehome housing with a certificate of occupancy within 15 years; qualifying recorded/subsidized affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners; and separately alienable property satisfying both owner-type restrictions and prescribed exemption-notice requirements. Qualifying local just-cause ordinances displace the section.
rules.quoted_span:
If the intended occupant fails to occupy the rental unit within 90 days after the tenant vacates or fails to occupy the rental unit as their primary residence for at least 12 consecutive months, the owner shall offer the unit to the tenant
who vacated it at the same rent and lease terms in effect at the time the tenant vacated and shall reimburse the tenant for reasonable moving expenses incurred in excess of any relocation assistance that was paid to the tenant in connection with the written notice.
rules.interaction:
A remedial return and reimbursement right following an owner-occupancy termination; it does not itself supply a termination ground. Prior relocation assistance offsets reimbursable moving expenses.
r-0429 coexists r-0270 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.
rules.temporal_notes: Section-wide operative date; supplied version amended effective January 1, 2026. Individual amendment changes are not identified. Repealed January 1, 2030.
rules.penalty: Section 1946.2(h) provides civil remedies for material violations.
limitations: This passage supplies no deadline for accepting the reoffer.
The death exception contains an internal reference to clause (vi); the substantive exception is preserved as written.

rules.requirement: Withdraw a conditional offer based on a criminal record only upon determining by a preponderance of the evidence that withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest. Perform an individualized assessment considering offense nature and severity, applicant age at the offense, elapsed time, rehabilitation and good conduct information, safety consequences if the offense recurred, and connection to property rented or leased by the applicant.

c.     (1)  A housing provider may withdraw a
conditional offer based on an applicant's criminal record only if the housing
provider determines, by preponderance of the evidence, that the withdrawal is
necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, and nondiscriminatory interest.
(2)   If a housing provider withdraws a conditional
offer, the housing provider shall provide the applicant with written
notification that includes, with specificity, the reason or reasons for the
withdrawal of the conditional offer and an opportunity to appeal the denial by
providing evidence to the housing provider demonstrating inaccuracies within
the applicant's criminal record or evidence of rehabilitation or other
mitigating factors.
(3)   The housing provider shall perform an
individualized assessment of the application in light of the following factors:
(a)   the nature and severity of the criminal offense;
(b)   the age of the applicant at the time of the
occurrence of the criminal offense;
(c)   the time which has elapsed since the occurrence
of the criminal offense;
(d)   any information produced by the applicant, or
produced on the applicant's behalf, in regard to the applicant's rehabilitation
and good conduct since the occurrence of the criminal offense;
(e)   the degree to which the criminal offense, if it
reoccurred, would negatively impact the safety of the housing provider's other
tenants or property; and
(f)   whether the criminal offense occurred on or was
connected to property that was rented or leased by the applicant.

rules.title: Security claims limited to reasonable amounts for statutory purposes
rules.requirement: The landlord may claim security only in amounts reasonably necessary for the purposes described in subdivision (b), subject to the additional restrictions in subdivision (e)(2).
rules.key_value: Amounts reasonably necessary for purposes in subdivision (b)
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential security within subdivision (b), which describes beginning-of-tenancy processing charges except as provided in section 1950.6, advance rent, and purposes including rent default, damage caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant excluding ordinary wear, move-out cleaning to the initial cleanliness level, and authorized restoration, replacement, or return of personal property or appurtenances excluding ordinary wear. The agreement must authorize security use for the subdivision (b)(4) personal-property purpose. The source states that amendments to the cleaning paragraph apply only where the tenant's right to occupy begins after January 1, 2003.
rules.exemptions: No claim for preexisting defects or ordinary wear; materials and work are limited to reasonable restoration costs; professional cleaning is chargeable only when reasonably necessary to restore the initial condition excluding ordinary wear. The list in subdivision (b) is expressly nonexclusive.
rules.interaction: Subdivision (e)(2) limits claims otherwise within subdivision (b); inspection and accounting provisions impose additional requirements.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Preserve the cleaning-paragraph occupancy-date condition after 2003-01-01. Subdivision (q) describes specified 1985 amendments to (e) as declaratory of existing law; no original onset is inferred from the footer's 2026-01-01 amendment date.
limitations: This record does not treat the enumerated purposes as exhaustive or independently resolve the external section 1950.6 exception.

“State law permits former tenants to reclaim abandoned personal property left at the former address of the tenant, subject to certain conditions. In general, these costs will be lower the sooner you contact your former landlord after
being notified that property belonging to you was left behind after you moved out.”
(2) Based on the inspection, the landlord shall give the tenant an itemized statement specifying repairs or cleanings that are proposed to be the basis of any deductions from the security the landlord intends to make pursuant to paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (b). (5) Nothing in this subdivision shall prevent a landlord from using the security for deductions itemized in the statement provided for in paragraph (2) that were not cured by the tenant so long as the deductions are for damages authorized by
this section.
(6) Nothing in this subdivision shall prevent a landlord from using the security for any purpose specified in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (b) that occurs between completion of the initial inspection when possession of the unit is returned to the landlord or that was not identified during the initial inspection due to the presence of a tenant’s possessions.

rules.title: Professional cleaning charges require reasonable necessity
rules.requirement: The landlord must not require payment for, or claim against the tenant or security for, professional carpet cleaning or other professional cleaning unless reasonably necessary to restore the premises to their condition at tenancy inception, excluding ordinary wear.
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rentals covered by section 1950.5 where professional carpet or other professional cleaning is charged to the tenant or security.
rules.exemptions: Professional cleaning may be charged when the stated reasonable-necessity and initial-condition standard is met, excluding ordinary wear; preexisting defects remain nonchargeable.
rules.interaction: Does not displace the general restrictions on preexisting conditions and ordinary wear.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Footer supplies a 2026-01-01 version amendment date, not this provision's original onset.
rules.quoted_span: (C) The landlord shall not require a tenant to pay for, or assert a claim against the tenant or the security for, professional carpet cleaning or other professional cleaning services, unless reasonably necessary to return the premises to the condition it was in at the inception of tenancy, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear.

rules.title: Ordered application review and first-qualified approval in fee process A
rules.requirement: When relying on subdivision (c)(2)(A) to charge a screening fee, completed applications must be considered in receipt order under the landlord's established criteria, which must be provided in writing with the application form. The first applicant meeting those criteria must be approved for tenancy.
rules.key_value: Receipt order; first qualifying applicant approved
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential property owners or agents choosing the paragraph (A) fee-authorizing process. This process must also comply with (A)(iii)-(iv)'s consideration-before-charge rule and its limited concurrent-submission exception; applicant includes guarantors and cosignors as defined in (j).
rules.exemptions: These paragraph (A) conditions are not imposed by this provision when the landlord instead uses paragraph (B)'s full refund process for all unselected applicants. This section does not preempt federal or state housing-assistance-program deposit and fee requirements.
rules.interaction: These selection constraints are conditional components of one fee process, not general screening restrictions independently imposed on every landlord.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. Original onset unspecified; version amendment effective 2026-01-01.
limitations: The supplied provision does not enumerate what substantive screening criteria are otherwise lawful.

rules.title: Permissible post-offer convictions and lookback periods
rules.requirement: After a conditional offer, consider only the listed serious convictions without an express lookback limit, or qualifying indictable offenses within the applicable lookback: first degree, six years; second or third degree, four years; fourth degree, one year. Measure from conviction issuance or, where the conviction resulted in a prison sentence, completion of that sentence, to issuance of the conditional offer.
rules.key_value: Listed serious convictions: no stated lookback; first degree: 6 years; second/third degree: 4 years; fourth degree: 1 year
rules.coverage_conditions: Post-offer screening of covered residential rental applicants. The listed serious convictions are murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, sexual assault under N.J.S.2C:14-2, the specified child sexual-act offense under N.J.S.2C:24-4(b)(3), and any crime resulting in lifetime state sex-offender registration.
rules.exemptions: Units in owner-occupied premises with no more than four dwelling units are excluded. Records prohibited by C.46:8-56(a) remain unusable.
rules.quoted_span:
After the issuance of a conditional offer to an
applicant, a housing provider may only consider a criminal record in the
applicant’s history that:
(1)   resulted in a conviction for murder, aggravated
sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, sexual assault in
violation of N.J.S.2C:14-2, causing or permitting a child to engage in a
prohibited sexual act or in the simulation of such an act in violation of
paragraph (3) of subsection b. of N.J.S.2C:24-4, or any crime that resulted in
lifetime registration in a state sex offender registry;
rules.interaction:
Consideration does not itself authorize withdrawal; C.46:8-56(c) imposes additional requirements.

rules.title: No rental denial because reasonable disability measures are needed
rules.requirement: A person may not be discriminated against or refused rental housing because the person needs a reasonable modification or accommodation.

(1) a refusal to permit or to make, at the expense of the handicapped person, reasonable modification of existing premises occupied or to be occupied by such person if such modification is necessary to afford such person full enjoyment of such premises; provided, however, that, in the case of publicly assisted housing, multiple dwelling housing consisting of ten or more units, or contiguously located housing consisting of ten or more units, reasonable modification shall be at the expense of the owner or other person having the right of ownership; provided, further, that, in the case of public ownership of such housing units the cost of such reasonable modification shall be subject to appropriation; and provided, further, that, in the case of a rental, the landlord may, where the modification to be paid for by the handicapped person will materially alter the marketability of the housing, condition permission for a modification on the tenant agreeing to restore or pay for the cost of restoring, the interior of the premises to the condition that existed prior to such modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted;
(2) a refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services, when such accommodations may be necessary to afford a handicapped person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling; and
(3) discrimination against or a refusal to rent to a person because of such person's need for reasonable modification or accommodation.

rules.title: HUD possession before sale ground
rules.requirement: The bulletin identifies recovery of possession to vacate property before sale as a no-fault ground when the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both owner and plaintiff.
rules.coverage_conditions: RSO- or JCO-covered property; HUD Secretary is both owner AND plaintiff; possession is sought to vacate before sale. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Eviction-related procedure is stated for ALL Los Angeles RSO OR JCO rental properties; verify relevant program property classification and keep disputed scope unknown. Substantive program scope: For these substantive no-fault grounds, require EITHER verified RSO property/tenancy coverage OR verified JCO property coverage AND (tenant has lived in the same unit for at least six months OR the original lease has expired, whichever occurs first). Apply the elapsed/original-lease test only to the JCO branch. Verify the particular ground and its other conditions separately. The all-properties filing rule in D040 lines 73-75 does not establish substantive JCO tenancy coverage.

evidence.quote:
The Secretary of Housing and Urban Development is both the owner and plaintiff and seeks 
to recover possession to vacate the property prior to sale (LAMC 151.09.A.12, 165.03.K.).

Rental Units Covered Under JCO
The JCO covers most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not regulated by the City’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO).
In order to apply to a tenancy, it requires that the tenant either has lived in the same unit for at least six months or that their original lease expired, whichever comes first.  There are other specific exceptions to the JCO including, but not limited to, transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner’s roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit facilities for the homeless or short-term treatment centers for substance abuse, and some properties owned by HACLA or the government.  The JCO can apply to buildings that are newer than October 1, 1978.  The JCO can apply to a property that contains only one single-family dwelling.

All tenant not- at-fault evictions require payment of relocation assistance and the filing of a 
Declaration of Intent to Evict form with the Los Angeles Housing Department (LAHD) before 
evicting tenants from units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause 
Ordinance (JCO). Failure to file the Landlord Declaration with the LAHD makes the eviction a 
violation of the RSO or JCO. Notices to terminate tenancy can only be served on the tenant after 
the landlord files the Declaration with LAHD, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD 
no later than 3 days after it is served. To file a copy, go to housing.lacity.gov/eviction-notices. 
 Not-At-Fault Reasons for Eviction
1. The landlord evicts for the occupancy of her/himself, spouse, grandchildren, children,  
parents or grandparents, or a resident manager (Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC)  
151.09.A.8, 165.03.H.). Evictions for the purpose of resident manager occupancy are

rules.title: Protection against discriminatory rental termination
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers may not cancel or terminate a rental agreement because of a protected characteristic. This is an antidiscrimination limitation on termination, not a general requirement to establish just cause for every eviction.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most California housing under FEHA. Protection covers actual or perceived protected characteristics, intersecting characteristics, and characteristics of associates. The listed characteristics include race, color, ancestry, national origin, citizenship, immigration status, primary language, religion, disability, sex and gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, genetic information, marital and familial status, source of income, military or veteran status, and age.
rules.exemptions: The guidance describes age-based limits for qualifying senior housing and, under unspecified circumstances, homeless-youth housing. It does not describe their consequences for termination. Its owner-occupied, one-additional-person exception expressly addresses applicant exclusion, not termination.
rules.quoted_span: Cancellation or termination of a sale or rental agreement

conditions.description: The termination protection concerns discriminatory grounds.

rules.temporal_notes: No operative date is stated.
limitations: The guidance supplies neither a general just-cause standard nor termination notice periods.
No statutory section is supplied.

evidence.quote: This law prohibits people or entities that provide housing from discriminating against or harassing tenants, homeowners, residents, their guests, housing or mortgage applicants, home buyers, and others.
Examples of actions that could be discriminatory if based on a person’s protected characteristic:
Cancellation or termination of a sale or rental agreement

California law protects individuals from illegal discrimination and harassment by housing providers based on certain protected characteristics, whether or not someone actually has that characteristic or is perceived to have it. The law also protects against discrimination and harassment that is based on more than one, or intersecting, characteristics. Finally, California law protects people from discrimination and harassment that is based on the protected characteristic of their family member, friend, roommate, or any other associate.

Protected characteristics include::
Race
Color
Ancestry
National origin
Citizenship
Immigration status
Primary language
Religion
Disability (mental or physical)
Sex and gender
Sexual orientation
Gender Identity
Gender Expression
Genetic information
Marital status
Familial status (families with children under 18 or people who are pregnant)
Source of income
(including the use of government rental assistance such as a Section 8 Housing Choice voucher)
Military or veteran status
Age
When an owner is occupying a home and is renting to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics.

Housing specifically for seniors may be limited based on age.
Under some circumstances, housing for homeless youth may be limited based on age.

What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act (also known as FEHA) applies to most providers of housing and services related to housing such as landlords, tenant screening companies, real estate agents, home sellers, builders, mortgage lenders, and housing authorities. This law prohibits people or entities that provide housing from discriminating against or harassing tenants, homeowners, residents, their guests, housing or mortgage applicants, home buyers, and others.
Examples of actions that could be discriminatory if based on a person’s protected characteristic:
Refusal to sell, rent, or lease rooms, apartments, mobile homes, condos, or houses
Refusal to negotiate for the sale, rental, or lease of housing
Informing someone that an apartment is not available for inspection, sale, or rental when it is in fact available
Denial of a home loan or homeowner’s insurance
Cancellation or termination of a sale or rental agreement
Refusal to permit, at a disabled tenant’s expense, reasonable modifications – such as adding a ramp, widening a doorway, or installing a safety bar in a shower – when necessary to accommodate a disability
Refusal to make reasonable accommodations in housing rules, policies, practices, or services where necessary to provide a disabled person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling
Rules that restrict only on families with children, such as a prohibition against children using an on-site pool or playing in common areas of an apartment complex
Refusing to rent to a tenant with a section 8 voucher.
Not complying with the requirements of a rental assistance or subsidy program (such as section 8) by refusing to complete required forms, sign documents, or allow inspections
Refusing to rent to anyone with a criminal history
Screening prospective tenants – including when done by a third-party such as a tenant screening company – in a way that discriminates based on a protected characteristic
Retaliation against someone because they filed a complaint with CRD, requested a reasonable accommodation for a disability, or otherwise tried to protect their rights to be free from housing discrimination
California law protects individuals from illegal discrimination and harassment by housing providers based on certain protected characteristics, whether or not someone actually has that characteristic or is perceived to have it. The law also protects against discrimination and harassment that is based on more than one, or intersecting, characteristics. Finally, California law protects people from discrimination and harassment that is based on the protected characteristic of their family member, friend, roommate, or any other associate.

When an owner is occupying a home and is renting to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics. However, the owner still cannot make, print, or publish discriminatory statements, notices, or advertisements.
When sharing a living area in a single dwelling, the owner or occupant may state or imply that the housing is available only to person of one sex.
Housing specifically for seniors may be limited based on age.
Under some circumstances, housing for homeless youth may be limited based on age.
Can a housing provider refuse to rent to families with children?
Generally, housing providers cannot discriminate against families with children. This is called “familial status” discrimination and protections include:
Prohibiting landlords and other types of housing providers from refusing to rent to someone because their household includes children.
Requiring that admission and occupancy requirements  be enforced the same for everyone, including families with children. For example, if a housing provider allows up to four people to live in a one-bedroom unit, they must allow a family of two parents and two children, or a mother or father with three children, to reside in the unit.
Prohibiting housing providers from having conditions or rules that discriminate against households with children, such as charging a higher security deposit to households with children or excluding children from playing in common areas open to other tenants.
However, housing that has been specifically designed for senior citizens (persons 55 and older in some cases or 62 and older in others) can exclude people based on age, including families with children. To qualify as “senior housing,” a housing accommodation must meet specific legally defined requirements, which may include a minimum number of units, age-based residency limits, and design features.
Is it legal to develop and market housing for seniors?
Yes, but only when the facility or community is:
Provided under any state or federal program that the Federal Department of Housing and Urban Development has determined to be specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons
Designed to meet the physical and social needs of senior citizens; or
A mobile home park that:
Is intended for, and solely occupied by, people aged 62 years or older; or

evidence.quote:
What types of housing are covered by the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
The Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) covers the sale, rental, or occupancy of most housing accommodations in California, including single-family homes, multi-family homes, condominiums, apartments, short-term rentals, mobile homes, subsidized housing, dormitories, sober living facilities,  group homes, residential motels,
emergency shelters, homeless shelters, shelters for survivors of domestic violence
, recreational vehicles (RVs) used as a home, farmworker housing, and boats used as homes.
Who must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act?
Most people and entities that are housing providers or who provide services related to housing must comply with the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). This includes landlords, homeowners, apartment managers, real estate brokers, state or local governments, owners of short-term rentals, appraisers, tenant screening companies, homeowners associations, mortgage lending companies, and public housing authorities.

criteria.condition: Provider cancels or terminates rental agreement because of a protected actual/perceived/intersecting/associated characteristic.

evidence.quote:
California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act (also known as FEHA) applies to most providers of housing and services related to housing such as landlords, tenant screening companies, real estate agents, home sellers, builders, mortgage lenders, and housing authorities. This law prohibits people or entities that provide housing from discriminating against or harassing tenants, homeowners, residents, their guests, housing or mortgage applicants, home buyers, and others.
Examples of actions that could be discriminatory if based on a person’s protected characteristic:
Refusal to sell, rent, or lease rooms, apartments, mobile homes, condos, or houses
Refusal to negotiate for the sale, rental, or lease of housing
Informing someone that an apartment is not available for inspection, sale, or rental when it is in fact available
Denial of a home loan or homeowner’s insurance
Cancellation or termination of a sale or rental agreement
Refusal to permit, at a disabled tenant’s expense, reasonable modifications – such as adding a ramp, widening a doorway, or installing a safety bar in a shower – when necessary to accommodate a disability
Refusal to make reasonable accommodations in housing rules, policies, practices, or services where necessary to provide a disabled person equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling
Rules that restrict only on families with children, such as a prohibition against children using an on-site pool or playing in common areas of an apartment complex
Refusing to rent to a tenant with a section 8 voucher.
Not complying with the requirements of a rental assistance or subsidy program (such as section 8) by refusing to complete required forms, sign documents, or allow inspections
Refusing to rent to anyone with a criminal history
Screening prospective tenants – including when done by a third-party such as a tenant screening company – in a way that discriminates based on a protected characteristic
Retaliation against someone because they filed a complaint with CRD, requested a reasonable accommodation for a disability, or otherwise tried to protect their rights to be free from housing discrimination
California law protects individuals from illegal discrimination and harassment by housing providers based on certain protected characteristics, whether or not someone actually has that characteristic or is perceived to have it. The law also protects against discrimination and harassment that is based on more than one, or intersecting, characteristics. Finally, California law protects people from discrimination and harassment that is based on the protected characteristic of their family member, friend, roommate, or any other associate.

criteria.condition: The owner-one-person and senior/youth exceptions are framed as admission restrictions; this guidance does not establish their consequences for termination. Do not transfer them automatically.

evidence.quote:
When an owner is occupying a home and is renting to one additional person, the owner may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics. However, the owner still cannot make, print, or publish discriminatory statements, notices, or advertisements.
When sharing a living area in a single dwelling, the owner or occupant may state or imply that the housing is available only to person of one sex.
Housing specifically for seniors may be limited based on age.
Under some circumstances, housing for homeless youth may be limited based on age.
Can a housing provider refuse to rent to families with children?
Generally, housing providers cannot discriminate against families with children. This is called “familial status” discrimination and protections include:
Prohibiting landlords and other types of housing providers from refusing to rent to someone because their household includes children.
Requiring that admission and occupancy requirements  be enforced the same for everyone, including families with children. For example, if a housing provider allows up to four people to live in a one-bedroom unit, they must allow a family of two parents and two children, or a mother or father with three children, to reside in the unit.
Prohibiting housing providers from having conditions or rules that discriminate against households with children, such as charging a higher security deposit to households with children or excluding children from playing in common areas open to other tenants.
However, housing that has been specifically designed for senior citizens (persons 55 and older in some cases or 62 and older in others) can exclude people based on age, including families with children. To qualify as “senior housing,” a housing accommodation must meet specific legally defined requirements, which may include a minimum number of units, age-based residency limits, and design features.
Is it legal to develop and market housing for seniors?
Yes, but only when the facility or community is:
Provided under any state or federal program that the Federal Department of Housing and Urban Development has determined to be specifically designed and operated to assist elderly persons
Designed to meet the physical and social needs of senior citizens; or
A mobile home park that:
Is intended for, and solely occupied by, people aged 62 years or older; or
Is intended and operated for occupancy by people aged 55 years or older and that meets a set of requirements including: at least 80% of the occupied units are intended to be occupied by at least one person who is 55 or older, the park publishes and adheres to policies and procedures demonstrating the intent for occupancy by people 55 or older, and the park complies with HUD’s rules for verification of occupancy.

rules.title: No discriminatory rental notices, statements, or advertisements
rules.requirement: A person must not make, print, publish, or cause a rental-housing notice, statement, or advertisement indicating a preference, limitation, discrimination, or intent to discriminate based on the protected characteristics in subdivision (c).
rules.coverage_conditions: Any person responsible for the described rental-housing communication. Subdivision (c) lists race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, and genetic information, including perceived traits and association under (m). Source of income includes lawful, verifiable income paid to a tenant or representative or on the tenant's behalf to the owner, public assistance and housing subsidies, Section 8, and HUD-VASH; a landlord is not the tenant's representative unless the source is HUD-VASH. The source separately applies to sale communications, outside this rental-only record.

rules.title: Prohibition on supplying coordinated pricing algorithms
rules.requirement: Prohibit selling, licensing, or otherwise providing Berkeley landlords with a covered coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or achievable occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley.
rules.key_value: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: A covered algorithm uses Competitor Data to calculate and recommend future lease rents, fees, occupancy rates, or other rental contract terms in coordination between a Berkeley landlord and at least one competitor, including through a vendor. Competitor Data must be nonpublic, less than 90 days old, and concern a property other than one owned or managed by the landlord receiving or using the recommendation. Products incorporating such algorithms are included. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Covered enacted definition requires future-lease coordination between a Berkeley landlord and >=1 competitor AND nonpublic competitor property data less than 90 days old, excluding recipient-owned or managed properties.
rules.exemptions: Excluded are aggregated anonymous rental-data reports, studies, or presentations that do not recommend future lease terms; products establishing rent or income limits under governmental affordable-housing guidelines; and information or processes used for project-financing market research, appraisals, or software-development research, testing, or training. The software-development exclusion permits processing Competitor Data for predictive or machine-learning models only when that data is not an operational input when a recommendation is calculated for publication or provision to a Berkeley landlord. Exclude anonymous aggregated reports without recommendations, government affordable-housing limits products, project-financing research, appraisal, or software-development research/testing/training. For the development branch, competitor data must NOT be an operational input when a landlord recommendation is calculated; training use alone is not equivalent to prohibited operational use.
rules.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley 
landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy 
levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.

evidence.quote:
This Chapter is not intended to prevent the development or sale of software to help 
landlords manage their units generally or through the use of public data. Nor does this 
Chapter regulate the amount of rent that a landlord may charge.

“Coordinated pricing algorithm” means any analytical or computation process that 
uses Competitor Data to calculate and recommend rent prices, fees, occupancy rates or 
other rental contract terms for future leases in coordination between one City of Berkeley 
landlord and one or more of such landlord’s competitors, including through a third-party 
vendor.

A “coordinated pricing algorithm” includes a product that incorporates a 
coordinated pricing algorithm, but does not include (a) a product or process that 
generates or presents any report, study, or presentation that publishes rental data in an 
aggregated and anonymous manner but does not recommend rent prices, fees, or 
occupancy rates or other rental contract terms for future leases; (b) a product used for 
the purpose of establishing rent or income limits in accordance with the affordable 
housing guidelines of a local government, the state, the federal government, or other 
political subdivision; or (c) a product or process that provides or uses, or the provision or 
use of, information for the purpose of (i) conducting market research for project financing, 
(ii) conducting an appraisal, or (iii) conducting research, testing, or training for software 
development.

For clarity, “research, testing, or training for software development” 
includes without limitation the use or processing of Competitor Data in the development, 
training, or testing of predictive or machine learning models so long as any such data is 
not used as an input in the operation of the model at the time a recommendation is 
calculated for publication or provision to a City of Berkeley landlord.

“Competitor Data” means information that is not available to the general public 
concerning actual rent prices, occupancy rates, lease start and end dates, and similar 
data regarding a property other than a property that is owned or managed by the landlord 
who is the recipient or user of the generated recommendation, when such data is less 
than 90 days old.

It shall be unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley 
landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy 
levels that may be achieved for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.

The City Attorney may file a civil action for violations of section 13.63.030, 
subsections A and/or B, for damages, injunctive relief, restitution/return of illegal profits, 
and/or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. The court shall award reasonable 
attorney’s fees and costs to the City Attorney if the City Attorney is the prevailing party 
in such a civil action.

evidence.quote:
A. “Coordinated pricing algorithm” means any analytical or computation process that 
uses Competitor Data to calculate and recommend rent prices, fees, occupancy rates or 
other rental contract terms for future leases in coordination between one City of Berkeley 
landlord and one or more of such landlord’s competitors, including through a third-party 
vendor. A “coordinated pricing algorithm” includes a product that incorporates a 
coordinated pricing algorithm, but does not include (a) a product or process that 
generates or presents any report, study, or presentation that publishes rental data in an 
aggregated and anonymous manner but does not recommend rent prices, fees, or 
occupancy rates or other rental contract terms for future leases; (b) a product used for 
the purpose of establishing rent or income limits in accordance with the affordable 
housing guidelines of a local government, the state, the federal government, or other 
political subdivision; or (c) a product or process that provides or uses, or the provision or 
use of, information for the purpose of (i) conducting market research for project financing, 
(ii) conducting an appraisal, or (iii) conducting research, testing, or training for software 
development. For clarity, “research, testing, or training for software development” 
includes without limitation the use or processing of Competitor Data in the development, 
training, or testing of predictive or machine learning models so long as any such data is 
not used as an input in the operation of the model at the time a recommendation is 
calculated for publication or provision to a City of Berkeley landlord.
B. “Competitor Data” means information that is not available to the general public 
concerning actual rent prices, occupancy rates, lease start and end dates, and similar 
data regarding a property other than a property that is owned or managed by the landlord 
who is the recipient or user of the generated recommendation, when such data is less 
than 90 days old.

rules.requirement: A foreclosing agency or new owner may make a written good-faith monetary offer to vacate without good cause, but acceptance is voluntary. The new owner must supply the separate NOTICE TO TENANTS with initial and final written or oral offers. Pressure through misrepresentation, claimed obligation or consequences, harassment, withheld utilities or maintenance, or unlawful or unconscionable rent increases is prohibited.

 However, it is important to note that the accepta nce of a bona fide monetary offer is 
voluntary.  The tenant shall not be pressured by anyone, including the person making the offer to 
accept any offer to vacate the property.  Pursuant to the New Jersey Foreclosure Fairness Act 
(N.J.S.A. 2A:50-69 et seq.), pressure tactics include but are not limited to (N.J.S.A. 2A:50-71(b)):

2. Implying the tenant is obligated to accept the offer;

4. Harassment, including but not limited to discontinuance of utilities, failure to maintain 
common areas or fa cilities, or any other failure to maintain the premises in a habitable 
condition; and 
5. An increase in rent in excess of any rent control or rent leveling ordinance, or if the property 
is not subject to rent control, an unreasonable or unconscionable rent increase.

rules.requirement: Pay security-deposit interest at the end of each year and a prorated amount when a tenant moves out before year-end.
rules.key_value: Annual interest; prorated on earlier move-out
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance. Additional source-reviewed applicability: Within Berkeley, full coverage generally includes most multifamily units built before 1980; single-family homes with current pre-1996 tenancies; and single-family rooming houses with >=5 individually leased rooms. Partial coverage includes construction AND certificate of occupancy after June 1980, single-family tenancies beginning >=1996-01-01, and most condominiums. Qualifiers most and overlap issues require verified legal resolution rather than automatic classification. Both fully and partially covered Berkeley units receive just-cause and security-deposit-interest protections; do not exclude a unit merely because its rent amount is not controlled.
rules.exemptions: Units outside full or partial ordinance coverage are not included in the stated requirement. rules.title: Public-housing lease breach involving illegal activity
rules.requirement: Substantial breach of a public-housing lease covenant concerning illegal controlled substances or other illegal activities can support eviction if the covenant conformed to federal guidelines and was effective at the start of the lease. No Notice to Cease is required; Notice to Quit must follow federal public-housing regulations.
rules.key_value: No Notice to Cease; federal Notice to Quit rules
rules.coverage_conditions: Public housing; qualifying lease provision effective at lease commencement.
rules.exemptions: The guide notes that household-member or guest drug activity may support eviction even without the tenant's knowledge.
rules.quoted_span:
In public housing, if the tenant has substantially violated or breached any of the 
covenants or agreements contained in the lease, pertaining to illegal uses of controlled 
dangerous substances, or other illegal activities, the landlord may file a suit for eviction.
rules.interaction:
State eviction ground expressly incorporates federal public-housing requirements.
r-0451 overrides r-0058 within the recorded coverage; see the relationship evidence.
limitations: The applicable federal notice text is not reproduced.
related_citations: Dept. of Housing and Urban Development v. Rucker, 122 S.Ct. 1230 (2002)

evidence.quote:
In public housing, if the tenant has substantially violated or breached any of the 
covenants or agreements contained in the lease, pertaining to illegal uses of controlled 
dangerous substances, or other illegal activities, the landlord may file a suit for eviction.

The covenant or agreement must conform to federal guidelines and must have been in effect 
at the beginning of the lease term.

The landlord does not have to give Notice to Cease the 
illegal activity before filing a Notice to Quit. A Notice to Quit must be served on the tenant 
in accordance with federal regulations pertaining to public housing

A public housing authority may evict a tenant when a member of the tenant’s 
household or guest engages in drug -related activity, even if the tenant did not know of

rules.title: Documentation for repair or cleaning performed by the landlord or employee
rules.requirement: When the landlord or an employee performs repair or cleaning charged against security, the itemized statement must reasonably describe the work and state the time spent and reasonable hourly rate charged. rules.title: Deposit does not cap recovery for intentional or malicious property damage
rules.requirement: Section 15B does not limit the landlord to the deposit when a tenant willfully or maliciously destroys or damages the landlord's real or personal property and repair or replacement cost exceeds the deposit.
rules.coverage_conditions: A residential tenant's willful or malicious property damage with repair or replacement cost exceeding the security deposit.
rules.exemptions: Section 15B does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy, or tenancy of 100 days or less where the lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose; both the duration and purpose conditions are required.
rules.interaction: The preservation clause does not enlarge ordinary deposit deductions for wear, preexisting damage, or unsupported repairs.
rules.temporal_notes: Query date: 2026-10-01. The supplied statutory text is treated as the source version for that date. The document does not separately state this provision's original effective date; the August 1, 2025 version notes expressly date only the introductory paragraph of subsection (1)(b).
limitations: This preserves a right to recover beyond the deposit; it does not itself establish every element or amount of an underlying damages claim.

Section 15B. (1) (a) No lease relating to residential real property shall contain a provision that a lessor may, except to inspect the premises, to make repairs thereto or to show the same to a prospective tenant, purchaser, mortgagee or its agents, enter the premises before the termination date of such lease.  A lessor may, however, enter such premises:
(9) The provisions of this section shall not apply to any lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of one hundred days or less in duration which lease or rental is for a vacation or recreational purpose.

(e) A security deposit shall continue to be the property of the tenant making such deposit, shall not be commingled with the assets of the lessor, and shall not be subject to the claims of any creditor of the lessor or of the lessor's successor in interest, including a foreclosing mortgagee or trustee in bankruptcy;  provided, however, that the tenant shall be entitled to only such interest as is provided for in subsection (3)(b).
(2)(a) Any lessor or his agent who receives, at or prior to the commencement of a tenancy, rent in advance for the last month of the tenancy from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give to such tenant or prospective tenant at the time of such advance payment a receipt indicating the amount of such rent, the date on which it was received, its intended application as rent for the last month of the tenancy, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom the rent is received, and a description of the rented or leased premises, and a statement indicating that the tenant is entitled to interest on said rent payment at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held payable in accordance with the provisions of this clause, and a statement indicating that the tenant should provide the lessor with a forwarding address at the termination of the tenancy indicating where such interest may be given or sent.
Any lessor or his agent who receives said rent in advance for the last month of tenancy shall, beginning with the first day of tenancy, pay interest at the rate of five per cent per year or other such lesser amount of interest as has been received from the bank where the deposit has been held.  Such interest shall be paid over to the tenant each year as provided in this clause;  provided, however, that in the event that the tenancy is terminated before the anniversary date of such tenancy, the tenant shall receive all accrued interest within thirty days of such termination.  Interest shall not accrue for the last month for which rent was paid in advance.  At the end of each year of tenancy, such lessor shall give or send to the tenant from whom rent in advance was collected a statement which shall indicate the amount payable by such lessor to the tenant.  The lessor shall at the same time give or send to such tenant the interest which is due or shall notify the tenant that he may deduct the interest from the next rental payment of such tenant.  If, after thirty days from the end of each year of the tenancy, the tenant has not received said interest due or said notice to deduct the interest from the next rental payment, the tenant may deduct from his next rent payment the interest due.
If the lessor fails to pay any interest to which the tenant is then entitled within thirty days after the termination of the tenancy, the tenant upon proof of the same in an action against the lessor shall be awarded damages in an amount equal to three times the amount of interest to which the tenant is entitled, together with court costs and reasonable attorneys fees.
(b) Any lessor or his agent who receives a security deposit from a tenant or prospective tenant shall give said tenant or prospective tenant at the time of receiving such security deposit a receipt indicating the amount of such security deposit, the name of the person receiving it and, in the case of an agent, the name of the lessor for whom such security deposit is received, the date on which it is received, and a description of the premises leased or rented.  Said receipt shall be signed by the person receiving the security deposit.

(iii) a reasonable amount necessary to repair any damage caused to the dwelling unit by the tenant or any person under the tenant's control or on the premises with the tenant's consent, reasonable wear and tear excluded.  In the case of such damage, the lessor shall provide to the tenant within such thirty days an itemized list of damages, sworn to by the lessor or his agent under pains and penalties of perjury, itemizing in precise detail the nature of the damage and of the repairs necessary to correct such damage, and written evidence, such as estimates, bills, invoices or receipts, indicating the actual or estimated cost thereof.  No amount shall be deducted from the security deposit for any damage to the dwelling unit which was listed in the separate written statement of the present condition of the premises which was required to be given to the tenant prior to the execution of the lease or creation of the tenancy pursuant to clause (c) of subsection (2) or any damages listed in any separate list submitted by the tenant and signed by the lessor or his agent pursuant to said clause (c), unless the lessor subsequently repaired or caused to be repaired said damage and can prove that the renewed damage was unrelated to the prior damage and was caused by the tenant or by any person under the tenant's control or on the premises with the tenant's consent.  Nothing in this section shall limit the right of a landlord to recover from a tenant, who wilfully or maliciously destroys or damages the real or personal property of said landlord, to the forfeiture of a security deposit, when the cost of repairing or replacing such property exceeds the amount of such security deposit.
